Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."

Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Could the man who murdered a Christian missionary and his sons walk free in India?
- Published
Warning: This article contains details of violent death that some readers may find distressing
One of India's most shocking incidents of anti-Christian violence is back in the news more than a quarter of a century after it drew condemnation from around the world.
The Supreme Court is hearing a petition seeking release from prison by a man who is convicted of killing Australian Christian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons in 1999.
Dara Singh - whose real name is Rabindra Kumar Pal - has been in jail since his arrest in 2000, serving a life sentence for burning alive the Australian missionary and his six and 10-year-old sons in a village in the eastern state of Odisha (formerly Orissa).
Staines had spent 30 years working with leprosy patients, but Singh and his associates from Hindu hardline groups had accused him of forcibly converting poor Hindus from disadvantaged castes and tribals to Christianity.
The viciousness of the crime sent shockwaves through India's minority Christian community and caused global outrage. Now reports that Singh may be set free have brought alive memories of the heinous crime.
Staines lived in Baripada in Mayurbhanj district, where he worked among the local tribal community.
On the night of their murder on 22 January 1999, Staines and his sons had attended a Christian gathering in Manoharpur, a remote village in the neighbouring district of Keonjhar. They were sleeping in their jeep when a mob of 60 to 70 people led by Singh surrounded their vehicle, set fire to it and prevented them from escaping.
As Singh went on the run after the crime, police put up posters all over the state, offering an 800,000-rupee (approximately $18,000 then) reward for information leading to his capture. Reports at the time said he was helped by villagers and tribals who eulogised him as "a modern-day Tarzan who plays with elephants and rides tigers". He was arrested a year later during an overnight raid on a jungle hideout.
In a sensational interview, external with the India Today magazine's Ruben Banerjee from prison a few months later, he denied killing Staines and his children but said he "did not like Graham Staines" and had "spearheaded the movement against missionaries".
"Missionaries have been targeting our religion. They have been converting Hindus by deceit and inducements. Our religion is under siege. As a true Hindu, it was my responsibility to oppose them," he said. "Since I was possibly the most famous name in the region, the police implicated me in the killings."
Singh added that he was "prepared to be a martyr for the cause of Hindus" but believed that he would never get convicted.
His optimism was misplaced - in 2003, a trial court sentenced Singh to death and 12 others to life imprisonment. Two years later, the high court commuted his death sentence. It confirmed the life term of his accomplice Mahendra Hembram but freed 11 others, saying there was not enough evidence to support their convictions.
In January 2011, the Supreme Court upheld Singh's life sentence, refusing the prosecutors' plea to reinstate the death penalty.
The Staines murder was not the only crime Singh was guilty of. In 2007, he was convicted for two other heinous crimes he committed against religious minorities in 1999 - the same year he murdered the Australian missionary and his children.
He received life sentences, external for leading a mob that set fire to a church and killed Catholic priest Arul Das with an arrow as he tried to flee the burning building and, in the second instance, for beating and burning to death a Muslim garment trader Shaikh Rahaman.
Police had registered 10 cases accusing Singh of involvement in hijacking trucks of Muslim traders transporting cows - an animal many Hindus consider sacred - and setting them free. In his interview, Singh denied being "involved personally", saying "my supporters might have done it". But he admitted that he was "actively involved in the movement against illegal trade in cows and cowslaughter" which "had to be stopped at any cost".
Church leaders had alleged the attacks were carried out at the behest of hardline Hindu organisation Bajrang Dal but Singh denied he was a member and an enquiry commission, led by retired top court judge DP Wadhwa, later ruled that he had worked alone.
Graham Staines' widow, Gladys, who stayed on in India with her daughter Esther until July 2004, said she had "forgiven" Dara Singh in the Christian spirit. "Forgiveness opens up the path of healing," she said.
In July 2024, Singh filed a plea for remission in the top court, saying he was entitled to be released because he had spent more than 25 years in prison. He said his conduct had been good in jail and expressed remorse for his actions.
The 62-year-old blamed the crime on "the fervour of youth" in his petition, external seeking early release.
"The petitioner acknowledges and deeply regrets the transgressions committed more than two decades ago.
"In the fervour of youth, fuelled by impassioned reactions to the brutal history of India, the petitioner's psyche momentarily lost restraint and it is imperative for the court to scrutinise not merely the actions but the underlying intent, noting that there was no personal animosity harboured towards any victim," he wrote.
Last year, the top court asked the state government to take a call on his plea, but the authorities have so far not told the court what they intend to do.
At the last hearing on 19 August, authorities told the court that the Sentence Review Board (SRB), which is examining Singh's plea, was waiting for some more paperwork and sought an adjournment.
The two-judge bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi expressed their annoyance at the several adjournments the state had sought in the case and said if the SRB failed to decide Singh's plea by 2 September, the court would. "You take a decision, whichever way you want. If you do not take a decision, then we will."
On Wednesday, though, the court did not hear the case. The date for the next hearing is yet to be announced.
Reports that Singh may walk free if the state government or the court accept his remission petition have led to some disquiet in India's 30-million Christian community - some of it because of unease over his earlier statements.
In his 2000 India Today interview, he said he had "no regrets" and "will never regret" killing Staines' children. "When Hindus die, others don't cry. Why should we weep when others die? Whatever has happened is right. Whatever will happen will also be right."
If released from prison, he said, he would "go back to what I have been doing - oppose cow slaughter and conversions".
"The government must stop them. If they are not stopped, more people might get killed. Anything can happen," he added.
In an article on the Union of Catholic News (UCN) website, human rights and Christian political activist John Dayal wrote recently that remission after decades in jail is "not unusual" in India and "the principle behind it - that punishment should allow for reform and eventual return to society - is humane".
But the anxiety among religious minorities in Odisha "is not abstract given the state's history of anti-Christian violence", Dayal points out, citing the Kandhamal riots of 2008, in which dozens were killed and tens of thousands were displaced.
"The Staines murders were not an ordinary homicide but a public, theatrical act of terror, intended to be seen and understood as a warning. The killings of Father Arul Doss and Sheikh Rehman extended that same message," he writes.
"What remains to be seen is not whether Singh will eventually walk free, but how the government conducts itself around that decision...and whether minority communities are given any reassurance," Dayal adds.

Prashanth Fertility launched ‘Prashanth Fertility at Home’, an initiative to provide select IVF-related support services at patients’ homes across Chennai.
The service is aimed at helping patients maintain continuity during fertility treatment, particularly those who may find it difficult to make frequent visits to the fertility centre because of work and other commitments.
Under the initiative, a dedicated team will provide services such as injection administration, eligible monitoring, follow-ups and treatment coordination at home, while patients continue to remain under the supervision of their treating fertility specialists.
A dedicated vehicle and team will operate across Chennai. Patients can schedule eligible services through the Prashanth Fertility app, which also allows them to manage appointments, follow-ups and treatment-related medical records.
Speaking at the launch, actor Khushbu Sundar, the chief guest, highlighted the stigma and emotional challenges associated with infertility and fertility treatment. She said couples often have to navigate not only the physical and financial demands of treatment, but also social expectations and questions around parenthood.
Samhitha Moturi, Director, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said fertility treatment involves multiple appointments, medication schedules, monitoring and follow-ups, and repeated travel to a fertility centre can be an additional challenge for couples. “The initiative has been conceived to take appropriate, clinically supervised aspects of care closer to the patient,” she said, adding that reducing practical barriers could help patients stay on track with treatment.
Geetha Haripriya, Chairman, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said the initiative was intended to make fertility care “more accessible, more personalised, and more connected to the patient”.
The service is currently available across Chennai. Patients can contact the 24x7 helpline 044-2888-2888 for details about eligibility and scheduling.

Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
- Published
Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction.
A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive.
A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box.
It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades.
For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states.
But the 2015 federal election was a seismic shock.
The PDP lost the presidential vote to Muhammadu Buhari and the newly formed All Progressives Congress (APC) - a coalition of opposition parties and disgruntled former members.
Thrust into the political wilderness the party's national leaders were bewildered - familiar with the trappings of federal power they had to work out what to do in opposition.
This was the beginning of the end, according to political analyst Ishaq Buhari.
"They were a party that was so used to power, being in opposition was a new challenge they struggled with from the start," he told the BBC.
If 2015 was a major blow, 2025 was the year the party's foundations were left in ruins.
It was marked by a dizzying wave of defections and bitter internal conflicts.
A group of state governors switched party allegiance, which had a particularly devastating effect.
At the start of that year, the PDP still held eight states. But by December, five state governors - from Delta, Akwa Ibom, Enugu, Bayelsa and Rivers - had gone over to the ruling APC.
They cited the PDP's declining viability and a desire for better co-operation with the federal government as reasons for their departure.
Early this year, the PDP held three states but that is now down to zero - with the Oyo governorship slipping from the party's hands just last month.
Internal power struggles, factionalism, insistence that power rotates through the regions and disciplinary measures have all added to the sense of disillusionment within the party.
The PDP has been robbed of high-profile figures and talent, including the loss of former Vice-President Atiku Aubakar last year.
The crisis was intensified by a debilitating leadership tussle.
In November 2025, a faction of the party, which observers say represented the majority of members, held a contentious national convention in Ibadan, Oyo state, despite court orders attempting to stop it.
The convention expelled Nyesom Wike, a prominent PDP member who is serving in President Bola Tinubu's APC-led government.
Wike, who helped found the party, heads a rival faction creating a political stand-off that has paralysed the PDP.
He had controversially helped the APC win Rivers state in the last presidential election leading to accusations that he had betrayed the PDP.
But in the eyes of the law the faction that he heads is the legitimate party.
This means that it has been able to submit its slate of presidential and parliamentary candidates to the electoral commission leaving the rival faction without any representatives on the ballot.
Despite the chaos, some die-hard loyalists remain optimistic.
Politician and staunch PDP member Aminu Adamu, part of the anti-Wike faction, believes a return to its former glory is possible.
He cites examples from Thailand and Argentina, where parties have bounced back after years in the wilderness.
"We have seen it happen before," he tells the BBC. "All we need to do is put our house in order and start to build from there.
"If we make all the necessary corrections, by 2032 I really think PDP can be a major force again."
Others point out that the party still has a grassroots network - essential to win and sustain power - with offices, activists, supporters and local leaders. But by 2032 it may be too late.
With the party in such disarray and candidates backed by Wike on the ballot - voters are unlikely to trust them.
Analyst Deji Olarenwaju believes the only thing that could save the once-mighty party is an alliance with the African Democratic Congress - now seen as the biggest opposition group or Peter Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
"Because on their own they are going nowhere," he says.

Every morning, many of us drink one or two cups of coffee and feel good, refreshed, and ready for the day. Some of us drink one or two more cups at work before lunchtime. Some use pure coffee while others add chicory to it. We prepare the powder using a filter, add milk and sugar, and take a swig.
While many Indians have a fondness for coffee, almost everyone in the U.S. and Europe drinks coffee, and more of it, every day.
Now, what are the effects of drinking coffee? How many cups per day? Should it be black coffee or can it include milk and sugar? And how does this affect our health? These are some questions that have been on our minds — and for which research has offered contradictory answers in the past. Fortunately, a new publication, titled ‘Caffeine and Cardiovascular Disease: A Scientific Statement from the American Heart Association’, may clear some doubts. The authors of the statement analysed several studies that examined the effects of caffeine, the active molecule in coffee that stimulates the brain and the central nervous system and encourages the body to produce and use more energy.
The statement reported that moderate caffeine intake, especially through coffee, may lower the risks of type-2 diabetes, stroke, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation. However, high doses, especially from energy drinks, may harm cardiovascular health, and unfiltered coffee can also raise LDL cholesterol levels.
Data from the Nurses Health Study at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Harvard Medical School and an analysis of 3 lakh people from the U.K. Biobank and Health Canada have indicated that drinking four cups a day may lower the risk of developing cancer, type-2 diabetes, heart diseases, and age-related disorders like dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. However, analyses also suggest that it would be prudent for pregnant and lactating women to limit their coffee intake to three cups a day.
Drinking hot black coffee is recommended, with little or no additives like sugar or milk. However, a group from Copenhagen, Denmark, pointed out in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Science in 2023 that adding milk to black coffee can be good as milk contains antioxidants, minerals, and vitamins and allays the bitter taste.
Chicory-blended coffee
Many people in South India prefer to have pure coffee, i.e. with no additives like chicory, which comes from a perennial herbal plant with coloured flowers. This herb contains no caffeine but a polysaccharide called inulin, which supports digestion and can help control blood sugar.
The benefits of a coffee and chicory blend and their implications for nutrition and health implications were discussed in a recent review paper by a group led by Pushpa S. Murthy at the Central Food Technology and Research Institute, Mysuru, published in the Journal of Food Science and Technology. Chicory contains several compounds that help protect the liver from inflammation, shield the stomach from damage, and may help defend against cancer. Adding chicory to coffee also improves coffee’s fragrance and taste.
The optimal blend of coffee and chicory was suggested to be 70:30 or 60:40, coffee to chicory, to strike a balance between taste and benefits. In fact, most coffee sellers across India have these ratios, unless of course a customer asks for ‘pure’ coffee. This writer himself used to prefer pure coffee until he read the review article by the Mysuru group!

World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
- Published
A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minster announced.
Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father.
The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US.
Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.
Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch, external, ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.
Announcing his death, Tooro's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki called his passing on Thursday an "immeasurable loss" to the royal family and the people of Tooro.
"I call upon all the people of Tooro to remain united, calm and prayerful during this profoundly difficult time," Akiiki said on Friday. "May His Majesty the King rest in eternal peace."
The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.
Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured".
"His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained.
When he became king in 1995 a regency, which included the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation.
The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness.
The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda.
Similarly, the Rwenzururu Kingdom also extended its condolences to "all those mourning this great loss", according to local media reports.
Others have also paid their respects to the late king.
The Federation of Uganda Football Associations, honoured King Oyo as a "true friend of the beautiful game", and announced a moment of silence before the kick-off of all matches until 4 September in memory of his "legacy, love, passion and contribution" to the sport.
Government minister Margaret Muhanga described the mood in the kingdom as "sombre... you can't see anyone smiling".
The king was "at the prime of his life", she said in a video shared on social media, "as young as he was, he had an impact on his kingdom".
Muhanga said they would be planting a million trees in his honour during the mourning period, and wants to ask the neighbouring districts in Tooro to do the same.
Uganadan musician Juliana Kanyomozi called it a "very dark day for Tooro", in an Instagram post. "Gone too soon. What a loss!!!!"
Meanwhile, pop star-turned-politician Bobi Wine, called for King Oyo's "soul to rest in eternal peace".

The Federal Trade Commission and 22 states sued Amazon yesterday, alleging that it has conducted a secret scheme to overcharge advertisers for seven years.
“Since 2019, Amazon.com, Inc. has secretly and systematically overcharged its approximately 1.2 million advertising customers by manipulating the ‘auctions’ that it uses to set the price of ads on its platform,” the lawsuit said. “Amazon represents, and advertisers believe, that competitive auctions set the prices for advertising on its leading e-commerce website. But, in reality, Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits.”
The FTC said it obtained internal documents and messages that reveal how Amazon secretly inflated auction prices for Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, and Sponsored Display advertisements that appear alongside results seen by consumers when they search for a product. The FTC investigation began in 2024.
“Based on numerous internal documents describing its ‘hidden’ ‘surcharges,’ Amazon’s scheme has likely illegally extracted over $20 billion from its unwitting advertising customers,” according to the lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Western District of Washington.
The FTC lawsuit was joined by a bipartisan group of 22 state attorneys general from Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Vermont, and Washington.
The lawsuit said Amazon has conducted “billions of rigged auctions,” imposing “hidden surcharges on advertisers almost every time a shopper clicks on an advertisement on the Amazon website. Amazon’s deception continues to this day” and deprives customers “of the benefits of competition and fair and transparent dealing,” the FTC said.

ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 22 జూలై 2026 నుంచే ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోలో ప్రియాంక గాంధీ, రాహుల్ గాంధీ భుజానికి నల్ల పట్టీ కట్టడం చూడవచ్చు. ఈ వీడియోని వివిధ మీడియా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కూడా ప్రసారం చేశాయి.
మీడియా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, 22 జూలై 2026న ఢిల్లీలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ ప్రెస్ మీట్కు ముందు ప్రియాంక గాంధీ ఆయనకు నల్ల పట్టీ కట్టారు. 21 జూలై 2026న ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనలో విద్యార్థులపై జరిగిన దాడిని ఖండిస్తూ, వారికి సంఘీభావంగా ఆయన నల్ల పట్టీ కట్టుకున్నారు. దీన్ని బట్టి, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో 28 ఆగస్టు 2026 నాటి రక్షా బంధన్కు సంబంధించినది కాదని స్పష్టమవుతోంది. అలాగే, రాహుల్ గాంధీ, ప్రియాంక గాంధీ సోషల్ మీడియా వేదికగా రక్షా బంధన్ శుభాకాంక్షలు తెలిపారు.
చివరిగా, రాహుల్ గాంధీ భుజంపై ప్రియాంక గాంధీ రాఖీ కట్టారంటూ వైరల్ అవుతున్న వీడియో రక్షా బంధన్కు సంబంధించినది కాదు.

India's GDP growth defies oil shock but stirs up controversy
- Published
"Doomsayers were doomed and India bloomed… Yet again," wrote Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on X, external, reacting to smart first quarter GDP data that came out earlier this week, widely beating forecasts, but also sparking a major controversy over its credibility.
On the face of it, the 7.8% number was a shot in the arm for the prime minister who's recently faced scathing student anger over his government's handling of exam paper leaks and rising youth unemployment.
While those longstanding concerns have not gone anywhere, the better-than-expected growth print suggests that his government may have deftly weathered the Middle East oil shock despite heavy dependencies on imported crude.
According to Sajjid Chinoy, chief India economist at JP Morgan, India's "cyclical growth recovery" had been visible for the past six months, driven by a huge fiscal stimulus, including direct tax cuts in February last year, a reduction of consumption taxes in September and interest rates which have come off by about 1.5% since early 2025.
"But the question was, could India insulate that recovery from events in the Middle East, and this is where the government deserves enormous credit," Mr Chinoy told India Today, external news channel, adding that the urgency with which Delhi diversified its energy imports in the face of the Hormuz blockade helped the country protect its growth.
What also helped Asia's third largest economy power ahead amid the disruption in global energy markets was a strong acceleration in exports and a surge in private corporate investments, which has long been a point of great concern for economists.
Exports grew by a sharp 12% despite tariff uncertainties on the back of strong global demand and a weak exchange rate. Economists reckon a 15% slump in the Indian rupee against the US dollar may have helped companies improve their competitiveness, driving up demand for Indian goods.
Corporate India, meanwhile, seems to be finally putting money into new buildings and factories. India's gross fixed capital formation, which serves as a core indicator of total domestic public and private investment rose, nearly 12% in the first three months of this year.
"Non-government data also points to the fact that investment intentions of companies have gone up in recent months, with announcements especially concentrated in industries like data centres, renewable energy and metals," Madan Sabnavis, chief economist with the state-run Bank of Baroda, told the BBC.
"Of course, private investment is not broad-based yet, but these are definitely signs of a pick up."
While the robust numbers pushed several private brokerages to revise their full year growth forecasts upwards, they also stirred up a roaring debate online and a war of words between politicians.
Opposition leaders like Jairam Ramesh , externalcalled the numbers "statistical gymnastics", accusing the government of repeatedly tweaking methodology to conceal what he said was "India's dire economic reality".
A former finance secretary also raised serious doubts, saying the GDP got a pop because it was calculated on the basis of newly revised numbers and a lower base for the same period last year - a view the government strongly rebuffed, external, saying revisions are a part and parcel of GDP calculations.
The government's view was supported by the World Bank's executive director for the country, Neelkanth Mishra, who said the new GDP series "cleaned up the data and also significantly improved the methodology", enhancing the credibility of the estimates.
But beyond the statistical minutiae, others like the former central bank governor Raghuram Rajan questioned why if the growth indeed was so rapid was India not creating more jobs or attracting more foreign direct investment.
To make matters worse, the stock markets also largely shrugged off the positive news.
The debate has muddied the picture for authorities who will have hoped the numbers would help them counter growing criticism about the uneven nature of India's growth trajectory.
There are also other more mundane reasons why it might be too early to celebrate a growth bump.
For starters, government spending is expected to ease off in the coming months as the compulsions to meet deficit targets get stronger. The impact of the goods and services tax cuts on spurring consumption is also soon likely to peter out, according to HSBC.
Moreover a sub-par monsoon and El Niño-like weather conditions have taken a toll on India's agrarian rural economy, which supports livelihoods for half of the country. As of 27 August, cumulative rainfall stood at 13% below the long-period average.
This will pose "clear risks to agriculture, rural demand and food inflation [even though] India appears better prepared than in past episodes", CareEdge, a rating agency, said in a note.
Sugar and onion prices have already spiked across the country, forcing the government to run special trains to cities to meet demand. India's retail inflation, meanwhile, hit a 15-month high of 3.9% in May and further rises are expected, with some economists predicting the rate will hit the upper band of the central bank's comfort level amid a weak monsoon.
Given the high-growth and high-inflation scenario, most brokerages are pencilling in a hike in borrowing costs. This, coupled with expectations of lower global growth (and hence lower demand for Indian exports), higher costs of inputs and energy because of volatile geopolitics could all mean this growth bonanza - credible or not - may well be nearing its peak.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar speaks during joint press conference with Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha in Kyiv, Ukraine.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Thursday said the Russia-Ukraine conflict cannot be resolved through measures targeting oil purchases, stressing that the war will ultimately have to be settled through dialogue, diplomacy and negotiations.Jaishankar made the remarks in Kyiv while responding to a question on whether India would consider reducing its purchases of Russian oil if the United States approves sanctions against countries buying Russian oil.
‘Conflict will not be solved by buying or not buying oil’
“This conflict, which is today in its fifth year, will not be solved because somebody is buying or not buying oil or alumina or minerals or metals or fertiliser,” Jaishankar said.“This conflict will be solved by dialogue, diplomacy, and negotiation. That is why, it is something we would encourage,” he added.His remarks came amid discussions over possible US sanctions targeting countries that continue to purchase Russian oil. India has maintained that its energy purchases are guided by national interests and the need to ensure affordable and secure energy supplies.
India-Ukraine trade sees resilience despite war
On India-Ukraine trade relations, Jaishankar said bilateral trade spans several sectors, including pharmaceuticals, food and agriculture, fertilisers, machinery, chemicals and consumer goods.
“Understandably, in the last four years, this trade has seen some disruption due to the war situation and logistical challenges,” he said.
At the same time, Jaishankar said there had been “visible resilience” in trade ties, with some new possibilities emerging.
“In our talks today, we will be challenged obviously by the issues of today as well as the prospects beyond, and we will be addressing them,” he said.Jaishankar also highlighted education as a longstanding area of India-Ukraine cooperation, noting that many Indian students are currently studying in Ukraine.“I take this opportunity, through you, Minister, to thank the authorities for taking care of them,” he said.Jaishankar’s remarks came during his visit to Ukraine, where discussions included bilateral ties, trade and cooperation, alongside the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict.

It's true that Talarico voted nay on the bill in question, SB 17, even though he had previously voted in favor of continuing to amend its language. The final version of SB 17 included amendments that its opponents said would broaden it beyond its intended scope. A spokesperson for Talarico said he voted nay on the final version to prevent giving the governor more power. The bill ultimately passed and became law in September 2025.
Rumors that Texas state Rep. James Talarico voted against a bill that would prevent the Chinese Communist Party from buying land in the state circulated on the internet in early September 2026 as Talarico, a Democrat, campaigned for a U.S. Senate seat.
People on social media claimed Talarico voted against a bill called SB 17, some accusing him of rejecting "the basic responsibility to protect the state's soil and food system."
(X user @EricLDaugh)
Supporters of Talarico's Republican opponent in the November 2026 election, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, unleashed a campaign ad amplifying the claim.
It's true that Talarico voted against SB 17, a bill aimed at preventing foreign interests from purchasing land in Texas. However, as Talarico and others pointed out, the bill had been amended such that it was likely to have effects beyond the scope of its original intent.
The legislation was initially aimed to prohibit real estate deals involving Texas land by countries identified by U.S. intelligence officials as national security threats: primarily China, Iran, North Korea and Russia.
The bill eventually passed by the Texas House in May 2025 was amended so that the governor, rather than federal intelligence officials, could ultimately "determine the countries whose residents, governments and other entities could be banned from buying property here," according to reporting by The Texas Tribune.
In the Texas House Journal from May 8, 2025, which also recorded Talarico's nay vote, a fellow critic, Democratic Rep. Mihaela Plesa, explained, "While the intent to safeguard critical infrastructure and land interests is valid, CSSB17, as amended, became too broad and open-ended. The bill now permits the governor and state agencies to unilaterally add entire countries to its prohibitive list, restricting land ownership by nationals of those countries without requiring future legislative approval or public oversight."
A spokesperson for Talarico told Snopes via email that Talarico voted nay on SB 17 to avoid giving the governor increased power. Talarico's team elaborated:
James doesn't support the Chinese Communist Party owning Texas land and his record reflects that, including by voting to stop countries like China from purchasing land near critical infrastructure like military bases. Ken Paxton is spreading lies about bills that sought to ban American citizens from buying land in this country — undermining our neighbors' God-given rights — in an effort to distract from his career of corruption. Paxton is the only candidate in this race that has cozied up to the Chinese Communist Party, going on a lavish all-expenses-paid trip to China and meeting with CCP officials while he was supposed to be serving us. There's a reason Republicans call him "Commie Ken."
The bill ultimately passed and was signed into law in September 2025.
The record also showed Talarico had voted yea previously on one of the amendments of the bill aimed at protecting U.S. visa holders, but ultimately voted nay on the final bill.
SB 667 and other related votes
Legislators voted on a different bill, SB 667, aimed at "prohibiting state entities from investing in Chinese-affiliated entities" as a means of funding state-funded pension plans on May 28, 2025. According to the Texas House Journal transcript of that meeting, Talarico had an excused absence that day and did not vote on the final version of the bill, which ultimately passed.
Talarico's votes on other bills with potential impact on Texans' dealings with foreign entities included:
- Yea on SB 1349, which was part of the legislative package that included SB 17, described as "creating the criminal offenses of transnational repression and unauthorized enforcement of foreign law." (The House Journal shows Talarico as first voting nay, with a correction that it was meant to be recorded as yea.)
- Yea on SB 2116, which was aimed at "business or governmental entities from entering into contracts or other agreements relating to state critical infrastructure with certain foreign-owned companies."
- Yea on HB 130, aimed at preventing the "use of biotechnology by foreign adversary countries as a component of military power and commercial advantage.
The "Commie Ken" reference in the statement from Talarico's team referenced to a 2023 report that alleged Paxton went on a "lavish" trip to China to meet with government officials, reportedly against the advice of his staff.
Paxton's opponent in the 2026 Texas Republican primary, incumbent four-term Sen. John Cornyn, called out Paxton's trip during his campaign and even built a website called CrookedKen.com that also labeled him "Commie Ken" and described him as "cozying up to the CCP."
For further reading, we've investigated other claims about Talarico, including that he once said he "hated" Christianity and that U.S. President Donald Trump once called him an "insult to Jesus."

Summer off England duty took me by surprise - Itoje
- Published
England captain Maro Itoje says he was initially shocked when head coach Steve Borthwick raised the possibility of him taking the summer off.
Itoje missed England's matches against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina in July, holidaying in Mauritius and Nigeria as he took a first proper summer break from professional rugby in more than a decade.
The 31-year-old, whose mother died in the weeks before he led England through a deflating Six Nations campaign that featured just one win, says he is now feeling the benefits of his time away.
"I spoke to Steve Borthwick two weeks after the Six Nations and at the end of a long conversation he mentioned we would have to think about what to do in the summer," Itoje told Rugby Union Weekly.
"I was taken aback a bit - it wasn't something that was in my mind.
"At the end of the season it is just the done thing to go on tour.
"But once I had digested it and had thought about it, the more I thought about it, the more I thought it was the best thing for me.
"I'm not annoyed by it at all. It was a wise and prudent decision, it has given me the best opportunity to perform well over the next period of time."
Itoje made his England debut in 2016 and has won 102 caps, as well as touring three times with the British and Irish Lions.
He played more than 30 matches in each of the 2023-24 and 2024-25 campaigns, breaching the recommended limit of 2,400 match minutes in the former and narrowly avoiding doing so in the latter.
"I would argue that the mental recovery was far more significant than physically," he said.
"I feel like I'm in a good physical condition, but mentally it was a heavy, busy year, both personally and professionally. So, it was nice to have just a bit of time to take a breath."
Itoje bumped into the England squad at Heathrow Airport as their return from a defeat by the Springboks in Johannesburg coincided with his own from Nigeria.
"I was on the shuttle train back to baggage reclaim and looked to my right and there was [Saracens and England team-mate] Jamie George, I looked to my left and there was Steve Borthwick, and they both looked at me in disbelief," he added.
Apart from that coincidence, Itoje kept his distance from the England set-up over the summer, sending the squad the odd good luck message, but opting against watching their games live.
"It was difficult to do, but when you're supposed to take a break, then if you're living and breathing every moment of a game..." he said.
"I watched them back in retrospect [knowing the final score], partly because I wanted to remove some of the emotion from watching it.
"That's the beauty of live sport - when you watch a game, you're in every nook and cranny, every tackle.
"But that also probably has a hidden emotional weight. The whole purpose of the rest was to get back on the even keel, so that was my methodology."
Itoje's rest precedes another busy period in his life.
Saracens' Prem season begins away to Leicester on 27 September before England take on Australia, Japan, New Zealand and a final's weekend play-off opponent in November's conclusion to the Nations Championship.
And the start of the Rugby World Cup in Australia is a little over a year away.
Meanwhile, his wife Mimi is expecting the couple's first child - a boy - imminently.
"I am very excited," Itoje added
"I want a minimum of three children, I don't really have a maximum.
"My cousin's grandfather must have 60 kids, but that isn't a route I am going down!"

The goat is now a celebrity - how this graduation gift went viral
- Published
When Promise Okoro walked out of his final degree exams earlier this month, he fully expected the usual end-of-term celebrations.
His cheering friends were already outside blasting music and snapping and filming this much-loved Nigerian "signing-out" ritual.
Their white shirts filled up with messages scribbled by classmates and well-wishers – a colourful record of a shared journey through education.
But then, through the crowd, came Promise's mother, Chinyere, pulling a goat.
It turned an already joyful afternoon into a moment Promise and his friends would not soon forget.
The 23-year-old pharmaceutical technology student initially thought the screams meant someone was about to propose marriage.
Instead, he found his friends gathered around his mother, who was making her way towards him, gently coaxing the farm animal behind her.
"I was so happy," he told BBC Pidgin. "I felt so emotional."
He says he was not embarrassed at all. Instead, his classmates cheered.
The moment was captured on video and quickly spread online, drawing thousands of warm reactions.
For some people outside south-east Nigeria, a goat might seem like an unusual gift to mark the end of university. But among the Igbo people, the animals can carry deep cultural meaning.
They are valuable gifts, often given to show respect, appreciation and goodwill and are associated with important occasions such as traditional weddings, family celebrations and ceremonies honouring elders or special guests.
Promise has not yet hit on a fitting name for his prized possession.
Some have questioned what the graduand now plans to do with the animal - but he tells the BBC it is very much his companion so he would never eat it.
"It's now my pet, it's too precious to me, I have no intention of killing it."
In fact, the plan is to get a female goat and start breeding the pair.
Until then, Promise's goat will continue enjoying special status at the student halls where he roams freely and even has some human-like habits.
"I have noticed it loves fried rice a lot! The way he eats up my fried rice leftovers - very voracious," laughs Promise.
Now something of a local hero, the goat accompanied Promise to a nearby supermarket where fans clambered to take photos of the animal.
"It got on a car ride with me from my hostel to the mall... it was calm [even though] it's now a celebrity - more popular than me.
"I also take it around my street for some evening walks".
Promise gained not just a new friend but also high praise from his mother Chinyere - this gift was her way of saying "I am proud of you" and she wanted everybody to know.
She had travelled, goat in tow, for more than an hour from Ubaha-Eze, the small farming community where the family lives, to surprise her son at the Federal Polytechnic Nekede in Imo state.
Chinyere had once dreamed of buying her son something very different – a shiny new vehicle.
"I did not have money for a 4matic Jeep - I love that car - so I said let me buy this little gift," she said.
The 4Matic is a Mercedes-Benz SUV – a car she said was beyond what she could afford.
Chinyere is a trader who sells consumer goods, including food, drinks and local snacks.
Business has been difficult but even with the financial pressures she was determined to keep her promise to her son.
When he got into university she had said he would be rewarded if he stayed away from violent gangs and other bad influences and not to drop out. Promise had done exactly that.
And now his mother wanted to stick to the pledge. She bought the goat for 120,000 naira ($88; £66).
"People love my son, I want[ed] to prove that he is [loved]," she said
"As I walked in and met loud celebrating and shouting, it gladdened my heart knowing that my son will rejoice together with us all when he comes out," she said.
For Promise, the relationship with his mother goes far beyond the celebrations.
"My mom is very cool," he said. "There is nothing I can hide from her and whenever she is confused about something, she always calls me to ask of my opinion or idea."
As a student of pharmaceutical technology Promise said he has always wanted to help sick people in Nigeria.
He knows that many health professionals have left the country in search of better opportunities abroad, while those who remain often work in difficult conditions.
But he wants to stay and contribute to improving Nigeria's strained health system.
Even as he waits for his final results, he believes he performed well. "If there is a list of the top 50, I will say that I am one of them."
Nigeria's tertiary education completion rate is 11.3 out of every 100 people. That is slightly higher than the average of 10.5 out of 100 across sub-Saharan Africa, but below the 17.6 out of 100 average for lower middle-income countries.
For Promise, completing his studies is therefore not simply another line on a certificate.
It is a milestone his mother has been waiting to celebrate. And now, he says, it is his turn.
"The way she has shocked me, I will make sure I reciprocate."
Whatever surprise Promise eventually finds for his mother, it may be difficult to match the one she gave him: a brown goat, brought from their village with love and determination – a simple gift that has united thousands of people who have watched the moment unfold online.

If you've been shopping for an Amazon Kindle or smart speaker in the past week, you might've noticed some brand-new prices. That’s right: Amazon has hiked prices by $20 to $100 on its popular devices like the Echo, Eero, and Fire Stick.
It's not alone in this move. We've seen similar increases from other tech companies like Apple and Kobo, both of which raised prices this summer. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED as to why it made these price hikes, but one Amazon spokesperson commented to CNET that it was due to rising prices in memory and storage components.
It's still hard not to feel like companies are raising prices simply because they can—and as a way to make upcoming Prime Day and Black Friday sales look better than they really are. The new prices spread across all of Amazon's hardware categories, hitting its Kindle e-readers, Echo smart speakers, Eero routers, and Fire TV devices—especially the more affordable and popular products in those categories.
In fact, many devices are already “on sale,” but the sale prices are around what used to be the base price. That means discounts will look good this holiday season, but you'll just be paying what the item used to cost a couple of months ago.
Here are all of the price changes on Amazon's devices, and my run-down on which devices remain a good buy.
New Kindle Prices
If you're looking for a Kindle, all of these models have faced a price increase of at least $30, if not more.
- Amazon Kindle (2024, 11th Gen): $150 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen): $200 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature (2024, 12th Gen): $250 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft: $290 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature: $320 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Kids (2024, 2nd Gen): $180 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Kids: $300 (up $30)
The only category untouched is, interestingly enough, the more powerful of Amazon's e-reader and digital notebook devices: the Kindle Scribe line. All of the Kindle Scribe models currently available (both the second and third gen, and the color version) have remained the same price-wise. You'd think those would have risen too since the price hikes are supposedly due to storage and memory costs, but it's Amazon's e-reader-only devices that all increased in price instead.
New Echo Prices
Many Amazon Echo speakers also raised in price, going up by anywhere from $10 to $100. The larger price increases are for the Echo Show devices, which come with a screen.
- Echo Dot (5th Gen): $80 (up $30)
- Echo Spot (2nd Gen): $110 (up $30)
- Echo Dot Max: $120 (up $20)
- Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen): $100 (up $10)
- Echo Show 8 (4th Gen): $200 (up $20)
- Echo Show 11: $250 (up $30)
- Echo Show 15: $350 (up $50)
- Echo Show 21: $500 (up $100)
Interestingly enough, Amazon already has many of these speakers “on sale” for around their old sticker price; the Echo Dot is a “deal” for $55 right now when it was $50 as recently as August 20, and the Echo Dot Max is “on sale” for $95 after costing $100 on August 20 as well. These current prices are likely Labor Day sales, and might be the same pricing we see come fall sale events, too.
But not all Echo devices went up in price. The fairly new second-gen Echo Studio still has the same $220 price tag it did when it launched, and is also on sale already for Labor Day (catch it for $195 right now). You'll also find the older Echo Show 8 that I like stuck to its $150 price point. And even if some did go up in price, some are having better deals than others—the Echo Show 11 is currently on sale for $190, a fine discount on its old price and a good one on its new $250 price tag.
New Eero Prices
Amazon owns the Eero mesh router system, and there was a price increase in that category as well. It only hit the Eero 7 and Eero Pro 7, but unfortunately, we think those are the best models.
- Amazon Eero 7: $400 (up $50)
- Amazon Eero 7 Pro: $800 (up $100)
You can still get the Eero 6 on a budget, since that one has stayed the same in price, but there are plenty of other mesh Wi-Fi routers we prefer over Eero if you don't want to deal with the price hike.
New Fire TV Prices
I wouldn't call Fire TV my favorite streaming setup (and neither would our reviewers), but if you're an Amazon Prime lover, maybe you feel differently. Amazon's Fire TV sticks had a couple of increases. While only a couple of products were affected, it did hit our favored models.
- Fire TV Stick 4K Max: $85 (up $25)
- Fire TV Stick HD: $40 (up $5)
Fire TV is still one of the cheapest systems around, but it wasn't the one we'd recommend before the increases, and I doubt you'll see it rank any higher with these new prices in mind. Still, the deals might be worth shopping; the Fire TV Stick HD is already on sale for Labor Day for just $18, while the 4K Max is on sale for less than its old sticker price (but only by $10).
What’s Still Worth It?
Not everything is still worth buying with these prices in mind. Here are the devices I'd still shop. For the rest, I'd wait for a sale event or look to another brand to get a similar product.

The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.
Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.
Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.
The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.
As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.
Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.
The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.
In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.
Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.
In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”
In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.
The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.
The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with the UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.
Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of about 20,000 rand for six years.
“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”
The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father, Samson, was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.
Mathinye did not initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”
Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but could not afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.
Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.
Sharpeville’s problems did not begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.
“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

Formula One’s governing body declared a heat hazard for this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix at Monza, the second time this season that it has taken such a step.
Race Director Rui Marques said in a statement temperatures in excess of 31 degrees Celsius (88 degrees Fahrenheit) had been forecast.
The Austrian Grand Prix in June was the last time a heat hazard was declared.
Declaring a heat hazard requires teams to fit a driver cooling system, such as a liquid-cooled vest, though drivers are not obliged to use them and can take a ballast penalty instead. The car’s minimum weight is increased to accommodate the hardware.
Sunday’s race is the 13th round of the championship, with 20-year-old Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli at the top of the standings for his home race.

Just 4 of 28 lifts at Queen Mary Hospital block set for service once repairs done
Architectural Services Department says remaining lifts had suffered frequent operational instability and requires urgent follow‑up
Only four of the 28 lifts at Queen Mary Hospital’s new clinical block will operate normally following minor repairs, while work must be carried out on the rest until the end of the year, according to Hong Kong’s architectural authorities.
The Architectural Services Department said on Thursday only four lifts serving non‑clinical facilities at the HK$13.5 billion (US$1.72 billion) block were in acceptable condition and would undergo minor repairs later.
The remaining lifts had suffered frequent operational instability and required urgent follow‑up, it added.
The department expected work to be completed in the fourth quarter of this year.
The block, part of the Pok Fu Lam hospital’s first‑phase redevelopment, was mostly completed last year and began opening in phases last November.
Clinical services have yet to move in, as repeated lift faults – including sudden drops that trapped staff – have kept most of the elevators out of service.
Authorities said last month that the defects emerged during final testing, with installation and performance failing to meet contract standards.
