On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods hit parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction (here, here, and here). Against this background, a video showing several houses being swept away by floodwaters is being shared on social media, claiming that the visuals are from the floods in Nepal’s Rasuwa area (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing the floods in Nepal’s Rasuwa area.
Fact: These visuals are not from Nepal’s Rasuwa area. They show the flooding in NEEPCO Colony in Posa, Kei Panyor district, Arunachal Pradesh, on 24 June 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
We conducted a reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video and found a longer version posted by an X account on 24 June 2026, with the caption stating that the video showed the flash floods and devastation caused by them in the NEEPCO Colony in Posa, Kei Panyor district, Arunachal Pradesh, on 24 June 2026.
Based on this, we performed a relevant keyword search and found videos of the flooding in the NEEPCO Colony posted by several social media accounts in Arunachal Pradesh on 24 June 2026 (here, here). These posts featured scenes matching those seen in the viral video.
Further, we found several media reports covering the incident from Arunachal Pradesh on 24 June 2026, which also featured the same visuals seen in the viral video (here, here, here).
To sum up, old flood visuals from Arunachal Pradesh’s Kei Panyor district were shared as recent visuals from Nepal’s Rasuwa area.

Wrexham complete signings of Ekomie and Kabore
- Published
Wrexham have completed the signings of Issa Kabore from Manchester City and Jacques Ekomie from Angers.
Burkina Faso international Kabore featured 32 times across all competitions during a loan spell with Wrexham in 2025-26 and has now signed a three-year deal with the club.
"I'm very happy to be back. It feels good to be here again," said right wing-back Kabore.
"Everybody knows our ambition is to get to the Premier League, and I'm here to fight for that promotion."
The deal for Kabore is worth up to £4.75m - with City having a 20% sell-on clause and matching rights.
Left-back Ekomie was in the final year of his deal with Angers and reportedly attracted interest from Wrexham's Championship rivals West Ham United and German side Hamburg.
On signing for Wrexham, Ekomie - who has put pen to paper on a four-year contract - said: "I'm excited to be here. It is a very big and interesting project for me - I'm here to progress, and I'm very happy to be here.
"I want to achieve great things at Wrexham. I think it's an ambitious project and I want to bring all my experience to help the team achieve our goals."
The Red Dragons recruited Liberato Cacace from Italian side Empoli during the 2025 summer transfer window, but the New Zealand international has been plagued by injuries since moving to north Wales.
Ekomie - signed for an undisclosed fee - will bolster Phil Parkinson's left-sided options, with the Gabon international joining right wing-backs Kabore and Danny Imray, goalkeeper Anthony Patterson and midfielder Ben Whiteman in moving to the Racecourse Ground this summer.
Kabore made a dream start to life with Wrexham last season as he registered a pair of assists on his debut to help the Welsh side earn a 3-2 win over Norwich City at Carrow Road.
His eight assists in the Championship were more than any other Wrexham player.
He was a mainstay under Parkinson before sustaining a hamstring injury while on international duty during the November break.
Kabore made his long-awaited return to action for Burkina Faso in the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations before again featuring prominently for Wrexham in the second half of the season.
The 55-cap international moved to Man City from Mechelen in 2020 before immediately returning to the Belgian club on loan.
He went on to have loan stints with Troyes, Marseille, Luton Town, Benfica and Werder Bremen prior to joining Wrexham on transfer deadline day in September last year.
He leaves Man City having failed to make a senior appearance for the club.
On Kabore's return, manager Parkinson said: "We're delighted to welcome Issa back to the football club.
"He had a successful loan spell with us last year, and we're looking forward to working with him again and watching him really develop as a player this coming season."

Ekomie started his professional career with Bordeaux but secured a switch to top-flight side Angers in the summer of 2024.
He made 21 appearances across all competitions in his debut season for the club, and his impact increased last term.
The 23-year-old featured in all but two of his side's Ligue 1 matches in 2025-26 - with 25 of his 32 league appearances being starts.
On Ekomie's signing, manager Parkinson said: "We're very pleased to sign Jacques. It's a transfer we worked very hard on.
"Jacques is a good young player and we're looking forward to integrating him into the group."
Ahead of his side's 1-1 draw with Watford, Wrexham manager Parkinson stated deals for various players to join the Red Dragons had fallen through in what had been a "difficult window".
But speaking in his post-match press conference after the Championship contest with the Hornets, the boss said there were "no guarantees" that Wrexham would further bolster their squad prior to the 23:00 BST transfer deadline on 1 September.
Midfielder George Thomason has operated as a makeshift wing-back in the absence of Cacace - who started just eight of Wrexham's 46 league games last season.
Cacace has missed all three of the Red Dragons' matches across all competitions so far this season and still has two years left to run on his contract at the Racecourse Ground.
Wrexham could yet add to their midfield and forward options in the final stages of the summer window.
Parkinson's men return to action against Birmingham City at the Racecourse Ground on Friday night (20:00 BST).

The EPA classified trifludimoxazin as having "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential," which essentially means that while there is evidence the chemical could potentially be one that causes cancer, there isn't enough data to say for sure. Additionally, the EPA does not consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS, though the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development does.
In late summer 2026, some people on social media claimed that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration approved the use of a potentially carcinogenic pesticide that's a "forever chemical," also known as PFAS. PFAS, an abbreviation for perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are long-lasting chemicals that persistently remain in the environment, capable of accumulating in things like rivers, plants, animals and people's bodies, that often have harmful health effects on people, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claimed that the EPA "just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin," to be used on crops including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples and tree nuts such as almonds. According to the post, environmental groups consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS pesticide and "forever chemical." 
The U.S. EPA just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin for agricultural use on a wide range of crops, including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples, and tree nuts such as almonds.
Trifludimoxazin is also considered by many environmental groups to be a PFAS pesticide because it contains highly fluorinated chemical structures and can break down into persistent fluorinated compounds - i.e. nature can't break it down properly as it's synthetic. Environmental organizations have described it as a "forever chemical" and have filed lawsuits challenging the EPA's approval.
Environmental groups have also pointed out that the company's own studies showed evidence suggesting cancer concerns and that the EPA downplayed those findings whe not was approved. The EPA claims the product is safe and that people shouldn't be concerned. Not a good look for MAHA.
Similar Facebook (archived) posts (archived) shared the same claims, which were also spread on X (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent us emails asking if the rumor is true.
The Trump administration's EPA proposed approving trifludimoxazin in June 2025 and went through with the approval in June 2026. Researchers have found some evidence suggesting the chemical may be carcinogenic, but it's not a "known carcinogen" like some posts claim. Trifludimoxazin is a PFAS as defined by the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, although not as defined by the more narrow EPA definition.
Trifludimoxazin is a pesticide, specifically an herbicide, that kills certain broad-leafed plants and grass weed species at agricultural sites farming "row crops (e.g., cereal grains, legumes, soybean) and tree orchards and groves (citrus, pome fruits, and tree nuts)," according to the EPA (PDF Page 6).
This wasn't the first time the EPA has tried to approve trifludimoxazin. In 2021, while Joe Biden was president, the EPA approved pesticide products containing trifludimoxazin, however; this approval was halted by lawsuits filed by environmental groups. The EPA then changed rules to require further EPA assessments before approving a new pesticide, and, ultimately, the makers of trifludimoxazin dropped their request for approval at the time.
The same environmental groups are attempting to halt the new approval for trifludimoxazin through lawsuits, as they did previously.
Potential carcinogen
The EPA did find evidence suggesting trifludimoxazin could possibly be carcinogenic, although it did not do enough research to confirm with certainty whether the chemical is carcinogenic.
In one study of rat carcinogenicity through chronic dietary exposure (PDF Page 8), the EPA found "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential." According to the EPA, such a classification means that the data raises a concern that the chemical has "potential carcinogenic effects in humans," but the EPA has determined the data is "not sufficient for a stronger conclusion."
Trifludimoxazin's entry on the pesticides properties database maintained by the U.K.-based University of Hertfordshire says that the chemical is "known not to cause a problem" as a carcinogen. The entry does report that trifludimoxazin is a potential liver toxicant, though. The database also notes "no serious health implications have been identified" with trifludimoxazin.
So while trifludimoxazin could potentially be a carcinogen, there currently isn't enough evidence to say with certainty that the chemical causes cancer.
Forever chemical
There are at least three definitions of PFAS, according to a 2022 paper in the peer-reviewed journal Digital Discovery: a broader definition from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development that is widely used internationally, a narrower definition used by the EPA and a definition that is a compromise between the two other definitions.
The University of Hertfordshire's database also classifies trifludimoxazin as a PFAS.
Where else has it been approved?
According to the University of Hertfordshire's database, trifludimoxazin has not been approved for use in the United Kingdom or the European Union as a whole. However, each individual state within the European Union has approved the pesticide for use in their individual countries. It has also been approved for use in Canada.
For further reading, Snopes has previously fact-checked claims about potentially toxic chemicals, including a claim about the use of paraquat by the parent company of the pomegranate juice brand Pom Wonderful.

India has been named the host of the inaugural Women’s Champions Trophy, ICC announced on Wednesday.
The Brabourne Stadium in Mumbai and the Vadodara International Cricket Stadium will host the T20 tournament, from February 14 to 28.
Missing from the host roster is the D.Y. Patil Stadium in Navi Mumbai, a popular women’s cricket venue in the country, and even one that the players of the national side have deemed the spiritual home of the women’s game in India.
The D.Y. Patil, a privately-owned venue within the D.Y. Patil University campus, was also the venue of India’s famous triumph in the Women’s ODI World Cup in 2025, where India beat South Africa in a high-octane and well-attended final. It is also a popular host in the Women’s Premier League, India’s top flight women’s franchise tournament.
ALSO READ | From Motibaug to Kotambi: Vadodara’s cricket passion finds a new home
D.Y. Patil earns NGT ire
During the conduct of the Indian Premier League’s 2026 edition, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) issued notices to six mainstream cricket stadiums and their respective associations raising concerns about sustainable use of water to maintain grounds and facilities.
The NGT bench comprised of chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava and expert members A Senthil Vel and Afroz Ahmad who passed the order on April 16, directing cricket associations to regular groundwater extraction and put in place rainwater harvesting for maintaining pitches. Even installations of sewage treatment plants were taken into consideration at venues where rainwater harvesting might not entirely be feasible for operations as a primary way.
The six stadiums in the firing line were Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi, Sawai Mansingh Stadium in Jaipur, Shaheed Veer Narayan Singh International Stadium in Raipur, Dr. DY Patil stadium in Navi Mumbai, Bharat Ratna Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee Ekana Cricket Stadium in Lucknow, Rajiv Gandhi International Stadium in Hyderabad and Barabati Stadium in Cuttack.
“In such a background, the submission of counsel for the applicant is that all the activities in these six stadiums should be completely stopped and they should not be allowed to carry out any sports activity therein,” the NGT noted in its order.
The tribunal had also questioned why sporting activities shouldn’t be stopped for failing to furnish disclosures to the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA).
It is unclear if this is why the venue has dropped off the radar for the prestigious Champions Trophy, but the stadium faces the question of receiving clearance for further sporting activity to happen at the premises.
Neither the ICC nor the BCCI has addressed reporters explaining the choice of venues or why D.Y. Patil Stadium has failed to make the cut.
The BCCI’s rotation policy for venues, which seeks to give more venues a chance to host marquee games, might have worked in favour of the Brabourne Stadium in Churchgate. This is also frequently used to stage WPL games across its four editions. CCI president Madhumati Lele Shrivastava was a member or the WPL Governing Council as well.
The Vadodara International Cricket Stadium, inaugurated in December 2024, has also found favour as a venue for women’s cricket fixtures in India from bilaterals to the WPL. Indian Olympic Association CEO Raghuram Iyer had even hinted at the city, 100km away from 2030 Commonwealth Games host city Ahmedabad, being considered to stage the cricket events of that edition.

Lando Norris reveals other 'opportunities' before signing new McLaren contract ahead of Italian Grand Prix
Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle caught up with Lando Norris to discuss his new McLaren contract and the title race in an interview that will air this weekend; watch Friday's practice sessions for the Italian GP at 11.30am and 3pm, live on Sky Sports F1
Wednesday 2 September 2026 19:54, UK
Lando Norris has revealed he had other opportunities before signing a new contract to stay at McLaren until at least the end of 2030.
Norris, who has won the last two Formula 1 races, has been with McLaren since making his F1 debut in 2019 and says the contract was "probably the easiest contract I've had to sign".
The 26-year-old admitted though, in a wide-ranging interview with Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle which will air at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix, that there were other options.
"There was opportunity of course. But opportunity that is positive. There's opportunities to gamble at times," he said.
"I'm a driver that personally I would take one or two tougher years over instant success - as I did a few years ago with McLaren.
"As much as I want to win every single year, not everything is about I need to be with a team tomorrow that's going to win the next race and do this and do that."
Norris pointed to the "strong" group of people at McLaren, led by team bosses Zak Brown and Andrea Stella, as a key reason to stay at the Woking-based outfit.
He added: "A good amount of it is also am I just happy? I was happy to be with McLaren even when we weren't winning because I'm still in an amazing opportunity and I still get to do the job I love and travel and do all these things. So not everything to me is about ultimate performance. A lot of it and a big part of it is the people that I'm with.
"Just the fact I feel I'm at home and I'm enjoying it. And that almost has enough control as saying 'I need to be with a team that is going to be performing and winning championships'."
Would Norris ever join Ferrari?
Norris is currently in great form after claiming pole position and the win at the last two Grands Prix in Hungary and the Netherlands to cut his deficit to championship leader Kimi Antonelli to 83 points.
He has another good opportunity this Sunday as Antonelli will start at the back of the field due to grid penalties for exceeding his engine allocation.
But, McLaren will still have the challenge of beating George Russell plus Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, who both have upgraded engines.
Hamilton and Leclerc will have huge support from the Tifosi at Monza, which features the most iconic podium as it overlooks the main straight and thousands of fans post-race.
Brundle pointed out Hamilton had previously stated he would stay at Mercedes before achieving his "dream" of joining Ferrari and asked if Norris would ever consider joining the Scuderia in the future.
The McLaren driver said: "That's not something I want to think about for now. Since I was a kid, you always think of yourself in different positions.
"My dream was always to be with McLaren. That's why I feel like I'm in a very fortunate position as I am. But you always want to experience the other side of things, whether that is Ferrari or other teams and Mercedes.
"It's just human. I think that you want to experience what it's like to be in this position and that position.
"Also, the history of other teams. The fact Lewis also went to Mercedes from McLaren and then to Ferrari, I think it's also pretty cool that you try different things and you experience different stuff.
"It depends a little bit on what you want to achieve in your career. Do you want ultimate success every single year? Do you want to just experience what it's like to go to a different team and experience Ferrari or Mercedes?
"For now, I'll say I'm not thinking of it. But ask me again at the end of 2030."

Trump Meant It Literally When He Said He Was Taking the Oil
The Venezuela operation is the purest distillation of his amoral foreign policy.
“We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Donald Trump said when he announced the capture of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro in January. And lo and behold, it has come to pass.
Trump announced last week that he had made a deal with Venezuela to develop its oil reserves. Well, not so much a “deal” as a payment by Venezuela of tribute at gunpoint. In a social-media post, Trump announced that the oil “is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.” This is a surprisingly generous offer from a country that is much poorer than the United States and, like most countries, disinclined to hand over its wealth to foreigners as a present.
Venezuela’s elected representatives did not approve this deal, because Venezuela’s representatives have not in fact been elected. The country also did not hold a referendum to approve it. Instead, after capturing Maduro, whom Trump had accurately denounced as a dictator, Trump installed one of Maduro’s cronies, Delcy Rodríguez, to govern in his place, in which capacity she has displayed roughly the same level of respect for democratic norms and civil society as her predecessor.
Trump’s Venezuelan-oil heist has received far less attention than either his ballyhooed promise to avoid foreign wars or his ongoing quagmire in the Persian Gulf. Yet this operation reflects Trump’s foreign-policy instincts in their most nakedly amoral—which is to say, quintessential—form.
The Trump administration laid the groundwork for its intervention by painting Maduro not only as a despot but also as the leader of a criminal syndicate. The Justice Department indicted Maduro and his allies for having “acted as leaders and managers of the Cartel de Los Soles,” a derisive nickname for the country’s kleptocratic rulers.
Trump, however, apparently viewed regime change as a way to exploit this arrangement rather than transform it. His invasion followed the logic not of an American president promoting democracy or regional security, but of a mobster angry to discover that a small-time crook is running a racket in his territory without giving him a taste.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, The New York Times reported in July, “has become the de facto viceroy of Venezuela, holding sway over a sovereign nation in a way that no American official has since L. Paul Bremer III arrived in Baghdad in 2003 to run U.S.-occupied Iraq.” A salient difference is that Bremer’s occupation was intended to establish the grounds for free and fair elections, which did eventually take place. Trump, in stark contrast, casually told the Times in January that he expects the United States to run Venezuela for years.
The new oil deal makes that outcome more necessary and therefore more likely. Rodríguez has tied herself to a policy that is toxic to both the left and the right sides of Venezuela’s political spectrum. Left-wing Chavismos despise foreign exploitation, and the opposition resents the Chavismos’ corruption. Exposing Rodríguez’s regime to free and fair elections creates a high risk of electing a government dedicated to unwinding Trump’s deal, which gives both her and Trump a strong motive to postpone such voting.
When Trump deposed Maduro, some right-of-center analysts credited him with taking the first step in what they imagined would be a democratization project. The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board celebrated the capture as “an act of hemispheric hygiene against a dictator who spread mayhem far and wide,” as did The Washington Post’s (headline: “Justice in Venezuela.”)
Both editorials mixed praise for the operation with caveats that the important work of transitioning to a legitimate government lay ahead, while fretting that Trump was confusing the issue with loose talk about running the country and extracting its oil. “The president often shoots from his hip in these press conferences and would be wise to reconsider,” the Post proposed. “Mr. Trump also talked about ‘the oil’ far too much,” the Journal cautioned, adding, “Sooner rather than later, Venezuela needs another election.”
It all sounded a bit like congratulating Michael Corleone for taking a stand against organized crime by murdering the heads of the Five Families, while urging him to clarify his intent to focus the family business on selling olive oil at market price.
Venezuela’s constitution expressly prohibits the sale of its untapped oil reserves to foreign interests. But Trump’s oil deal is designed to survive democratic scrutiny. Its “structure was deliberately intended to bind future Venezuelan governments to the agreement and make it difficult to unwind,” as The Wall Street Journal characterized the explanation given by a source involved in the deal. The Journal’s reporting suggests that Trump’s Venezuelan partners may not hold the highest regard for legal niceties. Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan businessman who leads the private company partnering with the Trump administration, has been investigated for, though not charged with, money laundering. Diego Arria, a former Venezuelan ambassador now in exile in the U.S., told the Journal that the U.S. is working with Venezuelan government figures who are wanted in the U.S. for drug trafficking and other crimes.
They are, in other words, Trump’s kind of partners. The president seems to despise democratically elected leaders (witness his current tantrum against Canada’s prime minister, or his yearslong feuding with South Korea, the European Union, and other erstwhile U.S. allies). He has always gotten along swimmingly with criminals (since his early days engaging in social and business dealings with mobsters in New York) and dictators (such as Vladimir Putin, whom he simply cannot quit). Trump’s favorite brand of partner combines disdain for the law and democratic norms with an absolute dependence on Trump.
Trump has been saying for years that a vital objective in any foreign conflict is to seize the enemy’s oil. Indeed, he has been saying for years that he has been saying this for years. “I’ve been saying it for years. Take the oil,” he told The New York Times in 2016.
Trump has shown time and again that his obsessions, even his most childish and comically sinister-sounding ones, are often quite earnest. In Venezuela, he is finally fulfilling a lifelong scheme.

China’s grey-zone game: Why India must prepare for ‘armed coexistence’

India-China ties have thawed since the border skirmish in 2020.
Former foreign secretary Vijay Gokhale argues that China waits for a strategic opening, acts pre-emptively and then builds a narrative of self-defence.His new book, “China’s Wars: The Politics and Diplomacy Behind its Military Coercion”, examines past conflicts and China’s recent grey-zone tactics.In an interview with Indrajeet Rai, Gokhale explains why the India-China relationship has entered an era of “armed coexistence”, why a full-scale war is not the most likely outcome but cannot be ruled out, and how political uncertainty after Xi Jinping could produce global economic shocks or military adventurism. Edited excerpts:You describe China as an opportunistic power. What does that mean, and when does Beijing decide to act pre-emptively?By opportunistic power, I did not intend to suggest that China is very different from other major powers. In the case studies in my book, China waited for the international situation to turn favourable, or for some advantage to accrue from its relations with other major powers, before carrying out conflict with a neighbour or another country. It used opportunity strategically to achieve its goals.The Chinese idea of preventive deterrence or preventive conflict differs from the Western concept. In the West, deterrence is a counteraction intended to stop the adversary from escalating. In the Chinese context, it is pre-emptive: China acts even before the adversary has had the chance to act first. The aim is to deliver a political and psychological shock so the adversary desists or fears retaliation.The 1962 conflict is one example. There was no indication that India intended to launch a military assault. But China used the words of then PM Jawaharlal Nehru and an international situation dominated by the Cuban missile crisis to act pre-emptively against India.
China often depicts its own aggressive action as defensive and blames the other side. How central is this narrative warfare to its strategy?The Chinese Communist Party utilised China’s difficult circumstances after the collapse of the empire and projected itself as the only organisation capable of pulling the country out of its problems. It placed the blame for China’s declining economy and global influence on external circumstances. It played the victim’s card: China was perennially the victim, and the party was the instrument that would restore it as a major power.
China’s grey-zone strategy seeks to steadily pressure and exhaust rivals while avoiding the escalation of tensions into full-scale war.
The blame, therefore, was always placed on somebody else: The colonial powers, the United States in the Korean War, India in the 1962 war and the Soviet Union in the 1969 conflict. There was never an acknowledgement that some responsibility also fell on China.This is not limited to foreign policy. The party does not take responsibility for major domestic failures either: The Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution or the 1989 Tiananmen incident. Blame falls on an external force or a few bad elements, never the party itself.You argue that China is pursuing sustained grey-zone coercion. How does this work against India?Since 1979, China has not fought a real conflict. The leadership made economic development the priority, and successive leaders after Mao Zedong focused on reform and opening up.But China was not willing to give up the use of force; it changed the manner in which force was used. Instead of hot wars or major conflict, it engaged and continues to engage in very low-intensity military conflict, popularly known as grey-zone warfare.Grey-zone warfare uses threats or actual force while staying below the threshold that might tempt the rival to launch a counteroffensive. It punishes or deters, but stops short of making the rival feel compelled to push back with force. We see it along the Line of Actual Control, in the South China Sea and in the East China Sea.I have characterised the situation on the LAC after 2020 as the end of peaceful coexistence and the beginning of armed coexistence. Armed coexistence does not mean conflict. It means China will continue to take grey-zone military action around the LAC to keep us tied down and to exhaust us not only financially - because keeping forces and equipment at those heights costs a lot - but also in terms of men and material.This fulfils a key Chinese objective: Keeping India confined to South Asia.
Apart from the United States, there are few potential rivals in this century, and India is one. If you look at India, it's geographical location, its population size, its territorial size, its talent, it's economic potential. All of it lends a credence to the belief that India can become a major power in this century. And clearly, China would like to delay that possibility.Does that mean a large-scale India-China war is unlikely in the foreseeable future?Nobody can predict this definitively. China and its decision-making processes are opaque, and there are no alternative channels of information such as free media or civil society.China is a mature state focused on becoming the strongest economy and power in the world. On a rational cost-benefit analysis, the price of a major war with India could exceed the benefits. Logically, China would be reluctant to engage in such a conflict.At the end of the day, however, it is impossible to predict. We have to be prepared for the worst, while logically understanding that a hot conflict with India may not be in China’s interest in the foreseeable future.China’s capabilities against Taiwan have grown, while the US is distracted by several conflicts. Could Xi Jinping move on Taiwan to secure his legacy?An American commander of the Indo-Pacific Command, Admiral Philip Davidson, suggested that by 2027 China would have the military capability to launch an assault on Taiwan. Some interpreted that to mean China would attack by 2027, but he did not actually say this.China’s capabilities for an assault on an island have substantially increased: Landing craft, area-denial capabilities, communication systems and anti-ship missiles.It is one thing for a major power to bomb another country and destroy its infrastructure, and quite another to occupy or conquer it. That requires a very large commitment of forces and material, with no assured guarantee of victory.China’s demographic decline is already causing anxiety. An assault would mean mass casualties because boots on the ground would be required. After Galwan, India acknowledged within days that 20 soldiers had been martyred; China took much longer to admit fatalities. With Taiwan potentially producing casualties in the hundreds or thousands, Beijing will worry about the domestic impact.This is where democracy, for all its weaknesses, becomes a strength. A democratic government has electoral and constitutional legitimacy to act, including in war. In China, the party claims it has popular support but has never tested that proposition. The reaction to large-scale war casualties is unpredictable.Xi has removed the age and term limits that helped institutionalise succession. What happens after him and why should India worry?Deng Xiaoping introduced two reforms that stabilised succession: Those above 68 could not continue in top party positions, and the president was limited to two five-year terms. This helped ensure smooth transitions from Jiang Zemin to Hu Jintao and then to Xi Jinping.Xi has abolished the age and term limits. In an authoritarian system, no leader will voluntarily give up power because enemies may find it easier to target him, and he cannot be certain a successor will not misuse authority against him.China could enter a period of political uncertainty and potentially turmoil as Xi ages and factions emerge in a contest for power. It is unclear whether this happens before or after his death, or whether he intends to stand for a fourth term.Because China is the world’s second-largest economy, domestic turmoil would affect its economy, military and diplomacy and create huge ripple effects abroad. Beleaguered regimes also sometimes use an external threat to divert attention. India must consider whether turmoil could produce military adventurism and how to preserve its national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity.China has few formal allies and did little visibly to support Iran. Does it lack the partnerships needed to become a global leader?China lacks the United States’ large network of treaty allies. But we should not underestimate the goodwill it enjoys. The Belt and Road Initiative has been welcomed as an alternative route to development. Western assistance often came with harsh conditions; China offers fewer and less onerous strings. Nobody gives aid for free, but China has built substantial diplomatic influence.There was little need for China to do more in the Iran war. It could neither persuade the United States to stop nor force peace. It protected its oil interests and relations with Iran and the Gulf countries without entering the mediation game.
When the conflict ends, Iran will rebuild using its oil and gas wealth. It is unlikely to trust the West, while China can build infrastructure at a scale few others can match. China needs energy; Iran needs infrastructure and money. That creates an enormous downstream economic opportunity and a win-win situation. Why would China get significantly involved now when there seems to be no clear way out of the conflict?As US-China rivalry intensifies, which side of the emerging world order should India prefer?India should not look at the world order through an either-or lens. The United States and China will both remain major powers. The question is how, in a triangular or quadrangular relationship, including the European Union if it acts as a union, we create an international framework relevant to this century.
India has objective advantages: Its location, demographics and consumer base; tested political stability; an independent military capability and growing defence industry; and talent.I do not see how India can fail to become a major power in this century. The international order is disintegrating and all states are hedging their bets; India is doing so too. The task is not to choose a US-led or China-led order. It is to help build an order in which India is one of the leaders.
Indrajeet Rai is the editor for TOI Online. He holds a PhD in International Politics from JNU. He has experience in both research and the social sector. He enjoys the fast-paced world of “breaking news”—as well as the equally important work of breaking down news for readers.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Nvidia to buy Hugging Face for US$13 billion in big bet on open AI models
Nvidia will buy popular developer platform Hugging Face for US$12.93 billion, betting that support for open AI models will drive future demand even as its biggest customers develop their own chips to reduce reliance on the semiconductor giant.
Shares of the company were up 1.5 per cent after the deal was announced on Thursday (Sep 3), which ranks among its biggest.
The deal will cement Nvidia as a central player in the market for open models that users can freely download, run and customise, unlike the closed systems built by OpenAI and Anthropic.
Nvidia has already played an active role in backing the open AI industry with its widely used Nemotron model.
Acquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to collaborate, test and share tools using various open AI models, potentially providing valuable insight and data to help it narrow the technology gap with top US and Chinese labs.
Demand for open-weight models has surged from businesses baulking at the steep bill of deploying the technology, with Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Z.ai emerging as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks, including generating computer code at a lower cost.
That surge has fueled fears that some American firms could become reliant on Beijing's models as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future.
"Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said, adding that his company's chips would not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face.
Under the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9 billion to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention programme of up to US$1 billion for employees who join Nvidia.
The two companies already work together to help developers use Nvidia's computing services on the platform.
BALANCE SHEET STRENGTH
Hugging Face was valued at US$4.5 billion in its last disclosed funding round in August 2023, when it raised US$235 million from investors such as Salesforce, AMD and Amazon.
Nvidia, meanwhile, exited its July quarter with US$22.44 billion in cash and cash equivalents, more than double January's US$10.61 billion, giving the chipmaker substantial capacity to fund the deal.
That financial strength reflects a rapidly expanding business. Late last month, Nvidia issued a rare year-ahead outlook, forecasting revenue growth of about 70 per cent in fiscal 2028 as the AI infrastructure boom rages on.
But the chipmaker's use of its balance sheet has also drawn scrutiny. Deals such as its agreement to guarantee up to US$105 billion for OpenAI's Ohio data-centre lease have intensified investor concerns that Nvidia is supporting the demand driving its growth.
For Nvidia, building up open source may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance on its costly and supply-constrained processors.
Hugging Face has also been in the news recently after a hack by rogue AI agents that escaped OpenAI's testing environment. Beyond hosting AI models, it offers datasets, software libraries and cloud services used to build and deploy AI applications.
The New York-based startup was founded in 2016 by French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf.

Masked men ransack, loot TMC leader Abhishek Banerjee’s office in Kolkata
TMC lawmaker Abhishek Banerjee alleged that police did not respond for at least two hours and blamed the ruling BJP for the attack
A group of armed masked men ransacked and looted Trinamool Congress (TMC) lawmaker Abhishek Banerjee’s office on Kolkata’s Camac Street in the early hours of Thursday. Banerjee called the attack outrageous, unacceptable, and a disgraceful assault on the rule of law. He alleged that police did not respond to calls and emails for at least two hours and blamed the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) for the attack.
“At around 4.30 am, BJP hooligans, armed with weapons, stormed our party office in the heart of Kolkata. They attacked our people, snatched their phones, smashed furniture, ransacked the premises and destroyed electronic equipment,” Banerjee wrote on X.
Banerjee, nephew of former chief minister Mamata Banerjee, posted a video on X, purportedly showing men wearing masks and helmets fleeing with what appeared to be monitors and smart television sets. Some of the attackers could be seen carrying two smart televisions and other gadgets at a time. A second video showed the ransacked office, shattered glass, broken furniture, and damaged electronic gadgets.
“This is what the BJP has done to my party office in the early hours of this morning. Will the Governor of WB [West Bengal] act? Will the Union Home Minister act? Will the PMO [Prime Minister’s Office] act? Or will they continue to look the other way? It is high time the judiciary, particularly the Calcutta High Court, takes serious note of what is happening and acts to uphold the rule of law in West Bengal,” Banerjee wrote.
Police said an investigation has started and they have detained some people for questioning.
BJP legislator Sajal Ghosh denied the charges of the ruling party’s involvement in the attack, saying it was part of Abhishek Banerjee’s attempt to stay relevant.
“...the BJP is in no way associated with this attack. The people of Bengal have discarded the TMC and voted for the BJP with a huge mandate. He [Abhishek Banerjee] is trying to stay afloat and politically relevant. That is why he is making such allegations. What were his workers doing in the office at that time?” Ghosh asked.
On August 27, the Kolkata Municipal Corporation removed an allegedly unauthorised TMC billboard from the building where Abhishek Banerjee’s office is located. This week, a team from the fire department audited the office. A case was registered against Abhishek Banerjee, and police on Tuesday questioned him in connection with a clash between his supporters and government officials who removed the billboard.

Another close mom friend recently sent me a photo of her three children's school supplies; it was a literal mountain of Amazon boxes. I only have one child and easily spent $100 give or take on school supplies each year — until I started teaching.
Once I was on the other end of the school supply list, I realized there were so many ways to save. As a former teacher and now a mom of a middle schooler, I have these top tips for saving money on school supplies.
Not every supply needs to be brand new
A common misconception among parents is that every school item needs to be brand new.
I've recycled my son's headphones for three school years now. They're still in good condition, and they weren't lost because I labeled them with his first and last name. That way, when he inevitably leaves them behind in a class, they get returned to him. His calculator is another item that's labeled and reused year to year.
Cleaning goes a long way in reusing supplies, too. At the end of each school year, I dump my son's book bag out and wipe down everything that can be reused with a disinfectant wipe. This includes unopened glue sticks and unused colored pencils, while items like scissors and highlighters look brand new after a good wipe-down.
I only splurge on 2 items
The only two items I spend money on are my son's backpack and lunchbox.
I wash my son's backpack and lunchbox throughout the school year. Quality bags can be washed again and again, and last you several years. I also let my son pick out a cute and discreet pencil bag to serve as a safe place for his valuables, including lunch money, his cellphone, and other personal items. And because I let my son pick out his own bags, he doesn't mind reusing them year to year.
For the book bag supplies, I always try to buy off-label, even if the school supply list states otherwise. For instance, if Clorox wipes or Ziploc bags are listed, any off-brand disinfectant wipes or plastic bags with zip-tops will do.
I shop at different stores to maximize savings
Both Target's and Walmart's prices on supplies are comparable. For example, Target's Dealworthy composition notebooks are $0.39 each, while Walmart's Pen+gear notebooks are $0.38 each.
When it comes to durability, I do prefer Target's products. Their Mondo Llama markers and colored pencils, for instance, are as good as Crayola's, in my opinion, and half the price.
As long as you're willing to go to a couple of stores, some supplies are even less at Dollar Tree, including their highlighters and glue sticks.
Then I pick out some of their two-packs of cute folders and colorfully designed notebooks that my son doesn't really need. But these things help with back-to-school jitters, and they only cost $1.25 each, which is a fraction of the price on the same items anywhere else.
If I can, I donate stuff to my son's classroom
I always pick up markers and colored paper while they're on sale, because my son will inevitably need them for projects during the school year. And while I'm no longer teaching, I still buy desk supplies for my home office. Even as an adult, I never get tired of fresh pencils and cute pens, while pretty folders and post-its always get used.
As a former teacher, I know how much classroom supply donations are appreciated. If I can, I like to apply my own school-supply savings toward donations to my son's classroom teachers. My No. 1 supply request was always a box of tissues. I would go through two to three a week, and I bought them myself for my classroom. Trader Joe's still sells a box of tissues for $0.99, which is less than anywhere I've seen.
After tissues, the top teacher requests are likely to be extra pencils for students, antibacterial wipes for desks, and bags of individually wrapped candy. I know candy may seem like an odd request, but teachers use it as a small reward in the classroom to increase engagement. Just like tissues, teachers are buying bulk candy out of their own pockets several times a school year.
I buy things off the school supply list
Middle and high school students will always need an endless amount of loose-leaf paper and pencils. When Target's Dealworthy packs of 175 sheets are priced at $0.89 during back-to-school, I get at least four.
I don't know why students lose their pencils, but they do. This year, I bought my son a box of 50 Up & Up mechanical pencils for $5.99 to keep at home and to restock his book bag as needed.
In both elementary and secondary, I really believe every student should get used to carrying a small hand sanitizer. My students loved wearing them on their book bags as keychains, too. Trader Joe's sells a 2-ounce lavender-scented sanitizer spray for $1.99 that would last me all school year at my desk.
After PE class and sports practices, I get my son a pack of 30 Arm & Hammer Kids Body Wipes from Dollar Tree for $1.25. On-the-go hygiene items like these are something a lot of parents forget about, but are so appreciated by an athletic middle schooler.

JAIPUR: Food regulator 
FSSAI
 on Thursday said it has directed CG Foods India Pvt Ltd to stop production of 'Veg Bhujia Namkeen' after inspections found multiple violations, including hygiene-related lapses.
The food safety and standards authority of india (FSSAI) said it had initiated enforcement action against CG Foods India in view of "unsafe processing, unlicensed bhujia manufacturing, and predated packaging".
FSSAI conducted an inspection at the company's unit in Roopangarh, Ajmer, Rajasthan, to check manufacturing practices and hygiene compliance, news agency PTI reported.
"The unit was found re-processing floor-collected, broken noodles into bhujia products without heat treatment, along with using predated packaging dates. Unlicensed manufacturing of 'Wai-Wai MaMa' and 'Wai-Wai Mama Punte' bhujia variants was identified in direct violation of Section 31(1) of the FSS Act, 2006," FSSAI said.
The regulator seized 32,107.2 kg of stock at the premises, including loose broken noodles.
"The inspection revealed several hygiene and documentation deficiencies, including inadequate pest-control records and other deficiencies relating to food hygiene and safety," FSSAI said.
Samples were collected for laboratory analysis, while 1,925 boxes of expired finished goods were detained, PTI reported.
FSSAI also initiated strict legal proceedings against the company.
The regulator directed the company to "discontinue the production of the Veg Bhujia Namkeen products without proper approvals and measures".
FSSAI warned that further regulatory action would follow based on the laboratory analysis and inspection findings.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday (August 28, 2026) submitted in the Supreme Court a proposal to provide information relating to added sugar, fat and salt in pictorial form on the front-of-pack (FOP) of food products, in line with international regulations.
“The proposal is intended to provide a simple, prominent and easily comprehensible warning to consumers regarding food products which are high in specified nutrients of concern,” an FSSAI affidavit filed in the Supreme Court said.
The affidavit proposes an FOP warning label in red hexagonal shape for food products which are high in any two or more “nutrients of concern” such as added saturated fat, added sugar and salt, based on thresholds specified under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024.
The warning label would read ‘High Fat’, ‘High Sugar’, ‘High Salt’ or ‘Highly Sweetened Beverage’ and be displayed in a font one point larger than that used in the nutrition information table on the back of the pack to help customers readily identify at-risk foods.
The FSSAI said single-ingredient food products and those which are “inherently rich in fat, sugar or salt, like ghee, edible oil, jaggery, honey” are proposed to be exempted from FOP warning requirement.
Phased implementation
The affidavit said the FOP labelling mechanism is intended to be implemented in phases to “facilitate consumer acceptability and provide industry adequate time for reformulation”.
Phase I would cover products high in two or more specified nutrients and specified sweetened beverages. Phase II would extend the warning mechanism to products high in any one of these nutrients.
The affidavit in the Supreme Court came in a petition filed by NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi. Mr. Dvivedi said the NGO would file a comprehensive rejoinder to the FSSAI’s compliance affidavit in the apex court after inviting public comments.
The compliance affidavit by the food regulator follows scathing comments on August 13 from a Bench headed by Justice J.B. Pardiwala on the state’s obligations to protect public health. The court had observed that not only developed but even developing countries were adopting international standards of packaging food products.
Bringing awareness
“A positive step in that direction would further accelerate our country’s endeavour to be fully developed, by bringing awareness to the public in general of the ill-effects, emanating even from indigenous foods, despite our conviction that indigenous foods coming from diverse cultures in this country were never intended to be packaged,” the court had recorded in its August 13 order.
The court had noted that the Economic Survey has already suggested FOP labelling, and the Union government would not have any impediments in implementing the changes.
“We are doing this in public interest. Keep it in mind,” Justice Pardiwala had addressed the government on August 13.

- The claim that U.S. President Donald Trump diverted 300 first responders to work on his Washington, D.C., beautification projects, thus making those workers unavailable for immediate rescue efforts in the aftermath of the Aug. 29, 2026, Grand Canyon National Park flash floods, is unproven.
- The rumor stemmed in part from users sharing a Sept. 1 article from the online publication The Lever, which reported, "Trump reassigned 300 National Park Service emergency responders to golf course and reflecting-pool renovations before the Grand Canyon flooded."
- The Lever cited a CNN article published days before the flooding reporting hundreds of NPS first responders were reassigned without saying exactly when the staffing shifts occurred. The CNN story cited its own review of internal communications and department data, as well as anonymous sources.
- Snopes has not been able to review the same internal CNN documentation, nor have we located information confirming or debunking the claim that Trump's reported diversion of first responders hampered flood rescue efforts.
- An Interior Department spokesperson said of the rumor that the reported diversion of workers hampered the flood response, "That is 100% false." We reached out to numerous other relevant parties and will update this article if we receive further details.
A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump diverted 300 first responders to Washington, D.C., to work on his administration's beautification projects circulated online in early September 2026. People sharing the claim suggested they would have proved key in rescue efforts, possibly saving lives, had they been available immediately following the Aug. 29 flash floods inside Arizona's Grand Canyon National Park. We have not yet found evidence that would confirm or debunk this rumor.
The National Park Service, an agency under the Interior Department, announced closures to bridges, the Colorado River, lodging and trails, as well as confirming two deaths, one person missing and around 80 people rescued or evacuated.
An NPS news release said the two people who died, John Giusti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, both of Granbury, Texas, were hiking in Bright Angel Canyon and were a part of the same group as the missing person. A key water pipeline sustained severe damage, as well.
In one example of the rumor, on Sept. 1, an X user posted (archived) a message appearing to place blame for the deaths on Trump.
(@factpostnews accessed via X)
Other posts featured the claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived).
Some posts directly cited the online publication The Lever, which published an article on Sept. 1 with the headline "Before Deadly Floods, Trump Diverted Emergency Responders To Beautify D.C." The story's subheading reads: "Trump reassigned 300 National Park Service emergency responders to golf course and reflecting-pool renovations before the Grand Canyon flooded."
The Lever's article cited a CNN story published prior to the floods on Aug. 25, telling of Trump's administration sending 300 NPS incident management team workers — a division responding to wildfires and other incidents — to work on what CNN dubbed Trump's Washington, D.C., "pet projects," such as the past renovations for the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and the future overhaul of the East Potomac Park golf course. The CNN article does not say exactly when the purported staffing shifts occurred.
The CNN reporters cited their own review of internal communications and department data, as well as anonymous sources regarding other information.
Neither the Lever's article nor users' posts explicitly said the Trump administration's reported diversion of 300 workers hampered rescue efforts surrounding the flash floods. Either way, users inferred it, some believing Trump very recently diverted the workers, with one Snopes reader emailing, "Did tRump divert 300 specialized emergency first responders from American national parks to work on his Reflecting Pool, in the midst of needing them for Grand Canyon rescues?"
Snopes has not been able to review the same internal documentation CNN cited, nor have we located information that might allow us to conclusively rule on the veracity of the claim that Trump's reported diversion of first responders hindered Grand Canyon flood rescue efforts. This claim is therefore unproven and we have left it unrated.
Via email, the White House referred us to the Interior Department, where a department spokesperson said of the rumor that the reported diversion of workers to Washington harmed the flood response, "That is 100% false."
We requested documentation, information and/or comment from the Arizona Department of Public Safety, CNN, Coconino County Emergency Response, Grand Canyon National Park, The Lever and NPS, and will update this article if we receive further information.
A brief timeline of rescue efforts
Within three hours of the flooding on Aug. 29, NPS Grand Canyon shared details about officials evacuating 50 people by air. By the next morning, the division reported 62 total evacuations out of the roughly 80 rescues to date, and said it had gotten assistance from the Arizona Public Safety Department.
A Sept. 1 notice from NPS Grand Canyon announced the continuation of search-and-rescue operations, as well as that the "NPS Western Type 3 Incident Management Team" — the same as the incident management teams CNN and The Lever reported about — would be taking over command as of that morning. The Arizona Daily Sun published a photo reportedly showing a member of that same team observing an Aug. 31 news conference, two days following the flooding.
For further reading about Trump's beautification efforts in the nation's capital, we previously reported about an allegation that his administration chopped down dozens of beloved cherry trees to renovate a golf course, as well as that his motorcade ride inside the reflecting pool caused damage he later blamed on others.

We actually know how to help mothers with postpartum depression
The Lindsay Clancy trial reveals our failure on postpartum depression. Here’s how it gets better.
The trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children, is laden with painful what-ifs: What if she had more support? What if she had more people to confide in? Could all of this suffering have been avoided?
Those are urgent questions, whatever the outcome of this particular case, because millions of women experience postpartum depression. Severe postpartum psychosis may be extremely rare, but every year at least 1 in 8 women who give birth in the US experience some depression symptoms — and that is likely an undercount.
A jury will ultimately decide whether or not to convict her for her children’s deaths; by Tuesday morning, the jurors were still unable to reach a unanimous verdict but the judge in the case ordered them to keep deliberating. Their verdict will rest in part on whether they believe that Clancy was in her right mind when she killed her children — the defense does not contest the underlying facts — or whether, as her attorneys are contending, she was experiencing severe psychosis that should render her not culpable for her actions.
Clancy’s case has become a national flashpoint for maternal mental health — a gripping courtroom drama that also exposes how new moms’ mental well-being has been neglected by the health system and researchers for years.
It’s easy to feel hopeless in the face of such a tragedy, and much of the coverage has — rightly — focused on the gaps it exposed in the system for women getting the care they need. But even now, there’s good reason to feel optimistic.
Doctors and health workers across the United States are experimenting with strategies that can improve postpartum mental health care. They have found a secret ingredient that can help new mothers when they are struggling: other moms who have been through the same thing before.
“You just had a baby. You’re responsible for a new human life. And it’s really hard to juggle everything in your life,” Dr. Jessica Gaulton, a pediatrician who founded FamilyWell Health, a postpartum mental health support service that incorporates peer coaches into its program, told me. “Oftentimes what women need is just somebody to be there and have their back.”
Postpartum depression is a health system problem, a public health problem — but it’s also a deeply personal one. Helping people make connections that make them not feel so alone is one way we can start to improve the postpartum outlook for American mothers.
And a wave of local programs — and research showing that they really work — is offering some promising new ideas about how to deliver more compassionate and effective care for postpartum depression.
How to help new moms with postpartum depression right now
During the Clancy trial, the Maternal Mental Health Alliance has listed five steps that could be taken to improve postpartum care. One of their top priorities is better care coordination among the different healthcare providers who see a new mom after she’s given birth.
The so-called “collaborative care model” has been building momentum for years now, since it was first introduced for postpartum care for Medicaid patients in Seattle’s King County more than a decade ago. The model has since spread to other places, but the basic tenet is this: It takes a whole team to care for a new mother and watch out for her mental health, and they need a point person to help manage their care.
In Los Angeles, for example, where a group of nonprofits is wrapping up a five-year pilot program based on the collaborative care model, new mothers are assigned to a behavioral-health care manager. The manager performs assessments and brief interventions, works with a psychiatric consultant to continually assess how the patient is doing, and cooperates with the OB/GYN or primary care doctor to manage the patient’s treatment. Rather than waiting for a psychiatrist to have an open appointment when she’s struggling right now, the new mom’s preexisting healthcare providers can step in with support from a mental health professional to manage postpartum depression symptoms.
In evaluations, the model has consistently outperformed other standards of care in reducing symptoms. But while we have started to see collaborative care spread to other parts of the US, its progress has been halting for various logistical and financial reasons. The Maternal Mental Health Alliance is urging health systems and health insurers to invest in more care coordination programs.
And now some providers are building on the collaborative care model with an important new element: peer support. In Washington, the MOMCare program is now experimenting with peer “navigators” to help their patients figure out the appropriate place to get the care they need. In Massachusetts, Gaulton’s FamilyWell Health, which works with OB/GYN practices to provide mental health services, launched a pilot program that added certified behavioral health coaches.
These people were recruited because they had their own life experience of giving birth and having postpartum depression symptoms; the coaches were frequently doulas, nurses, and midwives. Patients would talk once or twice a week with their coach to set goals and receive positive feedback, while the coaches had a protocol to follow if it seemed their patient required more serious support. A study published in April found that this new coach-driven approach was successfully reducing depression and anxiety symptoms. Patients experience remission of their depression symptoms within an average of nine days with a peer coach, versus eight days with a licensed therapist. In other words, the mothers assigned to a peer got better almost as quickly as those who saw a professional.
Gaulton said she introduced the peer-coach concept to FamilyWell Health because of her own experiences as a new mom. She struggled to recognize her own depression symptoms. When she did, she leaned on a friend and fellow neonatologist at the hospital where she worked for help. Then during Covid, she saw moms with otherwise healthy babies struggling during that world-altering public health emergency.
“What I realized was that we were underutilizing coaches,” Gaulton said. “For decades, we’ve been using peer groups, peer coaching in this field to support, but it has never been formalized. There was no formal training.”
So she decided to found a new company dedicated to supporting new mothers’ mental health — and she brought those lessons with her.
This idea — training experienced moms to help new moms — has been gaining traction across the country. In Colorado, researchers from the University of Colorado launched a program called Alma, which connects new moms with another woman who has been through the same experiences and received specialized training to provide emotional support. The program’s mentors receive 80 hours of training and then meet up to 10 times with a new mother, either in person or virtually, to talk about what makes them feel good and how to incorporate it into their day, following long-held protocols for depression treatment called “behavior activation.”
“There is a special kind of trust that can develop when someone feels that the person sitting across from them understands something about their life and their community — someone who has walked the same path,” Sona Dimidjian, a University of Colorado clinical psychologist who helped found the program, said in an email. “A peer can often say, in effect, ‘I have been there too, and I know how hard it can be.’ That shared experience can also help reduce the stigma and shame that many women feel about depression during pregnancy or the postpartum period.”
The concept was based on research from India that found “lay counselors” were effective at reducing mental health symptoms. With the US in a permanent mental health provider shortage, being able to tap into the general population to support new moms was an appealing idea. And evaluations of the program found that it significantly reduced symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress among the Spanish-speaking Latina women who were its initial focus.
The biggest endorsement of a peer-support approach like Alma or the peer coaches in FamilyWell Health’s coordinated care program is its target audience. A nationwide survey of new and expecting Latina mothers in the US found that the vast majority thought talking to a peer would make them feel less isolated and more understood compared to a mental health professional. And providers and policymakers around the United States have started taking notice: English and Spanish-language versions of the Alma program are now being implemented in California and New Jersey.
There is no panacea for postpartum depression. As Amritha Bhat, who has worked on the MOMCare program at the University of Washington, explained it to me: “Having a multipronged approach is a good way to ensure that treatment reaches those most in need.”
There are big-picture institutional-level changes that need to be made. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM, the bible of American psychiatry, currently does not categorize postpartum depression as its own distinct diagnosis. As NPR reported, primary care doctors and pediatricians often do not receive sufficient training to help them recognize the signs of postpartum depression and provide patients with the support they need. There is never enough funding for research or for programs for maternal mental health: The Maternal Mental Health Alliance has been pushing Congress to add millions of dollars in funding for the federal programs that focus on new moms. Peer coaching has not traditionally been covered by health insurance; figuring out how to pay for programs like this is another system-level challenge.
But connecting moms to other moms can help the people who need support right now. Sometimes that can happen through organized programs like Alma or FamilyWell; the experts working on those initiatives want to make them an integrated part of post-delivery medical care. But that support might also be found informally in a new parent’s everyday life. There are a lot of social media and in-person groups for new moms to get together, sometimes at a local library or other community organization. Gaulton leaned on a friend when she was struggling after her own pregnancy.
As Gaulton emphasized to me, most cases of postpartum depression never escalate into a tragedy. This is a scary condition — but it’s treatable.
“I just want laypeople to know that the typical case is someone like me who had some symptoms of depression, anxiety,” she said. “I found help. I got better.”

Court case shows how cocaine traffickers got creative during N.L.'s COVID-19 restrictions
Man gets 39-month sentence for plot to move drugs via sale of used truck
A pandemic-era police operation has resulted in findings of guilt against three men who concocted a scheme to bring more than $1 million worth of cocaine into Newfoundland amid COVID-19 travel restrictions.
Dion Wilson Lee Rodgers is the first of the trio to be sentenced for his role in importing 3.4 kilograms of cocaine stashed inside a pickup truck. The Dover man was sentenced to 39 months imprisonment.
The case offers a rare glimpse into the movements of narcotics to the island, especially during a time of heightened isolation.
"I accept that Mr. Rodgers was an integral part of the conspiracy to conduct a high-level trafficking operation in this province," Justice Leanne O'Leary said in her sentencing decision, which was published on Wednesday. "He facilitated the importation of a large quantity of high purity cocaine."
The investigation began in 2018 and centered on Steven Armstrong — an Ontario man who was making frequent, short trips to Newfoundland via the Marine Atlantic ferry system.
In December of 2019, investigators with the RCMP kept a close watch as Armstrong and Rodgers travelled in separate vehicles from Nova Scotia to Newfoundland. Officers moved in on Armstrong as he drove off the ferry in Port aux Basques. Despite their search efforts, they were unable to find any drugs in the vehicle.
Throughout the early part of 2020, the RCMP went to court to obtain warrants to surveil and intercept Armstrong's communications.
Through the wiretaps, investigators heard Armstrong was planning to move a Honda Ridgeline from Ontario to Newfoundland in early 2020. The world had other plans.
The COVID-19 pandemic reached the island in March. Travel in and out of the province came to a screeching halt, throwing a wrench into Armstrong's plan to move the truck and its illicit contents.
"The government restrictions surrounding the pandemic at the time prevented his travel into the province," Justice O'Leary said. "Tracking of Mr. Armstrong’s communications revealed his ongoing efforts to get a vehicle to this province when he was prevented from travelling himself."
Travel opened up to the Atlantic provinces in the summer of 2020, and the investigation showed Armstrong began trying to reach Rodgers again in September.
"Mr. Armstrong called the home line of Mr. Rodgers and his stepfather," O'Leary summarized. "Mr. Armstrong advised [the stepfather] that Mr. Rodgers couldn’t let him down and he needed him to check his phone. The parties were using encrypted applications which could not be traced by the police for investigative purposes."

- N.L. cocaine case stopped after Jordan timeline exceeded by 7 days
Later that month, police followed Armstrong as he drove the Honda Ridgeline from Ontario to the ferry terminal in Nova Scotia. The investigation determined he'd prepared a bill of sale for the truck, with Rodgers listed as the buyer.
Police also watched on the other side of the gulf, as Rodgers and his stepfather drove onto the ferry in Port aux Basques. They watched as his stepfather took control of the Honda Ridgeline in the terminal parking lot in Nova Scotia.
Upon returning to Newfoundland, officers followed the truck across the island before pulling him over in Dover. They then encountered an unexpected problem.
"An initial search of the Honda Ridgeline revealed no drugs," O'Leary said.
The surveillance didn't stop there. Police continued to track communications between Rodgers and Armstrong, and picked up a tidbit of information that led to another search of the truck soon after the arrest.
"The police located 3.4 kilograms of cocaine within a hidden compartment of the Honda Ridgeline," O'Leary said. "The compartment included a customized hydraulic release system within a modified passenger side air bag module."
The RCMP said the cocaine was worth an estimated $1.4 million.
Tests determined the drugs had a "very high" purity, ranging between 84 and 87 per cent pure.
An officer told the court at trial that the volume of cocaine would likely increase between two and four times after processing, cutting and packaging.
A jury found Rodgers guilty of conspiracy to traffic in cocaine.
Armstrong was initially charged in Newfoundland and Labrador, but his case was later shipped back to Ontario. He pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced on Sept. 10.
