It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

Crude oil is back in focus as fresh hostilities in West Asia revive concerns over supplies from the region. Brent crude is trading above $95 per barrel after US military strikes on areas along Iran’s southern coast.
Brent crude has risen around 20% from about $79 a barrel in early July to around $95 currently, reversing the easing seen during a month of relative calm in the US-Iran conflict. Renewed US strikes on Iran on 31 August, followed by Iranian retaliation, have pushed supply disruption risks back to the forefront.
Mint explains the volatile price trend, its impact on oil supplies and what it means for the Indian economy.
What has been the recent crude price trend?
Over the past one week, crude prices have traded on a volatile note, in the range of $88-$97 per barrel, amid a sharp escalation in the war in West Asia.
Al Jazeera reported that the US and Iran exchanged the biggest barrage since July and that the death toll from the latest US strikes has reached 18. The US military struck cities and areas along Iran’s southern coast, while Iran retaliated with attacks on US bases across West Asia. The escalation has further clouded oil supply prospects from the region.
Why does crude price volatility matter for India?
Given India's dependency on oil imports, uncertain supplies and price volatility affect the Indian economy. Nearly 90% of India's oil requirement is imported. The import bill in the last fiscal stood at around $123 billion, and an increase of $1 per barrel for a year may raise the country's annual import bill by ₹18,000 crore.
Already, India has imported crude worth $63.4 billion in the first four months of this fiscal (FY27), more than half of the total import bill of FY26. The import bill has grown about 56.5% on a year-on-year basis.
A higher import bill could add to inflationary pressures if the increase in costs is passed on to downstream products and consumers. This, in turn, could affect GDP growth or widen the country's current account deficit.
How could the West Asia war affect India's oil supplies?
Traditionally, West Asia catered to about 60-65% of India's total oil imports, with Saudi Arabia, Iraq and UAE being the key suppliers. These supplies have now declined drastically with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Although a few tankers are coming in through the Strait, which earlier used to handle 20% of global oil trade, and some supplies are coming in through the Red Sea route and Emirati and Omani ports towards the east of the Strait of Hormuz to India, refiners have significantly diversified.
Russia continues as the top supplier, while the US and Venezuela have emerged as other key sources. While availability and supplies are not major concerns for Indian refiners, alternative sources come with higher costs. Supplies from the US and Venezuela involve longer routes, while the dense and viscous nature of the crude from America adds to the cost.
Is India's petroleum consumption also rising?
Being the third largest crude importer and fourth largest refiner in the world, the country is a major petroleum products consumption hub.
Data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) showed that India's petrol demand in August was 3.82 million tonne, about 7.88% higher on a year-on-year basis, while diesel consumption was up 6.46% to 7 million tonne.
So far this fiscal (April-August), petrol and diesel consumption has increased 6.48% and 4.29%, respectively. With consumption rising, India's crude oil import requirement is expected to grow going ahead.
According to the Organization of Petroleum Exporting countries, India is set to become the major driving force for the world's petroleum products demand by the end of this decade.
What is India doing to strengthen energy security?
India has well diversified its oil imports in the past few years to about 41 countries to ensure energy security and continues to look for newer sources.
On the domestic front, the government and oil marketing companies are eyeing an increase in local oil and gas production. The recent approval by the Union cabinet for the 'Samudra Manthan-National Offshore Exploration Scheme', with an outlay of ₹84,000 crore, aims to boost the hydrocarbon exploration and production sector.
According to the government, India’s eastern and western offshore basins are estimated to hold over 5,600 million metric tonnes of oil equivalent of hydrocarbon potential.

Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.
The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.
Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.
The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.
Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.
While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.
The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.
Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.
“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.

What will Jackson bring to Villa with Watkins set for exit?
- Published
Aston Villa have completed the signing of Nicolas Jackson in a deal worth up to £65m, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.
Unai Emery's Villa are undergoing a major overhaul this summer, with key players including Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne having already departed.
Jackson, 25, joins a number of new additions including Johan Manzambi, Joao Gomes, Zion Suzuki and Matteo Ruggeri.
That level of squad disruption was evident on the opening weekend, when Emery's side slumped to a 4-0 defeat at Brighton.
With Watkins, 30, unavailable and both Tammy Abraham and 17-year-old Brian Madjo injured, Villa started without a recognised centre-forward - Emiliano Buendia led the line.
The arrival of Jackson - who overtakes Manzambi to become Villa's record signing - from Chelsea gives Emery a specialist striker to work with.
It also looks set to coincide with the end of Watkins' six-year spell at Villa, during which he scored 108 goals in 278 games and became one of the defining players of the rise under Emery.
However, the stats suggest Jackson is not just a like-for-like replacement for the England international - he is a different type of number nine.
More involved, more shots - but a smaller sample
On the surface, Jackson's numbers at Bayern Munich last season compare favourably with those of Watkins at Villa.
The Senegal forward scored 11 goals and provided three assists in 1,320 minutes across all competitions, averaging 1.0 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Watkins recorded 21 goals and five assists in 3,837 minutes, an average of 0.6 per 90.
Jackson also generated more attacking opportunities. He averaged 3.8 shots per 90 compared with Watkins' 2.6, and 2.2 shots on target to 1.2.
His expected-goals (xG) figure was also higher, at 0.7 per 90 compared with 0.5, while he averaged 8.5 touches in the opposition box to Watkins' 5.6.
That fits a pattern which predates his spell in Germany. Among players with at least 5,000 Premier League minutes since January 2020, only Erling Haaland has registered a higher non-penalty xG figure per 90 than Jackson's 0.55.
Getting into scoring positions has rarely been Jackson's main problem - it is his ability to finish chances which has attracted scrutiny.
During his two Premier League seasons with Chelsea, he scored 14 goals from 18.7 xG in 2023-24 and 10 from 12.3 xG the following campaign.
Jackson has converted 18 of 61 big chances in England so far, although Watkins has also missed plenty of high-value opportunities (scoring 24 of 73 since joining Villa in 2020).
Interestingly, last season's numbers suggest the gap between them was negligible. Jackson converted 19.6% of his shots and 40.9% of his big chances, compared with 18.9% and 43.2% respectively for Watkins.
There is, however, an important caveat.
Watkins started 43 matches and played almost three times as many minutes. Jackson started only 15 of his 34 appearances, and Opta says his relatively limited, substitute-heavy sample could make some of his per-90 figures look stronger than they might over a full season.
Are Villa getting a different type of striker?
Both players were predominantly used as centre-forwards last season, making the comparison reasonably fair.
Watkins played 100% of his 3,837 minutes as a striker, with 92% coming as the central striker in Villa's 4-2-3-1.
Jackson spent 95% of his 1,320 minutes up front, with the remaining 5% on the left. At Bayern, 86% of his playing time came as the striker in a 4-2-3-1.
The similarity largely ends there. Jackson averaged 46.6 open-play touches per 90, compared with Watkins' 29.5, and completed almost twice as many passes - 24 per 90 to Watkins' 11.6.
He was also considerably more involved in creating and progressing attacks. Jackson averaged:
- 1.6 shot-ending carries per 90, compared with Watkins' 0.8
- 1.6 successful take-ons per 90, compared with 0.82
- 2.5 passes into the penalty area per 90, compared with 0.7.
Opta's touch maps reinforce the difference. Watkins' involvement was concentrated more heavily around the centre of the final third and penalty area, while Jackson received possession across a wider range of attacking zones.
Among a sample of 1,577 top-five European league strikers over the past 10 seasons, Jackson ranked in the 85th percentile for chances created, 77th for progressive carries and 73rd for touches.
Watkins ranked in the 28th, 53rd and eighth percentiles respectively. That points towards Villa moving from a relatively low-touch focal point to a forward who is more comfortable becoming involved in attacks earlier.
Greater intensity without the ball
There is another possible difference when Villa lose possession. Jackson averaged 34 high pressures per 90, slightly above Watkins' 31.4, but the distinction becomes clearer in where possession was recovered.
Jackson won the ball 2.7 times per 90, compared with Watkins' 1.8, and regained it in the final third 0.9 times per 90 to Watkins' 0.6.
His percentile for possession won in the attacking third was 88th among the Opta striker sample, compared with Watkins' 43rd.
The two were almost identical for runs in behind, Jackson averaging 13 per 90 and Watkins 12.7, although the Englishman made slightly more runs which finished inside the penalty area.
Watkins also offered more aerially, winning 1.2 aerial duels per 90 compared with Jackson's 0.7, and carried the ball more directly towards goal. So Jackson would not necessarily reproduce every aspect of the player he is replacing.
Why Emery believes he can unlock Jackson
Villa's interest also comes with an element of familiarity. Emery worked with Jackson at Villarreal, where the forward made 27 appearances under him, scoring three goals and providing three assists in 1,195 minutes.
Jackson has subsequently credited Emery with transforming his understanding of the game.
"Unai taught me everything about football," he said,
Jackson has explained that, when he arrived from Senegal, he possessed natural dribbling ability but had much less understanding of how and when to move.
Emery helped turn that instinctive talent into a more structured game.
Jackson's development accelerated after Emery left Villarreal. During the 2022-23 La Liga season he produced 0.56 non-penalty xG plus xA per 90, a rate bettered by only seven players with at least 1,500 minutes, all representing Barcelona, Real Madrid or Atletico Madrid.
Jackson's ability to carry the ball was already evident too. Ten of his league goal involvements followed carries, fewer only than Vinicius Jr, despite Jackson playing substantially fewer minutes.
Chelsea subsequently signed him in 2023. He scored 30 goals and supplied 12 assists in 81 appearances for the club before spending last season on loan at Bayern.
His time in Munich was complicated by circumstances rather than simply performance.
Bayern's obligation to buy would have been triggered if he reached a demanding appearance threshold, but Harry Kane remained fit and prolific, while the displays of Luis Diaz and Michael Olise limited opportunities elsewhere across the frontline.
Jackson still produced 11 goals across all competitions, and only Kane recorded a better rate of open-play Bundesliga goals per 90.
Bayern coach Vincent Kompany publicly defended him when criticism resurfaced, pointing to the quality of the forwards ahead of him and saying Jackson had trained and performed well.
A replacement - but not necessarily a replica
Watkins has provided Villa with reliability, running power and goals throughout one of the club's most successful periods of the modern era.
Jackson arrives with a different profile. He is five years younger, gets more touches, carries the ball more frequently, creates more for others and, in limited minutes last season, generated shots and high-quality chances at an impressive rate.
There remain questions around whether those per-90 numbers would survive a heavier workload, while his finishing record at Chelsea explains why doubts have followed him.
But Villa are not buying an unknown quantity. Emery has coached Jackson before, knows the qualities he wants to develop and would be replacing a 30-year-old striker with a 25-year-old whose underlying numbers suggest there may still be considerable room to improve.
If Jackson joins and Watkins does depart, the Europa League winners will be doing more than just changing their centre-forwards.
They will be changing the way their number nine plays.

The wife of a British man detained by police in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation has pleaded with Andy Burnham to get involved in the Brexit catastrophe unfolding for many British citizens in Sweden.
Charles, who does not want to be fully identified, and his Swedish wife, Lily, were summoned to the police station at 10am on Tuesday, where he was told he would be held at a detention centre and deported within the next two weeks.
Lily, who is a lawyer, was told to go home and get his passport despite her protests that there was a court process under way appealing the deportation order.
“I feel shame,” said Lily, who asked that their family’s surname not be published.
“To me, Britain represents freedom for human beings, and then to see this British man in detention just because he wants to be with his wife and live in his house, this is not right.
“What kind of country are we living in? Is this civilisation? They don’t care about human rights. This is a European country, but it looks like Sweden is like somewhere like Afghanistan,” she said.
Lily met her husband in the UK after starting a law degree in London in 2010.
She now works for the local authority in Stockholm and returned to Sweden in 2015, with her soon-to-be husband joining her in 2017, three years before Brexit.
A former business consultant, now retired, Charles made an application to remain in the country before the deadline for applications after Brexit.
His application was rejected two years later in 2022 and the family have been fighting deportation ever since with “six or seven” appeals, said Lily. “The Migration Agency has hunted us for five years.”
During the summer the couple received a text asking them to show up at their local police station on 1 September.
“They told us they needed to talk and we should show up at 10am. They didn’t say anything about deportation or to bring passports.
“When we arrived they told us that they needed to talk to Charles privately, and after three hours they told me they were taking him to the detention centre and that they would deport him.
“I told them that they can’t do this because his case is in court and they have to wait for the outcome, but they told me they were going ahead,” said Lily.
She has pleaded with Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, to intervene.
“Why can’t Andy Burnham talk to the Swedish government? How many British families have to suffer in Sweden before Andy Burnham gets involved? How many families have to leave their homes, be forced into selling their houses?
“This is not humanity. This is not right. They should threaten the trade agreement,” she added.
Charles’s case comes amid growing controversy over Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement, which is supposed to have protected EU citizens in the UK and British citizens settled in the bloc before Brexit.
Among those threatened with removal in the past month are 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, who has been in the country for 21 years, and George Mason, a 74-year-old man in dementia care who has been in the country for 24 years.
A 34-year-old man revealed this week he was deported from Sweden in January despite having been in the country since he was 10 and being married to a Swedish woman in Gothenburg.
Two years ago another British woman, Kathleen Poole, was threatened with deportation because she had not provided financial statements to the Migration Agency while in full-time dementia care.
The Swedish migration minister defended the country’s implementation of the withdrawal agreement, saying the Migration Agency was following the rules and had granted a number of residency permits for Britons who had “reasonable grounds” for late applications.
However, concerns have been raised formally by the UK government through the EU-UK specialised committee, the official platform to raise issues over the working out of the Brexit deal, over the high number of late applications for post Brexit residency being rejected.
Sweden, along with 12 other EU member states, opted for a constitutive system requiring citizens to formally apply to extend their residency rights post Brexit. Others, like Spain, opted for a declaratory system requiring Britons to simply register their presence initially.
Lily says she and her husband phoned the authorities and used the correct form for residency and have been fighting ever since.
The latest statistics from the 2024 European Commission annual report show that 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency have been decided in Sweden.
According to analysis by the UK government, 27.5% (3,918) of applications have been refused, “a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3 and 4%”.
Sources added that this “constitutes 12% of all refusals across the EU member states, even though UK nationals in Sweden makes up only 1.55% of the total population of WA beneficiaries in EU member states”.
Denmark faced a similar controversy two years ago, but legislation was introduced to give British nationals a second chance to make the residency application.

Seoul – South Korea announced plans Thursday to put a second presidential office and legislative complex in the administrative city of Sejong, as it accelerates efforts to move hundreds of institutions out of Seoul in a bid to lessen the capital’s dominance.
The nation has long struggled with a widening divide between regions, with about half its 51 million people concentrated in the Seoul metropolitan area for jobs and education opportunities.
The plan, which also includes relocating the gender equality ministry and prosecution service, is the latest in a decadelong push to move state bodies out of Seoul and promote balanced development.
Relocations began in 2012, when the prime minister’s office moved to Sejong, about 120 kilometers south of Seoul.
Since then, 44 central government bodies — including the finance and health ministries — have relocated to the city.
Officials said 350 public institutions based in the Seoul metropolitan area will have their relocation plans finalized in 2026.
“Balanced growth is now no longer a matter of choice, but a survival strategy for a sustainable South Korea,” Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said in a briefing.
The government aims to complete a second presidential office in Sejong by August 2029 and a second National Assembly building by 2033, Han said.
The foreign and unification ministries could also be relocated once the presidential office and National Assembly complex are completed, according to Interior Minister Yun Ho-jung.
The announcement follows plans by chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to invest 800 trillion South Korean won ($589 billion) in a chip hub in the country’s southwest, also aimed at reducing regional inequality.
Many regions face shrinking and aging populations, forcing schools and children’s clinics to close, as the country grapples with one of the world’s lowest birth rates.
As of 2024, 130 of South Korea’s 228 cities, counties and districts — or 57% — were classified as being at risk of disappearing due to population decline, according to the government.
The Seoul capital region accounts for just 12% of its land but 53% of national gross domestic product — and more than three-fifths of the country’s research and development investment, according to Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development data.
“The starting point of virtually all the major problems South Korea currently faces is the extreme imbalance in the country’s development,” said South Korean President Lee Jae Myung last week during a meeting.

Top court sets aside ₹425-crore fine on Gujarat diamantaire, cautions on AI use
The court ordered the case to be reconsidered by an officer of the same rank after finding the original order relied on non-existent case laws.
The Supreme Court on Wednesday set aside an order issued by a customs officer in Gujarat slapping a penalty of ₹425 crore against a diamond trader which had relied upon AI-generated case laws that did not exist.
Remanding the matter back to be decided by an officer of the same rank, a bench of justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu said that while Artificial Intelligence can be an “assistive tool”, it will be imprudent and dangerous if it assumes the driver seat in adjudicating decisions.
“Artificial Intelligence (AI) may well serve as training wheels but entrusting it with the pilot’s seat would be both imprudent and dangerous,” the bench said. Setting aside the order of October 8, 2025 passed by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat, the court remanded the matter back to the same authority requiring that the case be decided not by the same individual but by an officer of the same rank.
SC leaves action against officer to appointing authority
Sparing any action against the said officer, the order said: “We leave it to the wisdom of the appointing authority to initiate such action against the author of the order as may be warranted in the circumstances, in accordance with law.”
The appeal was filed before the court by the aggrieved trader, Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya, who was slapped with a penalty of ₹425.27 crore under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962, for misdeclaring a consignment of natural diamonds as lab-grown diamonds to pay a lower tariff.
Also read: ‘Catastrophic, invisible’: Supreme Court flags use of AI in legal process as ‘misconduct’
AI may assist but cannot replace
The court said that the use of AI is not prohibited as it can always be an “assistive tool” that can expedite the decision-making process. However, sounding a note of caution, the bench said, “Assistance can never be substituted for adjudication,” as it noted the fallout of this mistake in this case.
“The use of AI in this case, resulting in reliance placed by the Additional Commissioner of Customs on material which is dubious, proves fatal to the sustainability of the order imposing penalty on the appellant. Such circumstances compel us to interfere and remand the case,” the bench said.

Kennedy did not explicitly that hospice patients cost taxpayers too much money because they received treatment for too long. Instead, he was specifically referring to instances of suspected hospice fraud in California.
In late August 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said people in hospice care weren't dying fast enough and were costing taxpayers too much money.
For example, independent journalist Aaron Rupar shared a clip of Kennedy speaking on X and wrote, "RFK Jr complains that people in hospice aren't dying quick enough and therefore cost too much money."
Similar claims about Kennedy's alleged comments on people receiving hospice care also circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
Though Kennedy did speak about hospice care during an appearance on the Fox News program "Saturday in America" on Aug. 29, summaries such as Rupar's on X did not accurately reflect his words.
Kennedy did not explicitly say that hospice patients cost taxpayers money because they received treatment for too long. Rather, he said hospices in California had fraudulently received federal funds, pointing to billing for patients over multiple years instead of the typical several months as one example.
In August 2026, The Associated Press reported on one incident of fraud where a California hospice billed Medicare for a healthy 71-year-old woman.
In a recording of the "Saturday in America" town hall featuring Kennedy, he said (at 52:52):
We closed down thousands of hospices in California, they didn't have patients, they were just billing us. And the way we found them is because the patients would never die. And so, we could see, we've been paying for this guy for five years — usually, if you go to a hospice, it means you've got three months left to live — these people were never dying, they just had the patient numbers and we were being charged $6,000 a month and just paying, I think 8,000 of them, of these hospices. We're talking about tens of billions of dollars stolen every year.
Given the above, we find claims that Kennedy said hospice patients weren't dying fast enough and costing taxpayers money false. Instead, he was specifically referring to instances of suspected hospice fraud.
We contacted the Department of Health and Human Services to ask when it closed the 8,000 hospices Kennedy mentioned and how much money the department estimated hospice fraudsters had received and await a reply.
Medicare, the U.S. federal health insurance program for people 65 and older, covers hospice care for eligible patients. According to Medicare's website, a patient is eligible if one or more doctors certify they are terminally ill, with a life expectancy of six months or less — not three, as Kennedy said. The insurance program covers hospice care for two initial 90-day periods and successive unlimited 60-day periods.
The Associated Press reported in August 2026 that fraudsters opened fake hospices and tricked real patients into enrolling, or stole people's identities to bill Medicare for hospice services they did not receive.
In May 2026, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced six-month moratoriums on Medicare enrollment for hospices and home health agencies. The centers said they had worked with Vance's anti-fraud task force to suspend federal payments to 800 hospices and home health agencies suspected of fraud in Los Angeles. The suspected fraudulent companies received $1.4 billion in Medicare payments in 2025, according to the news release.
The release noted that hospice fraud was especially prevalent in Arizona, California, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada and Texas.
California's Department of Justice described hospice fraud as "an epidemic" in the state. The department said it carried out its own investigations into hospice fraud within Medi-Cal, California's state-level health insurance program and that it had secured 51 "hospice related convictions" since 2021.
For further reading, Snopes routinely investigates claims about Medicare.

A US federal judge has sided with Google, ruling that the company will not have to sell its online advertising exchange (previously known as AdX). The US Department of Justice (DOJ) sought this remedy in the long-running ad tech antitrust trial, which Google lost in 2025. However, the remedies imposed upon Google for that loss are shaping up to be minimal.
In this case, the DOJ and a coalition of states sought to prove that Google leveraged its immense market power in online display ads to reduce the reach of competitors. Government lawyers argued that Google had “rigged” ad auctions to give itself an advantage. While the court agreed that Google illegally locked publishers into using its exchange, it did not agree that Google had broken the law when it came to the tools used by advertisers.
Despite the mixed ruling, the DOJ argued during the remedy phase that forcing Google to sell its ad exchange, which facilitates connections between ad buyers and sellers, was the best way to level the playing field. But that won’t happen. While the ad exchange represents a relatively small part of Google’s revenue, forcing the company to sell may have sent ripple effects through the rest of its ad business. It would also have been a powerful message to Big Tech firms, which have successfully knocked back a recent wave of antitrust cases.
That doesn’t necessarily mean Google gets off scot-free. While divesting the ad exchange would have been the most serious penalty, the government also asked for fines and court-ordered changes to Google’s business practices. It’s likely that the DOJ will get a lot of that, but we don’t know the specifics yet. Judge Leonie Brinkema has sealed the order for 14 days, giving the parties a chance to request redactions. So we’ll know the exact nature of the remedies in two weeks, but Google’s legal team will undoubtedly be celebrating today.

Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice in South Africa
- Published
Abraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators.
A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg.
"We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government.
"All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told."
The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted.
Mofokeng is now part of a legal case set to be announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.
At least 69 protesters were shot dead by police on that day in 1960, becoming a pivotal event in the history of the anti-apartheid movement.
Though Sharpeville may be a place name rich in historical resonance, it scarcely looks like a site that symbolises the struggle: the township is slowly crumbling.
The once tarred roads of this area south of Johannesburg are returning to dirt. Many of the houses are still the small, brown-faced brick homes built under the apartheid-era government. The earth is dry and barren - heaps of rubbish are piling up throughout the neighbourhood.
While the legalised system of racism was buried in 1994 when the country held its first democratic election and elected Nelson Mandela as president, its scars remain.
There have been attempts at redress - not least through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) - set up by Mandela's government to investigate crimes committed during the apartheid era.
But the Sharpeville survivors feel they have not seen justice.
Sharpeville's local memorial park, the Human Rights Precinct, tells the story of how the streets of township became the scene of a bloodbath.
Inside the park stand 69 white pillars, one for each life lost.
The victims were killed while demonstrating against the racist pass laws.
At the time, black people were forced to carry a document known as a passbook, known as "dompas" in Afrikaans, which restricted their freedom to move around the country.
A person could be beaten and jailed if found without it - or if found in a "whites-only" area without permission.
Many heeded the call from the leaders of the Pan Africanist Congress in March 1960 to march in protest against the dompas, including then-20-year-old Mofokeng.
"The life we were living under apartheid was a life of oppression. We could not move around freely. We ended up planning to march to the police station against these passbooks that were being used to oppress us," he says.
Thousands turned up to what they thought would be a peaceful protest.
"[The police] had rifles, machetes, even shields. We explained to the police that we didn't want the passes anymore and we were prepared to go to prison. There was a commotion, then all hell broke loose when the police started shooting."
Mofokeng was among the more than 200 people injured and recent estimates by South African researchers have revised upwards the number who died to as many as 91.
Another survivor, Larazus Magotsi - now 90 - walks along the long row of graves in the cemetery where most of those who died are buried. Among them is a headstone marking where a 12-year-old was laid to rest.
Magotsi's eyes are filled with tears as he struggles to compose himself.
"We heard gunshots and ran and hid inside a store, peeping to see what was happening outside," he says.
"People were lying on the ground. When we looked out again, we saw that some were trying to get up, but the police were just shooting at them.
"Others were using machetes to strike the heads of people who were still moving."
It is thought that more than 1,300 bullets were shot into the crowd. Archive photos show policemen walking among the corpses, lying where they fell, in the immediate aftermath of the massacre.
The only legal case that followed the killings was a failed attempt to charge the protesters with affray.
Now, survivors and relatives of those who were killed are hoping to overturn the law they say prevents them from getting justice.
The 1961 Indemnity Act was passed by the apartheid government in the wake of the massacre and protected the police and government from having criminal charges or even civil claims brought against them in relation to what happened at Sharpeville.
Despite more than 30 years of democratic rule, that law remains on the statute books.
But now South African non-governmental organisation Lawyers for Human Rights, together with UK-based law firm Leigh Day, has filed a case at the High Court arguing that the law is unconstitutional under the new constitution that came into effect in 1994.
"Apart from the individual damages, what the community's looking for is basically reparations to enable their healing. They feel as though Sharpeville is a forgotten community," says Charne Tracey, one of the lawyers on the case.
Part of their court application includes getting a class action certified - if approved this would mean that for the first time dozens of victims and relatives of those killed could collectively sue the state. It could also possibly lead to criminal charges being brought against the alleged perpetrators, if any are still alive.
"Nothing has been done that assists with their healing and improvement of their quality of life, or remedy the long-term effects of what they've suffered," Tracey says, adding that 70 people could be involved in the class action.
Constitutional law expert Prof Frans Viljoen believes having the old law repealed is important because it would help to "clean up" the legislation and "close a chapter on the past".
"Although South Africa has a very transformative constitution… The principle of continuity of statehood still applies, which is why the case can be brought against the current state," says Viljoen.
"So if there were laws in our statute book in 1994, the constitution explicitly says they remain in force until parliament repeals them, abolishes them or changes them," he adds.
But he backs attempts to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional "to cleanse us of that past".
The TRC, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was generally praised for bringing together victims and perpetrators who were granted amnesty as long as they, among other conditions, fully disclosed what they had done.
But the greatest criticism of the process was that it did not bring about justice for some as people were not jailed for their acts and no police officers applied for amnesty for the Sharpeville shootings.
The government told the BBC it had supported apartheid victims over the years, and would continue to do so, but did not oppose survivors and families pursuing legal remedies.
When it comes to reparations the justice department said 560 TRC-recognised victims of apartheid-era violence had received individual grants amounting to some $31m (£23m) and though not all Sharpeville survivors and relatives had been identified it encouraged them to come forward.
For many in the community of Sharpeville, there is hope that restitution will help heal decades of lingering trauma.
"Apartheid is dead and buried. A win would bring complete healing, not just for us, but for future generations as well," says Mofokeng.
"Considering how people died, many have not completely healed."

Why Nepal floods should worry India
- Published
Nepal's devastating floods have exposed a risk that does not stop at its borders.
India and Nepal share the rivers that rise in the Himalayas, but the relationship between a flood in Nepal and a disaster in India is more complicated than a simple story of water flowing downstream, say experts.
Some floods can race out of the mountains carrying enormous quantities of mud, rock and debris. Others may lose much of their force as they reach the plains, leaving behind a more conventional flood.
And whether that water becomes a disaster in India depends not only on how much rain has fallen in Nepal, but also on rainfall, river levels, embankments, drainage and development on the Indian side.
Nepal's floods are a warning for India - not simply because water flows south across the border, but because the two countries share a vast and increasingly volatile Himalayan river system.
How many Nepal rivers flow into India?
Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges.
Three major systems dominate: the Kosi in the east, the Gandaki (Gandak in India) in the centre and the Karnali (Ghaghara in India) in the west, with the Mahakali (Sharda) along the western border.
A dozen smaller rivers rising in the Siwaliks and Chure - including the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai - are less famous but can produce faster, more unpredictable floods because their catchments are small and steep.
Seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into the Indian plains, and they are responsible for flooding in India, according to Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).
India's Central Water Commission identifies the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati and Ghaghara as some of the main transboundary rivers.
Which Indian states are most exposed?
Bihar is by far the most exposed Indian state, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone.
Almost all the major rivers that flood the state originate in Nepal, with the Kosi - the "sorrow of Bihar" - the most notorious, followed by the Gandak, Bagmati and Kamala.
But the risk extends beyond Bihar.
Eastern Uttar Pradesh is vulnerable to the Ghaghara, Rapti and Gandak rivers. Districts like Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti are regularly affected.
Uttarakhand state shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers. North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda.
"Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported," says Pradeep Man Dangol, hydrologist at ICIMOD.
Bihar bears the greatest burden, but Uttar Pradesh is a significant and often overlooked part of the risk.
When Nepal floods, what determines India's fate?
Think of it as a three-part chain, say hydrologists.
First, the rain: where it falls and how heavily.
Flood peaks reaching India are often generated not in the high Himalayas but lower down, in the Siwaliks, Chure and Terai, where intense monsoon rain can fall on steep, small catchments.
Second, the river.
Nepal's rivers cross a sharp break in slope at the mountain front, drop their sediment, and spread across the plains as braided, shifting channels.
Third, when the water meets India.
How bad the flooding becomes depends on what the water encounters - the volume of rain on the Indian side, how full the Ganges is, embankments and barrages, and blocked drainage from roads, railways and settlements on the floodplain.
So the peak flow at the border is largely determined by rainfall in Nepal. The severity of flooding depends at least as much on conditions in India.
The 2008 Kosi disaster shows why: the river was carrying far less water than the embankment was designed to handle. The catastrophe was caused by the embankment failing, not by an exceptional flood.
So how much depends on Nepal v India?
"For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal's rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions," says Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD's intervention manager for disaster risk reduction.
How Nepal's rain becomes India's flood risk
The 2008 Kosi disaster is a powerful illustration.
Nearly 400 people died in Bihar after the Kosi breached an embankment in Nepal. But, remarkably, it was not an extraordinary high-flow event on the river.
According to Rajiv Sinha, a professor of earth sciences at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, the flow was only about a tenth of the river's carrying capacity. The catastrophe was caused by a breach in an embankment built decades earlier and inadequately maintained.
"The embankments constructed in the 1950s and 1960s had not been properly maintained. They had become eroded and eventually developed a weak point. The river breached its embankment through these vulnerable points and entered parts of India that had not seen flooding for perhaps 100 years," says Sinha.
The failure, in other words, was "structural, not hydrological", adds Sanyal.
How much warning can India get from Nepal?
For ordinary monsoon floods, India may have "roughly 12 hours to two days of warning", according to Sanyal, depending on how quickly the water travels downstream.
Water can take about a day to reach the Bihar plains from the Nepal mountain front along the Kosi and Gandak, and somewhat longer along the Ghaghara.
Flash floods from the Chure rivers can arrive within hours.
A landslide-dam burst or debris flow can be even faster - in the current floods, the peak surge from Rasuwa reached Triveni, near the Indian border, in about seven-and-a-half hours.
India and Nepal do share real-time rainfall and river-level data from a network of stations. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology feeds rainfall and river levels to India's Central Water Commission, which uses them for flood forecasts.
But important gaps remain, says Sanyal.
They include too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing Chure catchments. There's also no single shared forecasting model between the two countries; and limited routine sharing on embankment conditions, river-channel changes and sediment.
And then there's, crucially, the last mile.
A warning reaching a district office is not the same as reaching a family in danger.
For these transboundary rivers, Sinha says, "cooperation on information sharing and early-warning systems is extremely important. We need rapid continuous monitoring of glacial lakes, their outflows and how they are changing over time".
What is the biggest misconception around Nepal and floods in India?
A common misconception is that Nepal "releases" water into India, say scientists.
Nepal has almost no large reservoirs capable of doing this: its main storage dam, Kulekhani, holds less than a tenth of a cubic kilometre, "so there's nothing to release", says Sanyal.
The Kosi and Gandak barrages are operated by India. When floodwater reaches the border, it is overwhelmingly because rain has fallen upstream - not because Nepal has opened a gate.
But there is an important truth behind the claim: much of the water that floods north Bihar and eastern UP has fallen as rain in Nepal, so Nepal's rainfall largely determines the timing and size of flood peaks reaching India.
Nepal supplies around 40% of the average annual flow of the Ganges - and a much larger share in the dry season - making its hydrology critical to India.
"What is too simplistic is treating that as a story of cause and blame. Rain is not a decision," says Sanyal.
Whether a given flow becomes a disaster depends on conditions in India as much as in Nepal the Ganges' level, Indian rainfall, embankment integrity, drainage and sediment.
"And the effects run both ways: embankments and barrages built for India's protection have raised water levels and caused backwater flooding in Nepal's Terai, which is Nepal's long-standing concern,' says Sanyal.
Nepal and India share one river system, with one country upstream and the other downstream.
The answer is therefore not blame, but better shared data, forecasting and river management.
So what should worry India the most?
"India should be worried. but not necessarily because of the Kosi river in Nepal," says Rajiv Sinha.
In other words, experts say, the real warning is about what is happening in the Himalayas - and what happens when water, rock, ice and enormous quantities of sediment suddenly combine.
Sinha says the latest Nepal disaster resembles a series of catastrophic events that India has experienced in recent years, including the 2021 Chamoli disaster and the 2025 Dharali disaster in Uttarakhand. The Nepal event, he says, was "perhaps five to 10 times larger".
"The fundamental point is that these are not normal hydrological floods," Sinha says.
A conventional flood is largely water. But when water from intense rain, melting ice or a sudden discharge mixes with huge quantities of sediment, the result can become a thick, high-energy slurry capable of destroying almost everything in its path.
That was the lesson of the Chamoli disaster in 2021, when a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people and damaged hydropower infrastructure.
It was also evident at Dharali in Uttarakhand in 2025, after heavy rains triggered a flash flood and the flow of debris buried parts of a village under metres of material.
And then there's climate change.
Extreme rainfall is intensifying: the region is warming faster than the global average, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, and the monsoon is delivering more rain in fewer, heavier bursts, say experts.
High-mountain hazards are also growing. As permafrost degrades, glacial lake outbursts and rock-ice avalanches are expected to increase, producing faster, debris-laden floods that are harder to forecast.
And more extreme events mean more landslides and sediment in rivers, raising riverbeds and reducing channel capacity on both sides of the border.
They are manifestations of the same broad Himalayan hazard system. And India's exposure is considerable.

Jailed HK activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to foreign collusion
- Published
Prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy campaigner Joshua Wong has pleaded guilty to collusion with foreign entities, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison under Beijing's sweeping National Security Law (NSL).
The 29-year-old, who has become the poster child for political activism in Hong Kong, is already serving a sentence of four years and eight months after being convicted of subversion – another NSL violation – in late 2024.
The court said Wong would be sentenced at a later date. His earlier jail term is due to end early next year.
Wong was at the forefront of the Umbrella Movement in 2014 and massive pro-democracy protests in 2019.
The latest charge accuses Wong of conspiring with other campaigners, including exiled activist Nathan Law, to ask foreign countries and entities outside China to impose sanctions or blockades against Beijing.
These include activities that took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard. That was the year China introduced the controversial NSL, which critics say has created a climate of fear and quashed dissent in Hong Kong.
Beijing and Hong Kong authorities argue the law is necessary to maintain stability and deny it has weakened autonomy.
On Tuesday, the court heard that Wong and Law had participated in "international lobbying on numerous occasions", including via visits to the US, Germany and Italy.
The duo are among several leaders who founded the pro-democracy party Demosistō in April 2016, and ran for the Hong Kong Legislative Council elections that year.
Among other things, prosecutors on Tuesday also accused Wong, along with Law, of promoting the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act: a US federal law that came into force in November 2019, during Donald Trump's first administration. The Act compels the US government to impose sanctions against mainland China and Hong Kong officials if they are deemed responsible for human rights abuses in Hong Kong.
Even after Demosistō disbanded, Wong had maintained that he would not abandon his political stance and would continue to seek support from the international community, the prosecutors said.
Wong, dressed in a dark blue shirt and dark-rimmed glasses, did not dispute these allegations.
About 40 of Wong's supporters, including fellow activists and some of his close friends, gathered in court on Tuesday. Some shouted: "Hang in there, Joshua!"
Wong was seen smiling and nodding in response from the dock.
Tsang Kin-shing, a former member of the now-dissolved League of Social Democrats, said he hopes the court will impose a lenient sentence, noting that Wong has by now spent more than 2,000 days in prison.
Fellow activist Louis Lee said Wong and his supporters were disheartened that he was handed another NSL charge while already serving time in prison.
Wong has continued seeking out new interests while in prison, including learning how to play the guitar and working out.
"I hope everyone can learn from him," Lee says.

Opening summary: race to rescue tunnel workers
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the aftermath of the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Rescuers in Nepal and China are still trying to locate thousands of people who are missing days after a wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region.
The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to at least 750 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepali officials confirmed 734 dead and 2,498 people missing. There were reports of some dead swept downstream as far away as India.
China said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing on the Tibetan side of a border crossing with Nepal: the highest number was from Nepal at 104, while 49 Indian, 33 Latvian, 18 American and 15 British citizens were also unaccounted for.
In a breakthrough late on Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.
“We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” said the home minister, Sudan Gurungd. More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.
Here’s the other main developments:
- 
  Four days after the disaster, authorities said some bodies being recovered had decomposed beyond recognition. They would be buried after legal formalities because of health risks and a fear of disease outbreaks. “DNA samples will be collected, and the bodies will be buried in an open space,” the Chitwan district administration said in a notice.
- 
  The foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said Nepal required specialist assistance to rescue people trapped in tunnels; restore transport and communication lines where bridges had been destroyed; identify bodies; conduct DNA testing; and store bodies for longer periods.
- 
  A team of Indian tunnel experts arrived in Nepal on Saturday, Khanal said. China’s Xinhua news agency reported Beijing had dispatched five tunnel experts to support rescue efforts, with four more due to join them.
- 
  The US will provide $3.6m in humanitarian aid to Nepal, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households,” the state department said in a post on X.

The Guard That Won’t Be Changing
Massachusetts Democrats chose progressivism over relative youth.
Many Democrats of a certain age took the same message from the party’s 2024 debacle: Voters are sick of the old guard and craving younger, more aggressive leaders. Better to retire on your own terms than suffer the fate of Joe Biden, forced to stand down from his reelection campaign after a public humiliation. Nancy Pelosi, the 86-year-old former speaker, announced her exit from the House, as did her longtime lieutenant, 87-year-old Steny Hoyer. Senators Dick Durbin (81) and Jeanne Shaheen (79) passed up reelection bids this year, and so, too, did two senators merely in their late 60s.
Senator Ed Markey, 80, heeded no such warning, and evidently, he didn’t need to. The Massachusetts Democrat is one of just two current senators whose tenures in Congress date to the presidency of Gerald Ford. But tonight, the oldest Democratic senator on the ballot this year trounced his much younger primary opponent, Representative Seth Moulton. The AP called the race a half hour after polls closed, with Markey leading by nearly 50 points.
In a race that pitted ideology against age, Massachusetts Democrats opted for a progressive stalwart who will be 86 at the end of another six-year term over a more moderate 47-year-old challenger. Moulton, an Iraq War veteran who is concluding his sixth term in the House, moved left to appeal to a statewide primary electorate. But he could not hope to outflank Markey, who won support from Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Instead, Moulton urged voters to embrace “a new generation of leadership” and argued that he could more effectively fight for liberal causes than an incumbent in the twilight of his career.
Markey had already faced that kind of challenge before, and won. Six years ago, he handily defeated then-Representative Joe Kennedy III, a grandson of Robert F. Kennedy who contended that the incumbent, after so many decades in office, was no longer up to the task. Young progressives, unimpressed with what remained of the Kennedy aura and appreciative of Markey’s record championing the Green New Deal, rallied to Markey’s side. But that race preceded Biden’s flameout in 2024 and the reckoning over the Democratic Party’s gerontocracy.
Some Massachusetts Democrats believed that Markey could be newly vulnerable, especially if a popular progressive such as Representative Ayanna Pressley, who is 52, decided to challenge him. Mary Anne Marsh, a longtime Democratic strategist in the state, told me that after seeing the reception Pressley received at a party convention last year, she became convinced that “if Ayanna runs, she wins.” But Pressley opted to run for reelection to the House, leaving Moulton to challenge Markey.
Moulton has never lacked ambition—he led a failed bid to oust Pelosi as party leader in 2018 and waged a short-lived presidential campaign the following year—but he’s neither as progressive as Pressley nor as well liked. He built a reputation as a moderate in the House Democratic caucus, and after President Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024, Moulton angered many on the left by accusing his party of being “afraid” to say that transgender athletes should not play women’s sports. He has since offered a partial apology to the transgender community, but the line became fodder for Markey, who said that he’d thrown “trans kids under the bus.” The issue was emblematic of Moulton’s struggle to convince progressives in Massachusetts that he shared their values. “He’s tried to become a progressive, but he does it by defining progressive in a way that nobody believes,” Marsh said. “He tried to become something that he’s not.”
The Massachusetts race was a rare Democratic primary this year in which U.S. policy toward Israel did not become a flash point, as both candidates criticized Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and opposed new military aid to Israel. (Moulton announced last year that he would return donations from AIPAC.)
Both public polling and Markey’s internal surveys showed a closer race until earlier this summer, when the incumbent began to pull away. A Markey adviser told me that voters had not really tuned in to the campaign yet, and media attention was focused on higher-profile Democratic primaries elsewhere. Markey’s age also did not become a big factor, perhaps because the years since 2020 have been kinder to him than they were to Biden. His support reflected a frequently overlooked nuance in the debate over whether the party needs new leadership: Older progressive leaders, particularly the 84-year-old Sanders, remain popular. “There’s a difference between being old and being part of the old guard,” the Markey adviser, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said. “Younger voters love Ed Markey, younger voters love Bernie Sanders, younger voters love Elizabeth Warren, and I think that has a lot to do with the fact that they take younger voters seriously.”
Moulton tried to align Markey with a Democratic establishment that he said has failed to deliver progressive wins. He frequently invoked the name of Senator Chuck Schumer, vowing to oppose the New Yorker if he seeks to remain the Democratic leader. And Moulton even accused Markey of having ties to the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, an attack that, according to Marsh, backfired so badly that it might have sealed Moulton’s defeat. (Markey denied any affiliation with Epstein.)
In the end, Massachusetts Democrats preferred Markey’s progressivism over Moulton’s relative youth. Markey might have been helped by the fact that the stakes in this primary were not as high as they were elsewhere this year—and certainly much lower than when the party pushed Biden to withdraw in 2024. Massachusetts is not in danger of going Republican in November. Democratic voters wanted a trusted fighter to wage battle against Trump for the next two years and—they hope—for transformative progressive policies in the four years after that. They didn’t seem to care much that the fighter they chose happens to be 80 years old.

A rumor that the CEO of a popular chain of convenience stores in the southern United States said the the company would no longer pursue locations in so-called "blue states" circulated online in August 2026.
Users on Facebook and a popular thread on Reddit suggested Buc-ee's CEO Arch "Beaver" Aplin III said the company was focused on building in "conservative, business-friendly states."
The quote was correctly attributed to Aplin.
The Buc-ee's CEO said it during public remarks on Aug. 17, celebrating the opening of a Buc-ees location in Benton, Arkansas, after being introduced by Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
Aplin's full remarks are viewable on YouTube.
The quote in question began at the 2:11 mark, when Aplin revealed Sanders had asked him to build a Buc-ee's in Arkansas. He said:
We're building in a lot of places but when you find a conservative, business-friendly state with a phenomenal workforce, it makes a difference. And I'm starting to realize life's too short to try and build in places that people don't appreciate what you're bringing. Versus a place like this, where people do appreciate what you're building.
So that leadership, that concept, that idea of conservative, business-friendly, family-oriented concept, works so much better if it trickles down from the very leadership from the very top at the governor's office.
A Buc-ee's news release said the Benton location was the company's 58th store and would create more than 200 jobs for the community. Buc-ee's was founded in 1982 and operates primarily in the South.
Local media covered the store opening, including NBC affiliate KARK, CBS affiliate KTHV and the Arkansas Democrat Gazette. The local reports didn't mention Aplin's specific comments nor did they report anything about the chain avoiding blue states.
On Aug. 18, Sanders posted a clip of Aplin's remarks to her Facebook page and wrote, "That's why red states like Arkansas are surging and people and businesses are fleeing blue states."
Later reporting from The Comeback and Fox Business homed in on Aplin's comments, as well as Sanders' takeaway that the chain intended to stop pursuing locations in so-called blue states. It was these reports that started circulating wider online and got increased media pickup, resulting in the claim gaining popularity.
While we found this to be a reasonable interpretation of Aplin's comments, it's crucial to note that Aplin himself didn't explicitly say the company would be "avoiding blue states" during his remarks on Aug. 17. We reached out to Buc-ee's for clarification on the company's plan's for development in red vs. blue states and will update this article if we hear back.

Russia to close German culture centres after Moscow blamed for airport drone plot
A drone laden with explosives was found near a Ukrainian plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport
Russia has said it will close German cultural spots across the country in response to being blamed for an attempted attack on an airport.
Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov announced the move on Thursday after Berlin blamed Moscow for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month. He announced the closure of both the Russian Consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in the German capital.
Lavrov said that cultural centers belonging to Germany's Goethe-Institut would be closed in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg, adding that any other response would show a lack of "self-respect" on Russia's part.
Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Lavrov said that Germany "could not have failed to understand" that the closure of Russian House would "signify the end of their cultural presence in Russia."
A drone laden with explosives was found near a Ukrainian plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 and later defused. The airport is a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine.
Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations.
Putin has dismissed the allegations, saying Berlin wants to distract from its own failings and dissatisfaction among voters. Any proof being offered "has been planted," Putin said.
European Union ministers on Wednesday weighed how best to respond to the attempted drone attack but struggled to find new ways to meet the challenge without resorting to military means.
"It is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism. The question is: what do we do about this," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters before chairing a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Ireland. They discussed sanctions, visa restrictions and shutting Russian consulates, among other measures.
The EU has slapped almost two dozen packages of sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine, hitting more than 3,000 officials, oligarchs and entities including banks, energy companies and drone makers. The EU was already preparing to impose more travel bans and asset freezes on another 1,600 people, Kallas said.
Germany insisted it was "not at war" but had become a "daily target" of the Kremlin's hybrid campaign. Putin dismissed the allegations, saying Berlin wants to distract from its own failings and dissatisfaction among voters. Any proof being offered "has been planted," Putin said.
But German Foreign Minister Johan Wadephul said Berlin had carefully prepared its response "and now Russia must live with these consequences." He called on Russia "to show that it is also ready for reasonable talks and negotiations, particularly regarding the situation in Ukraine."

Bulgarian filmmaker Theodore Ushev, Oscar-nominated in the animated short film category in 2017 for “Blind Vaysha,” is in pre-production on feature film “Light Boxes,” which he will present at the Venice Production Bridge’s Gap-Financing Market, running Sept. 4-6.
The film, which will include stop-motion animation and live-action sequences, is an adaptation of Shane Jones’ cult novel exploring the tension between escaping war through imagination and confronting its reality.
Set in a war-torn Ukrainian town, the story follows Anna, a 13-year-old girl who, despite restrictions imposed by Russian occupying forces, ventures into a ruined library and rescues a burning book titled “Light Boxes.”
Popular on Variety
Seeking refuge from constant bombardment, Anna discovers Bianca, her imaginary double, living in a fantastical town imprisoned by a war of its own. There, the tyrannical February has condemned its inhabitants to eternal winter and forbids them from flying, while a masked resistance movement known as The Solution fights to restore light and freedom.
With neither reality nor imagination offering an escape from tyranny, the film asks whether hope, memory and love can persevere when war threatens to extinguish them all.
For Ushev, survival lies in imitation. “The characters are constantly trying to reproduce what they have lost to convince themselves it can somehow return,” he tells Variety. “That is what I find fascinating about every totalitarian regime – no matter how oppressed people become, they will always find ways to recreate what has been taken from them, to keep hope alive.”
Until “Light Boxes,” the director had never wanted to make an animated feature, believing a project of such scale would “risk the individual touch, the imperfection” that defined his work. That changed in 2010, when, while presenting his short “Lipsett Diaries” in Toronto, he stumbled upon Jones’ novel. “As soon as I read ‘Light Boxes,’ I immediately imagined how I would recreate it with puppets,” he recalls.
Producer Jacqueline Wagenstein, founder of lead production company Cinelibri, acquired the adaptation rights, previously held by American filmmaker Spike Jonze, and set the fable up as a five-country co-production between Bulgaria, Canada, France, Belgium and Poland. The project is to become the largest Bulgarian-led animated feature production to date.
Visually, “Light Boxes” will distinguish its two worlds through different media: Anna’s reality will unfold in live action with a predominantly Ukrainian cast, while Bianca’s world will be rendered in stop-motion using puppets designed and crafted by Ushev. “Bianca’s world will be the main one,” he explains. “For me, the puppet animation is at the heart of the film.”
Symbols are at the story’s core. With natural light extinguished, its inhabitants recreate it through floating lights, drifting dandelions and artificial suns – man-made substitutes for the warmth and hope their world no longer provides. “Lighting will play a very important role in how we shoot the film, but also in the sets themselves. The materials used to build them will include fabrics recycled from parachutes, kites and other objects designed to fly,” comments the director.
That symbolism extends to February’s ban on flight, which Ushev sees as stripping people of their capacity to dream. “When you fly, you dream,” he says. “And the first thing every tyrant does is take away people’s dreams – their hope that things can change.”
The film acts as a reminder that preserving the light requires more than hoping it will endure. “The present is crucial to what happens in our future,” he says. “If we don’t act now and change things, then the future will also exist in the dark.”
