- "Technoblade Never Dies" is a feature documentary now entering production.
- Riot Games and Hypixel Studios are financing it and donating their profits to charity.
- The film has no release date yet and is targeting a major festival before theatrical distribution.
Technoblade’s legacy is officially heading to the big screen as a feature-length documentary titled “Technoblade Never Dies” is now in production.
The documentary is made with the full cooperation of his family and is financially backed by Riot Games and Hypixel Studios. Both Minecraft Hypixel and Riot Games have committed to donating their profits from the film to charity.
Directed by documentary filmmaker Steven Lake and produced by Candle True Stories, the film will explore the life of one of the best Minecraft players of all time. The project is made with full cooperation from Technoblade’s family and friends, along with hundreds of hours of his existing stories from the members of his worldwide community.
The Minecraft Technoblade documentary will examine the creator’s rise from a California teenager making Minecraft videos to a global gaming icon. It will also explore the personality, comedy, and extraordinary skills that made him one of the platform’s biggest stars.
The film has only just entered production, so there is currently no confirmed release date. The producers are targeting a premiere of the film at a major film festival, followed by a wider distribution. However, a distribution agreement has not yet been announced.
Lake says that the documentary will explore the lasting impact of Technoblade and how his famous catchphrase, “Technoblade Never Dies,” is always remembered by the community.
It will also revisit his battle with cancer, which Technoblade disclosed in 2021, while continuing to create content and interact with the community. He had also reached his goal of 10 million YouTube subscribers late that year, only months before his death.
The community became particularly important after Technoblade died in June 2022 at just the age of 23. His father also delivered his final message, “so long nerds”, while publicly revealing Technoblade’s real name, Alex.
The Minecraft documentary on Technoblade will also focus on how 400,000 fan messages were gathered through a virtual memorial. His influence still remains visible throughout gaming culture, as A Minecraft Movie also gave him a tribute with his famous crowned-pig character.

Following the devasting flash floods in Nepal on August 26, which claimed over 1,200 lives and caused massive destruction, a video has gone viral on social media, purporting to show the Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) phenomenon. It displays footage from a search helicopter, ostensibly showing the breach of a glacial lake in China. Users on social media have widely shared the clip, claiming that this was the immediate trigger to the Nepal floods.
X user Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) posted the clip on August 27, with the hashtag #NepalFloods. At the time of this article being written, the post garnered 2 million views, and was reshared close to 2,000 times. (Archive)
A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood #GLOF can happen when a glacier-dammed lake suddenly breaches. 🌊🧊
Pressure and fractures create a pathway for the trapped water to escape, sending a massive surge of water and debris downhill at terrifying speed#GlacialFlood #NepalFloods #Nepal pic.twitter.com/0zrw0SIEqO
— Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) August 26, 2026
Also Read: Nepal floods: Unrelated videos of past disasters, AI visuals falsely viral
A journalist with Dainik Bhaskar, Ashish Rai (@journorai) also posted the clip on X, which received 2 million views and close to 4,000 reshares. (Archive)
Several other X users, like former MLA Rajpal Singh Sekhawat (@Rajpal_BJP), Dr. Kiran J Patel (@kiranpatel1977), Pradhyumn Sharma (@pradhyu78651514), AH Siddiqui (@anwar0262) and (@greatandhranews) posted the clip with the same claim. (Archives: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
Fact Check
To check whether the claims surrounding this viral clip are authentic, we broke it down into keyframes, then ran reverse image searches on the keyframes. This led us to an Instagram reel, uploaded by an user with the handle (@helipilotleigh), on August 22. It contains the exact same footage as the viral clip.
View this post on Instagram
In the caption, the user, whose name is Leigh Coates, explains what a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, or GLOF is, and mentions that the video shows one happening over the Columbia Glacier in Alaska.
The description on her YouTube channel states that she is a helicopter pilot based in the United States, who specialises in ferry flights and advanced training for mountain flying, as well as airport landings.
We noticed that she had uploaded similar videos of glacial outbursts on her Instagram profile, and her YouTube channel.
In conclusion, the video that went viral recently in the context of the Nepal flash flood, showing a glacial outburst — purportedly in China — is actually from the Columbia Glacier in Alaska. It was uploaded by a helicopter pilot named Leigh Coates on her Instagram handle, a few days before the flash flood in Nepal. Thus, the claim that the phenomenon shown in this video was a direct trigger for the August 26 Nepal floods is false and misleading.

Jaguar Land Rover was one of the first automakers to announce a transition away from combustion engines. That transition timeline might have slipped somewhat—pesky things like pandemics, supply chains, and revanchism have all been barriers to more rapid electrification—but it’s still underway, and today is the debut of the Range Rover Electric, a new battery-electric vehicle variant that sits alongside the internal combustion and plug-in hybrid Range Rovers.
Until now, the only way to get a fully electric Range Rover was by going the restomod route. But classic Range Rovers drive like classic cars, with all their inherent faults, and the price tag can be eye-watering. No Range Rover is exactly cheap, but with a starting price of $138,000, the 2027 Range Rover Electric is about half the cost of one of those restomods and benefits from 21st century safety systems like airbags, advanced driver assistance systems, modern crash protection standards, plus the support and warranty of a major OEM. And there’s evidently demand: JLR told us that it already has 80,000 hand-raisers—half from North America—70 percent of whom are new to the brand, with 20 percent already owning an EV. (Obviously, only some fraction of those will translate to sales.)
Because the idea was to make the Range Rover Electric a Range Rover first and an EV second, it looks virtually identical to the other versions, albeit with a slightly more aerodynamic front grille and more aero-efficient wheels that together conspire to shave off a fraction of the vehicle’s drag coefficient. The lack of tailpipes at the back is probably the biggest giveaway that you’re looking at the electric one. There’s also a flat underbody, but hopefully you’ll never need to look at that.
The powertrain
The current Range Rover uses JLR’s MLA architecture, which was designed over a decade ago to be powertrain agnostic. The BEV actually only weighs 165 lbs (75 kg) more than the V8; getting rid of the front, center, and rear differentials plus all their driveshafts saves almost as much weight as the battery and drive units add back. The front and rear drive units are identical permanent-magnet synchronous motors with an output of 349 hp (260 kW); a front-induction motor was considered but dropped due to heat management concerns. Combined output is 542 hp (404 kW) and 627 lb-ft (850 Nm).

Professional organizations representing pediatricians, family physicians, obstetricians, and other medical professionals jointly released guidelines Wednesday for who should get vaccines aimed at staving off influenza, Covid-19, and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, this coming winter.
The combined effort, undertaken in conjunction with the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project, has two goals: to help medical professionals guide their patients, and to help individuals plan to get the vaccinations that should help them either evade these ailments, or minimize their risks of severe illness if they do become infected.
In previous times these organizations liaised with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to jointly issue such guidance. But that collaborative process has broken down following the dismantlement of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices — an expert panel fired in June 2025 by long-time vaccine critic and health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — and its replacement largely with vaccine skeptics.
A court challenge of that restructuring has left the ACIP and the recommendations the new version of it made in legal limbo.
The professional groups have each reviewed the evidence for use of the seasonal respiratory vaccines, with the help of the Vaccine Integrity Project, which works under UMN’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy, or CIDRAP. The renewed recommendations largely hew to previous ones from before the upheaval that has resulted in the second Trump administration.
A small but notable change has been made by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, which has extended the period during which pregnant people can be given an RSV vaccine to help protect their infants in their first RSV season.
Previously the vaccine was recommended for pregnant people during the period from Sept. 1 of a given year to Jan. 31 of the following year, with the vaccination recommended for late in the pregnancy. But Christina Davidson, ACOG’s chief medical officer, said given that recent RSV seasons have started later and run longer than what was previously seen, the period during which pregnant people can get the RSV vaccine has been extended to March 1.
The RSV shot for adults — pregnant and otherwise — remains, however, a once-only vaccine, because it is still not clear when or how often adults who have received the vaccine should be boosted. So pregnant people can get the vaccine in only a single pregnancy. In future pregnancies, their babies will be recommended to receive RSV monoclonal antibodies if they are 8 months of age or younger going into their first RSV season.
According to the American Academy of Pediatrics recommendations, all babies 8 months and younger going into their first RSV season born to mothers who did not receive RSV vaccine during pregnancy, or whose vaccination status is unclear, should receive monoclonal antibodies to protect against the virus, as should children going into their second RSV season who are at high risk of serious illness if they were to contract it.
The various medical groups stressed the need for patients of their members to receive flu, Covid, and RSV vaccines if recommended, and to get them at the appropriate time. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, noted for instance that because the effect of flu vaccination can wane over the course of the season, the best time to get an influenza shot would be in October, which is typically closer to the start of the season.
Bruce Gellin, from the Vaccine Integrity Project’s board of advisers, stressed that despite the upheaval in vaccination policy under the current administration, doctors still need clear and simple guidance to offer their patients, and patients need that information to make their fall vaccination choices.
“Americans should have access to the best available scientific evidence and recommendations from the physicians and medical experts who care for them, so they can make informed decisions about vaccination,” he said during a joint press conference the groups held on Tuesday. “Whatever happens to the federal vaccine policy process, we cannot lower that scientific standard.”
Papers outlining the rationale for the various vaccination recommendations were published Wednesday in the Journal of the American Medical Association, and an interactive tool to help doctors and the public review the science behind the decisions will be posted on the Vaccine Integrity Project’s website.

Saint John police apologize after woman told to cover up at beach
Letter from acting chief says there was no legal basis for telling Lacey Tompkins to cover up at beach
A Saint John woman who was told by police to cover up while topless at a city beach this summer has received a formal apology from the Saint John Police Force.
Lacey Tompkins was at Dominion Park Beach on July 25 when she took off her bikini top while sunbathing. She said a lifeguard approached her and told her to cover up.
When she declined, a police officer also told her she needed to alter her attire.
Tompkins said she was surprised by the request because she understood that women can be topless in public in Canada.
“I was a little shocked and a little bit confused,” she said.
Tompkins eventually complied with the officer’s request but later filed a service complaint with the New Brunswick Police Commission on July 27.
In an Aug. 11 letter to Tompkins, Neal Fowler, the acting chief of the Saint John Police Force, said the incident was reviewed.
The review included police records, a call to police for service, and body-worn camera footage from responding officers.
“Based on the available evidence, it was determined there was no legal basis requiring you to alter your attire,” Fowler wrote. “In these circumstances, the direction provided to you was not supported by the applicable law.”
Police said officers had been called to the beach following concerns raised by lifeguards. An officer then approached Tompkins and advised her that she was required to alter her attire.
According to the review, Tompkins questioned the basis for the direction and remained respectful throughout the interaction. No enforcement action was taken, although she complied with the officer’s request.
The police force said the incident identified a need for additional education about the applicable law and relevant case law.
The responding officer received immediate guidance from a supervisor. Frontline members and supervisors also received further education about Criminal Code provisions relating to indecent acts.
Fowler acknowledged that being directed by police to do something Tompkins believed she was not legally required to do would be concerning.
“As a police organization, we have a responsibility to ensure our members are properly informed, trained, and equipped to apply the law appropriately and consistently when responding to calls for service,” Fowler wrote.
“Please accept my apology on behalf of the Saint John Police Force for the interaction and the concern it caused.”
Tompkins said she welcomed the response.
“I think it’s a really good thing,” she said. “It just shines a light on people being aware of what they are permitted and not permitted to do.”
What does the law say?
The legal question goes back to a 1996 decision by the Ontario Court of Appeal. The court considered whether then-student Gwen Jacob's removal of her shirt while walking on a Guelph street in sweltering weather had constituted an indecent act under the Criminal Code.
The court found that toplessness, on its own, does not make a woman’s conduct an indecent act. The circumstances of the conduct are relevant, including whether it is sexual in nature.
Howard Sapers, executive director of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, told CBC News earlier this summer that municipalities cannot change how the Criminal Code is interpreted.
“The simple answer is no. A municipal bylaw can’t alter the way the Criminal Code is interpreted,” Sapers said.
For Tompkins, the issue is also about equality and the different standards applied to men’s and women’s bodies.
“We tend to lean towards sexualizing women’s bodies,” she said. “We are not applying the same standard to everyone.”
Tompkins has since returned to Dominion Park Beach and continues to go topless.
“Nothing happened,” she said. “I was there and I sunbathed and then I was left alone.”
She said she hopes other women will be able to exercise the same right without having to go through a similar experience.

Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
- Published
A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran.
Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates.
It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade.
"Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity."
That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north.
Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea. This is focused on a dispute with Saudi Arabia but heightens insecurity for international shipping.
"I guess the pirates believe that with those two external events in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, they believe that the international forces will be dedicated to those crises instead of looking for pirates," says Vice-Admiral Ignacio Villanueva Serrano, operation commander for the European Union's naval force that protects shipping off Somalia's coast.
Among the latest vessels hijacked by the pirates was a Cameroon-flagged ship, the MV Lutuf, which was attacked off the coast of Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region on 17 August. A few days later pirates boarded an oil products tanker, the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1, in waters near Yemen, on the other side of the Gulf.
The capture of the Lutuf has triggered unexpected consequences.
Thirteen men allegedly belonging to a network that supplies the pirates on the ship have been killed in two drone strikes since 18 August. No one has said they are behind the attacks, but local officials blamed them on Turkey, saying the vessel was carrying Turkish weapons.
The Lutuf is now among six vessels being held for demands of millions of dollars in ransom, four of which are anchored near the fishing town of Bander Beyla known as a hotbed for piracy, the BBC has learned.
That is nowhere near the peak levels of hijackings 15 years ago that cost the global economy billions of dollars. In 2011 Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks and held hundreds of crew members hostage.
A co-ordinated international naval response together with private security on commercial ships successfully drove down the scourge and contained a flare-up in 2023 and 2024.
But experts stress that while the pirate networks were suppressed, they remained intact, given the failure to address the poor economic and security conditions in Somalia that feed them.
Currently the resurgence is fuelled locally by anger over foreign trawlers which overfish in Somali waters, damaging the fishing industry that sustains communities in Puntland.
And there are more targets available now with a potentially bigger payload.
The regional maritime insecurity has driven some ships closer to the Somali coast as they divert south to avoid the conflict further north. Given the high price of oil, hijacking a tanker is more lucrative.
"You have that combined effect of less naval patrolling but more commercial shipping in these waters," according to the analyst Mahmood, "and that signals an opportunity.
"And once you've had a successful attack, I think that spurs other units to do copycat type incidents as well."
He and other researchers suspect there may be collaboration between the Somali pirates and Yemenis after several vessels were seized near Yemen's coast.
But Mahmood says these would more likely be criminal elements than Iran's Houthi allies, especially as one of the ships seized last week, the MT Sibu 1, allegedly belonged to an Iranian "shadow fleet" used to transport petroleum products trying to dodge US sanctions.
"I don't see something specifically Iran-directed," he says.
Turkey, however, reportedly has a stake in the latest hijackings.
Puntland security sources and a Somali government official have told the BBC that the Lutuf was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. Ankara has an agreement with Somalia to strengthen its maritime security, as part of a wider defence and economic partnership.
The security sources say six international warships are now in the seas close to the Lutuf - two from Turkey and one each from Spain, Denmark, the US and India, something the BBC has not been able to independently verify.
"There is military equipment on the [hijacked] ship meant for Turkey's operations in Somalia," the Somali government official said, speaking on condition of anonymity, adding that the cargo included satellite equipment for a space station that Ankara is building north of the capital.
He alleged that Turkey had carried out the second drone strike that killed nine armed men on Sunday.
"The men who were killed were criminals and I don't have sympathy for them," he said, "but taking it to that level is escalating the situation even more."
Turkey's defence ministry has stated that its forces are providing "necessary support" to Somali authorities regarding the incident involving a hijacked vessel in Somali territorial waters, within the framework of their security agreement. But it stopped short of addressing the accusations that Turkey had carried out deadly drone strikes.
Publicly the government in Mogadishu has said only that it is aware of the operations against pirate groups and will take measures to address them.
Puntland authorities have been more outspoken.
Speaking to the BBC's Somali Service, Deputy Minister of Security Abdirahman Yusuf said his administration had evidence that Turkey was responsible for the attacks, citing information about Turkish activity around the vessel and along the Puntland coast.
The BBC has not independently verified his allegations.
The security ministry also issued a statement expressing opposition to "bombings by international warships targeting civilians" that "undermined co-operation… in combatting piracy", and demanded an immediate explanation for why they were carried out.
Puntland is wary of Turkey's close military relationship with the Somali government, and the incidents risk further complicating a long-standing political dispute between the semi-autonomous region and Mogadishu that hinders a co-ordinated effort to fight piracy, analysts say.
There is not yet a full-blown resurgence. But without an end to the US-Iran war, or increased international efforts at deterrence, Somali piracy stands to continue raising the threat level in a crucial maritime space that is already dangerously squeezed.

'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis
- Published
"If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you."
The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back.
"They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service.
It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom.
Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people."
About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima.
She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.
Fatima is one of an estimated 800,000 Nigerians who the UN says have been displaced in the country's north-west. One of the main reasons people have left their homes is violence.
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by gangs, locally referred to as bandits, who often move around on motorcycles and attack quickly then ride away, escaping before security forces arrive.
Thousands of people have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fight, and the BBC spoke to one who said his armed group had killed many bandits.
But the gangs keep attacking in what appears to be a deteriorating pattern of violence and abductions that is spreading southwards.
Fatima says when the bandits attacked her home, she ran into the nearby forest with other villagers to hide: "The forest became our sanctuary. We ran with our kids, if you couldn't find your child you'd take your neighbour's child."
She says people slept in the forest before moving on to the state capital, Gusau, "where we found a little bit of peace".
Fatima now lives in an informal camp in Gusau with her seven children, who are aged between nine and 30.
Dozens of women sit in groups on the dusty ground of the makeshift compound, many wearing brightly coloured hijabs. More than 1,000 people are here, she believes.
Conditions are tough with "no proper place to even lay your head". Food is scarce and assistance arrives irregularly.
Fatima describes two occasions where "good Samaritans" brought rice or potatoes. Children are sent out to gather firewood to sell so families can buy food, but 22 have been kidnapped by bandits, she says.
Gesturing towards a nearby building, Fatima says that there "you will find 100 or more women… maybe just two or three have had breakfast.
"When we had peace, we had our own wealth, but now the tables have turned and we have become beggars."
Her eyes fill with tears and she cries for a few minutes, wiping her face with her hands.
Despite being 16 miles (25km) from her village, the threat Fatima fled has not disappeared.
When she first arrived at the camp, the sound of gunshots kept her awake at night. Things have since quietened, she says, crediting patrols by the army and government-backed vigilantes, but the atmosphere is still tense.
The bandits are mostly people from the Fulani ethnic group, who traditionally make their living by raising animals. Some of them have swapped cattle trading for kidnapping and extortion, which is seen as a faster, easier way to make money.
They attack towns and villages or ambush travellers, abducting people for ransom, stealing whatever they want - and sometimes killing those who resist. They also force communities to pay protection money, only allowing farmers into their fields if they hand over large sums of cash.
Attacks are now more frequent than ever. In the bandit heartlands of north-west Nigeria, the number of incidents recorded by the international conflict monitoring group Acled rose 78% in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025.
One security consultancy estimates that kidnappers across Nigeria collected nearly $5.8m (£4.3m) in ransoms over the past year as the number of abductions surged. SBM Intelligence estimates that 7,825 people were kidnapped between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase on the previous year.
The increase in bandit activity appears to be a key driver in this trend.
Malik Samuel at Good Governance Africa, a research and advocacy non-profit group, says that "there is no region in northern Nigeria currently that does not experience one form of mass abduction or the other".
Nigeria's battle with bandits is just one part of a more complex security situation facing the country.
As well as the bandit gangs in the north-west, there is an Islamist insurgency in the north-east, separatist unrest in the south-east and clashes in central regions, where the main grievance is over access to land and water for grazing and farming and where ethnic and religious elements have also fuelled some of the unrest.
Most analysts agree that armed groups have waged campaigns of violence that affect all communities, regardless of background or belief.
- The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria 
  - Published28 November 2025
Schools are a common target. When the Islamist Boko Haram militant group infamously kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from the north-eastern village of Chibok in 2014, it made global headlines.
At the time the group forced its captives into sexual slavery, domestic servitude or used them as suicide bombers.
But a range of groups across Nigeria now use kidnapping to raise funds, focusing on soft targets such as schools, churches, mosques and remote villages.
This was mainly confined to the Boko Haram strongholds of the north-east or the bandit zones of the north-west - areas that are largely Muslim.
Then, in May this year, gunmen on motorcycles attacked three schools in Oyo state, south-west Nigeria, one of the few regions that was previously considered relatively safe. Thirty-nine children, the youngest just two years old, were abducted along with seven teachers. One teacher was killed during the raid, another's murder was filmed and shared online.
After 56 days, the remaining 44 hostages were released. The government said it refused to pay a ransom and that the children were released after an operation by security forces. Three men were sentenced to life in prison for the attacks and confessed to being members of an affiliate of Boko Haram.
The abduction spread fear throughout the south-western town of Oriire, with parents in the community pulling their children out of school.
"There is fear because many residents have run away and are yet to return," says the traditional ruler of the area, Oba Tajudeen Abioye, whose niece was among the kidnapped children.
"And for those of us who are left here, we are relying on the security officials, the soldiers" who were sent to protect the community, he says.
Nigeria already has one of the highest numbers of out-of-school children in the world: the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) estimates the number is about 19 million.
The multiple, overlapping security issues mean Nigeria's military and police are overstretched and as a result struggle to tackle the violence.
A 2025 UN report said that police stations were often underfunded and not fully operational, citing independent sources that accused officers of lacking skills in hostage negotiation and forensic investigation.
President Bola Tinubu's administration has allocated the largest defence and security budget in the country's history, raising it by 10% in December 2025 compared to one year before. He has recently approved the recruitment of 28,000 new soldiers.
In the meantime communities are still suffering and in Zamfara thousands of residents have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fill the gaps in security.
But there are concerns about their involvement. In 2020 Zamfara banned a large vigilante group over concerns that extrajudicial killings were driving more violence, according to AFP.
The authorities say the new vigilantes are better trained, but Samuel, from Good Governance Africa, calls them a "time bomb waiting to happen".
"If citizens arm themselves how do you control them at the end of the crisis, how are you able to disarm them?" he asks.
One of the vigilantes meets us outside his group's headquarters, a single-storey concrete building, and agrees to speak on the condition of anonymity during our visit in July.
He perches on his motorcycle, an AK-47 slung over his shoulder, a scarf across his face as a makeshift balaclava, gold and silver skull rings on his fingers.
"We are some of the people the governor hired to protect the community," he says, explaining that they are sometimes told where the bandits are and "with the help of God we fight them and defeat them".
"Let the bandits understand that when they attack a place and kill, they can also be killed," he adds.
He estimates he has fought bandits at least 20 times and says the calls for his group's help keep coming.
"It's hard to go a week without these reports," he says. "There are regions that became safer… but there are other regions where the same cannot be said."
He calls on the state governor, whom he supports, to hire and arm more people to take on the bandits. "These people won't be afraid of you unless you have proper weapons to fight them," he says.
Fatima also calls for more action: "These kidnappers are in every nook and cranny.
"I am not saying the government has failed but even if it is trying, it needs to do more. There are problems and we think with more effort and more security agents, villages will be peaceful."
She wants to return home, but is doubtful that will happen as she has heard her village has now been turned into a camp for the gunmen that attacked it.
The local bandit leader has become the de facto authority, and that families look to him to solve domestic disputes, she says.
Another nearby village "is completely empty, not even a chicken lives there… empty villages like that are countless", Fatima says.
"Even if you go back to our area, it's just difficulty you will face. There's nothing there, no food… you farm and when you go to harvest, they stop you or kidnap you."

China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.
The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.
China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February.
How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.
The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.
This electrifying trend had begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic and strategic imperative of reducing petro-dependence.
In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.
Analysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” said Lauri Myllyvirta, the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.”
Myllyvirta noted this was the first time China’s overall emissions had fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption.
In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels.
Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst at Ember, which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further.
“The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

Google hasn’t released a frontier-level Gemini Pro AI model since early 2026, but it sure loves rolling out new Gemini Flash variants. Today, Google is announcing its third Flash model release in just six weeks, making it more likely that we’ll never see the promised Gemini 3.5 Pro. But no matter, says Google, because Gemini 3.8 Flash is its best reasoning and coding model yet.
Gemini 3.8 Flash comes in two variations. There’s the standard Flash, which Google describes as a “workhorse” model that’s good for anything from agentic tasks to software development. Then we have Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, which runs on the same foundations but has been tuned for vulnerability detection and mitigation.
For developers, Google has the same pitch as it did for the 3.7 Flash release just a couple of weeks ago. API access to the model is available at an “introductory rate” through the end of the year: $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens. The regular price will be $1.50 / $7.50, but it’s likely there will be new models available long before the price changes. Google probably sees the lower prices as a necessity given that other AI labs have recently dropped token pricing to keep increasingly wary businesses engaged with AI tools.
Google has offered its usual raft of benchmark numbers, which appear to show Gemini 3.8 Flash competing with (or even beating) larger and more expensive models. The numbers show a marginal improvement over Gemini 3.7 Flash in most tests, but the gains are larger in coding evaluations.

After U.S. President Donald Trump announced in August 2026 that he would rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America," social media users spread a screenshot appearing to show a Truth Social post from the president that announced the construction of the "Melania Canal" that would 
The screenshot circulated across Facebook (screenshot) and Threads. Here's what Trump allegedly said:
The FAKE NEWS is saying we need the Canadian canals that connect to LAKE AMERICA. Total lie! We don't need their small, low-energy Welland Canal! America built the Panama Canal, we built the Suez Canal — incredible, beautiful, high-IQ canals! I have officially instructed the Army Corps of Engineers to build a much BIGGER, DEEPER, WIDER, and far more powerful canal bypass connecting straight into Lake America! It is going to be magnificent! And we are naming it after my stunning, beautiful wife: THE MELANIA CANAL. Every American will be able to EASILY enter the Melania Canal from BOTH the front end and the back side for a very minimal fee! Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Some users seemed to interpret the rumor as true, and Snopes readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
A closer look at the screenshot indicated that this post was labeled as satire, both under the usual spot for "Likes" on a Truth Social post and as a watermark across the image.
According to the watermark, this post originated with a Facebook account called Mrs. Putin, which identifies itself as "Satire/Parody" in its description. Mrs. Putin first shared the post (screenshot) on Aug. 29.
As Mrs. Putin pointed out in a Facebook message conversation with Snopes in 2025, the account's posts often include several indicators that they are satire, including misspelled names. In this case, aside from the "satire" label, other indicators that the post is fake include that Mrs. Putin changed "Likes" to "disLikes" and misspelled Trump's social media tag, "@realDonaldTrump," as "@realDotardTurmp" and his last name as Turmp.
(Mrs. Putin)
A search of Trump's social media accounts using the databases Trump's Truth and Factbase also determined that, as of this writing, the president has not declared the construction of a "Melania Canal." He did, however, float renaming the Strait of Hormuz to "Trump Strait" in a Sept. 2 Truth Social post.
For more on Lake Ontario and its renaming, Snopes previously debunked a claim that Canadian officials were refusing passage to ships with "Lake America" in their documentation and confirmed that Lake Ontario was not named after the Canadian province.
Snopes also has previously written about numerous satirical Mrs. Putin posts.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Chirag vs Manjhi: SC ‘creamy layer’ debate puts Bihar NDA unity to test.
NEW DELHI: Could the open sparring over “quota within quota” between two prominent Dalit faces of Bihar last month open up a Pandora’s box for the BJP-led NDA government? Union ministers Jitan Ram Manjhi and Chirag Paswan engaged in an open war of words last week over a separate sub-category for the most deprived Dalit sections.Manjhi hails from the Musahar community and wants a sub-quota for the marginalised SC communities. Manjhi’s son Santosh Kumar Suman, who is the Bihar minor water resources minister, has demanded a review of the country’s reservation policy to assess which sections have benefited and which have remained deprived even after 79 years of independence. The father-son duo claims they are not against reservations but want either an increase in quota or separate arrangements for sections still deprived of its benefits after seven decades.Chirag Paswan, son of Late Ram Vilas Paswan, objected to calls to introduce the “creamy layer” provision in SC/ST reservations and insisted that those advocating such a move should first resign from their positions. He stressed that the reservation policy was not based on economic status but was designed to address centuries of social discrimination, exclusion and untouchability.
This is not the first time the two leaders have openly engaged in a war of words on issues.
There have been instances in the past when the two Dalit leaders have openly taken diametrically opposite stands. The latest point of friction was the Bharat Tiwari encounter case of Bhojpur district. While Chirag Paswan vowed to prevail upon Bihar's BJP-led government to ensure that punishment was meted out to all police officials involved in his encounter, Manjhi asserted that police were justified in having opened fire on the 28-year-old man with an "unlicensed" weapon. Tiwari, a self-styled social and political activist, was shot dead following a heated exchange on June 17 when officials of the local administration and police visited his place to interrogate him in connection with incendiary social media posts.Political observers feel the open friction between the two leaders is more of a political fight for Dalit leadership in the state. Analyst Naval Kishore Choudhary, who has observed Bihar politics for decades, says Manjhi and Paswan are engaged in a turf war."The two leaders represent two different constituencies within the SC community and are in race to establish themselves as a bigger leader within the NDA in Bihar. By taking contradictory stands, they are catering to their own constituencies within the community. There perhaps is a tussle between them to prove who is more important for NDA in Bihar," Choudhary said.However, the current issue of their discord, “quota within quota”, is not just contentious but also politically sensitive. The BJP has strategically avoided a debate on the issue of sub-quota within the Dalits, perhaps realising the uncertain fallout of any such debate.
Homogeneous group vs categorisation
A Supreme Court judgment in August 2024, in a 6:1 majority ruling, had allowed states to sub-categorise castes within the Scheduled Castes (SC) based on socio-economic backwardness and degree of under-representation in govt jobs to ensure that the larger pie of 15% SC quota goes to the backwards among them.It had also asked governments to devise suitable criteria to bar the ‘creamy layer’ among SCs and STs from availing reservation. In the process, the SC overruled an earlier judgment of a five-judge bench in EV Chinnaiah case, which had said the SCs were a homogeneous group and could not be sub-categorised.The Modi government had in 2017 constituted a four-member Commission headed by Justice (Retd.) G. Rohini in October 2017 to examine the extent of inequitable distribution of benefits of reservation among the OBCs and to work out the mechanism, criteria, norms and parameters in a scientific approach for sub-categorisation within them. The Commission submitted its report to President Droupadi Murmu on July 21, 2023. However, the report has not been made public yet.Clearly, the government perhaps wants to avoid opening a Pandora’s box. More so at a time when it faces a competing challenge from the upper caste communities also. There were protests against reservations in the national capital last month, and the government engaged with the protesters. On August 21, several people held a protest in the national capital following a call by Reservation Hatao Andolan (Scrap Reservation), an Instagram-based page. The protesters are demanding the scrapping of quotas, saying that economic criteria should be given precedence over caste in determining eligibility for government support and reservation.Later, the representatives of the group held a meeting with Union minister J P Nadda and engaged in a "cordial discussion". "Following the movement that took place at Jantar Mantar on 21 August, cordial discussions were held, as per the pre-determined schedule, with Harsh Dubey, Ran Bahadur Singh Chauhan, and Mrityunjay Pathak, members of the team. In this connection, we will meet again soon," Nadda said in a post on X after the meeting.Nadda's meeting with Reservation Hatao Andolan representatives drew questions from opponents. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke asked Nadda to explain the Modi government's stand on the anti-reservation movement and questioned what Prime Minister Narendra Modi has to say about the August 21 protest. AAP Delhi unit president Saurabh Bharadwaj also sought clarity from Nadda on the government's position, referring to the demand for reconsideration of reservations.
Two-fold challenge
These political attacks notwithstanding, the BJP has to keep in mind the upper-caste sentiments. The upper caste vote has largely been with the BJP barring some exceptions, but ahead of the crucial assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh there are reports of discontent in the community.For the BJP, the challenge is two-fold. On the one hand, it has to keep the anti-reservation protesters engaged without enraging the pro-reservation groups. On the other, it has to strike a balance between competing demands of allies on sub-categorisation within the SC community.The BJP already faces pressure from the marginalised groups after stay on University Grants Commission (UGC) rules calling out caste discrimination in universities. The saffron party is also battling opposition allegations that the 2027 caste census deliberately obscures caste data. The 40 questions which are part of the census ask for many personal details, which have not so far been required for any census. However, it does not have a drop-down box for caste, nor does it ask people to self-identify as OBC to allow for proper collation of caste data.Political analyst Uday Chandra says internal conflicts within the SC community is a reality. This is more so in Bihar where Dalit identity is not totally consolidated like in other states. “The “Jati” name takes precedence over the Dalit identity in Bihar and that explains why there is a competing interest between the two Dalit leaders in the state,” Uday Chandra says.“The BJP also faces the challenge of forming new social coalitions in the runup to 2029 Lok Sabha elections. The 2014 and 2019 social coalitions which helped the BJP electorally are starting to fray and may not be effective for electoral gains,” he adds.That perhaps explains why the BJP is treading cautiously and may not be averse to the idea of “quota within quota” like it exits within the OBCs. Nitish Kumar formed the group of EBCs in Bihar and they powered his politics for years.The BJP may also ponder at the prospect of making electoral gains by prioritising the deprived within the Dalits. No wonder, the opposition parties in Bihar are already accusing the BJP of using the two ministers to test people’s mood on the issue.
'BJP testing people's mood'
Bihar's leader of the opposition Tejashwi Yadav said: "The BJP is doing all this drama from behind. They are testing people's mood, putting pebbles in the water and seeing what happens." Referring to Majhi and Paswan, he said: "These people are merely characters. They only want posts. They are greedy for positions, chairs, bungalows and security, but have left society behind."Congress MP Pramod Tiwari said Union ministers making allegations against each other "goes against the Constitution". "Perhaps they do not realise that the principle of collective responsibility applies to the Council of Ministers. Whatever a minister says remains the government's position until it is contradicted," he said.But the BJP may not want to make any new experiment now as the very idea is fraught with huge political risks. Hence, to put the sparring Dalit leaders on the back foot, Bihar minister and senior BJP leader Lakhendra Paswan posed a pointed question to both the Union ministers.
Without directly endorsing either position, he asked how many people from their respective communities, beyond their immediate families, they had actually helped advance. He reiterated what he described as the BJP’s position on reservation, declaring, “If there is BJP, there is reservation.” BJP national spokesperson Dr Guru Prakash Paswan also reiterated that the government has a clear stand regarding the reservation issue. "Reservation will exist till discrimination exists in society, and our government has strengthened this system. Whatever one says on this can be their personal opinion, but for social justice, the BJP is committed to fulfilling the vows of B.R. Ambedkar," he said.So, while the BJP watches its two allies in Bihar fight, it would hope that the issue does not snowball into a controversy that goes out of hand.

Late-night transfer fallout sparks Chelsea-Monaco row
- Published
One source with connections to both Chelsea and Monaco said the clubs had "played with fire and got burned".
Indeed, the late-night transfer drama that involved Folarin Balogun, Everton, Monaco, Lamine Camara and Chelsea saw all parties lose out.
Camara - a 22-year-old Senegalese international midfielder - had been a target for Chelsea as they prepared for the £125m sale of Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City.
But Monaco were adamant he was going nowhere for the fee Chelsea were willing to pay.
"I've been speaking to them for the last 10 days," said Monaco sporting director Thiago Scuro said.
"At around 16:00 BST yesterday we got contact from Chelsea. The answer was the same: no."
Instead, the Ligue 1 club had allowed United States international striker Balogun, 25, to fly to Merseyside to complete a £40m move to Everton. According to Monaco, Camara had agreed to stay with the club.
With three hours remaining of the transfer window, Chelsea were content with their midfield options, despite the sale of Fernandez, after failing with enquiries for Camara and Roma's Manu Kone.
But issues with Balogun's Everton medical saw the door open again for Chelsea at the £47m price point Chelsea had previously offered. Negotiations were back underway with Monaco at 20:00 BST.
Meanwhile, Everton failed to find alternatives to Balogun and revived their move with minutes before the deadline.
Chelsea had completed all the necessary paperwork for Camara and did not need to submit a deal sheet - a request to the Premier League for additional time to complete a transfer, post the deadline.
But the plug was pulled. Monaco acknowledge Camara was disappointed after he had spoken to manager Xabi Alonso, passed a medical and signed a contract until 2033.
"What happened was that around 22:00 BST our time, maybe a bit earlier, Everton realised there was no issue and decided they were ready to sign the contract [for Balogun]," Scuro told reporters on Wednesday afternoon.
"As soon as we received that information, we came back to Chelsea and said there was no deal. Because that's also fair. It's part of the game."
Chelsea were left furious, claiming Monaco informed them in writing that the deal would not proceed rather than communicating the decision by phone.
Monaco thought - by signing a deal sheet, five minutes before the 23:00 BST deadline, to allow Everton extra time to complete the transfer of Balogun - they had secured the sale they needed to help comply with Uefa's financial regulations.
The Ligue 1 side were under pressure to generate 150m euros in player sales this summer, and had raised 106m euros from departures.
Balogun U-turn
Another twist was still to come.
In the early hours of Tuesday morning, the former Arsenal striker had a change of heart which saw him leave Everton's Finch Farm training ground without signing for the club.
Scuro claims Balogun felt he was mistreated while at Everton's training ground, something the Premier League club disputes.
"We had to respect his decision," Scuro added.
"We found solutions, challenged the medical assessment and worked through the issues.
"I don't want to create a war with Chelsea or Everton.
"My role is to protect Monaco and act in the club's best interests. That's what I've done since I arrived.
"It's not about being loved by people outside the club. It's about doing what Monaco needs."
Scuro says it is possible Monaco will look at selling other players to countries whose transfer window remains open in order to acquire the funds they need.
He is open to welcoming back both players and says he expects Camara to be back with "full power" for their upcoming match away at Paris St-Germain on Friday night.
"I really understand because a player can get excited by conversations with a coach and by everything a club like Chelsea can offer," Scuro continued.
"This is not the end of the world. It's one opportunity. For a player with his level of talent, I'm very confident he will soon have even better options and offers than the one he had yesterday."
According to sources close to Camara, Liverpool also retain a long-standing interest in a future deal.
Questions remain for Chelsea
Chelsea had been considering Camara as an option to replace Fernandez for the final 10 days of the window.
Of course, the Londoners could have forced a deal through sooner but it might have meant overpaying because, as sources had previously explained, Monaco saw Camara as not for sale throughout the majority of the window - barring those few hours on Tuesday evening - but for "exceptional" offers.
Chelsea were blindsided by the collapse of the deal and there was little they could have done to revive it or sign an alternative before the deadline.
They did, however, have the option of cancelling Fernandez's move to Manchester City but opted not to do so out of a sense of "professionalism".
Chelsea wanted a midfielder to replace Fernandez but there was never any desperation as the club only wanted to do so on its own terms.
Alonso sees captain Reece James primarily as a midfield option, alongside Moises Caicedo, Romeo Lavia and new signings Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco within his 27-man squad.
Yet injuries to Caicedo and Henderson, coupled with James' workload, meant full-back Malo Gusto was used in midfield during the 4-3 victory over Brighton, a match in which Chelsea recorded 25.6% possession, their lowest figure since records began in 2003-04.
Alonso could have selected Barco, 21, who came on as a second-half substitute, but the club want to carefully manage the signing from Strasbourg as he returns to the Premier League after a short-lived spell at Brighton.
There remains debate over whether Chelsea have sufficient depth and quality in midfield, with the club retaining the option of revisiting a move for Camara or another midfielder in January.
They could also look to strengthen other positions having been left delighted at making a net profit in the transfer market while adding quality.
Chelsea signed World Cup winner Emiliano Martinez, France international Maxence Lacroix and club-record £117m signing Morgan Rogers, as well as experienced striker Danny Welbeck and full-backs Pep Chavarria and Marco Palestra.
It's now on the manager and squad they have built to attempt to match Chelsea's ambitions on the pitch, starting with Sunday's trip to champions Arsenal.

The growing El Niño weather phenomenon to Australia’s east is already breaking heat records, with forecasts showing it will likely easily surpass previous events, according to Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology, as seperate research suggested climate change had greatly shortened the odds of the event hitting record extremes.
On Thursday the UN’s weather agency said the event in the Pacific was continuing to strengthen and would probably persist until early 2027, warning it had the “potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”.
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”
In an update this week, the Bureau of Meteorology said the El Niño was now forecast to peak in late spring or summer and “reach levels above the warmest observed since reliable records began in 1950”.
El Niño events tend to mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east in winter and spring, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires.
El Niño strength is assessed by analysing sea surface temperatures in a region of the equatorial Pacific known as Niño 3.4. The bureau has said the strength of an El Niño does not necessarily mean stronger effects for the continent.
However, bureau analysis of the unfolding event suggested this El Niño had already broken records.
“We have been looking at the rate of warming observed in the last two months and it has been faster than any other event. Not only is it strong, but it has escalated rapidly,” said Felicity Gamble, a senior climatologist at the BoM.
Gamble said the relative sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region for the month of August were likely to be between 2.2C and 2.3C above average – higher than any previous August since 1950 (the year after which records are considered to be more reliable).
She said forecasts were suggesting relative sea surface temperatures in that region could peak over 3C above average, compared to the highest previous figure of 2.6C observed in January 1983.
Gamble said the relative sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region had warmed by more than 2C between February and July.
She said: “No other period in the historical record exceeds that. This is the first event where we have had that change exceed 2C in the space of six months.
“We could be seeing a record in terms of the strength, and also the rate of warming and the duration.”
Climate experts have said El Niño will likely combine with climate change to push global temperatures to record highs next year.
Gamble said in the Pacific region, El Niño was already contributing to droughts in Papua New Guinea, with food and water shortages and major wildfires in Indonesia.
This winter was Australia’s third-warmest on record and the hottest on record for New South Wales, Tasmania and Victoria.
Scientists at the University of Melbourne have released preliminary research into the influence of climate change on the predicted peak of the El Niño. By analysing historical records and comparing climate models with and without the influence of greenhouse gas emissions, the scientists found climate change had made “an event of this magnitude” six times more likely.
The study has been submitted to a journal for peer review, but the authors said they had used a methodology common to many other published studies.
Dr Andrew King, one of the co-authors of the research, said: “This points to the fact that there is likely a climate change role here in the chance of having these extreme El Niño conditions. It seems likely there is a human fingerprint emerging in this event.
“We are seeing something that does not appear to have happened before and that is alarming.”
The bureau’s long range forecast for September to November points to an increased chance of below average rainfall for the south and east, but above average for most of the continent’s western half. Temperatures are also likely to be above average south of the tropics.

River water smashed into tunnel and chased me for 20 minutes, Nepal worker tells BBC
- Published
Nepalese hydropower workers have told the BBC about the catastrophic moment water from the Trishuli River crashed into their tunnel as the region was inundated by deadly flash floods last week.
It started with a sudden, strong gust of air, says Pemba Dundu Tamang, whose team of about 30 was constructing the tunnel's concrete lining.
The blast of wind sent plywood flying through the air and dislodged heavy machinery. Just outside, houses had already been swept away.
"I ran towards the tunnel entrance," he said. "The water was chasing behind me and I was running ahead of it."
Tamang lost several family members who were at home at the time. Nepal's death toll has exceeded 1,000 after last week's devastating floods, and officials say about 4,000 are missing.
A number of the missing - potentially in the hundreds - are labourers like Tamang, working in a vast network of tunnels at hydropower sites along the river. Engineers have been pumping air into these tunnels as part of a huge rescue operation.
"We are focused on search-and-rescue efforts at the tunnels, our work is continuing," Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP news agency.
"Our soldiers are also deployed to collect bodies and prevent the spread of disease."
Tamang says he ran for about 20 minutes to flee the violent deluge, which followed him uphill.
"I was almost unconscious with shock. I could not think clearly."
His colleague, Itha Ghale, says the powerful gust of air almost blew them away as they sprinted.
Over 99% of the electricity generated in Nepal comes from hydropower, and Tamang and Ghale had been working at a major production site helping to build the Upper Trishuli 3B Hydropower Project.
The plant, which was due to open next year, was designed to re-use water from a hydroelectric plant further upstream to generate additional electricity for Nepal's national grid.
There were several different teams operating there - and Tamang says the one operating the large tunnel-lining machine was the last to come out.
But soon afterwards came a crushing realisation.
"I could see where my house should have been. There was nothing left. That was when I realised everything was gone."
Six of Tamang's relatives - his mother, elder brother and sister-in-law and three of their children - are gone, he said. They were at home on the riverside when the floods hit.
Only his wife, son and one nephew survived.
"I feel life is meaningless now. Surviving feels miserable. I do not know where to eat or where to go," Tamang says.
"The dead are at peace. It is those of us who survived who suffer."
Ghale, who lost eight members of his family, says he does not know why he survived. "Perhaps it was not my fate to die."
The eight family members include his mother and eldest daughter. His three sons and wife survived.
Tamang dreads what the future may bring, especially if these hydropower projects are shut down. "If things continue like this, we will go hungry. Sometimes I feel it would have been better not to survive."
Tamang ultimately managed to take refuge with a few others in the village of Shanti Bazar for two days until the army came to rescue them.
He estimates about 50 to 60 workers were able to escape the tunnel alongside him.
He says more people could have been saved if proper resources had been in place.
This is echoed by a new report which says there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the disaster - and that better early warning systems could have saved lives.
Satellite images suggest the glacier surface was moving faster, meltwater was turning brown and a crack was developing in the surrounding rock, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment.
These are all possible signs the mountainside was becoming unstable.
The avalanche itself moved too fast for conventional warnings to help those closest to it, the scientists say.
But further downstream, where the flood took 10 minutes or more to arrive, they say a comprehensive warning system could potentially have saved a significant number of lives.
Right now, however, specialists from China, India and Nepal are continuing to use excavators and heavy machinery to blast through debris from the hydropower projects to try to reach workers still trapped at several hydropower sites.
"There are probably still some survivors inside. I would be happy if they were rescued quickly," Tamang says.
"I know many people who are still trapped there."
Additional reporting by Justin Rowlatt, climate editor
