The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on August 17 announced a new national social media team, replacing Amit Malviya with Deepak Mhaskey as its IT cell in-charge. The party also named four new social media co-convenors — Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav.
Alt News had earlier reported that within minutes of BJP’s announcement, a search on X revealed that the accounts of the four social media co-convenors had either vanished or their posts had become inaccessible. However, screenshots and archived versions of their past tweets, often containing personal and contentious opinions, are available, raising concern over the sudden disappearance of their accounts. Yadav, for instance, deleted more than 60,000 posts before making her X handle accessible again. Mhaskey deleted at least 1,342.
Gandhi’s X account, which has over 500,000 followers, remains ‘protected’ or hidden from public view at the time of this article being published. A notice from the platform states “Only approved followers can see @MrsGandhi’s posts”.
An earlier screenshot of her profile captured by us shows her following 2,015 handles, which has now gone down to 1,875. In other words, she has recently unfollowed 140 X users.
Alt News spoke to Gandhi, and asked her why she had hidden her X posts, but she refused to comment. Her Facebook profile bio describes her as ‘IT & Social Media National In-charge for all 7 BJP Morchas’ and ‘Official Spokesperson, Maharashtra BJP’.
Recently, in November 2025, Gandhi courted controversy after targeting Indian cricketer Jemimah Rodrigues over her expression of faith during a post-match interview. After India’s semi-final victory against Australia, in which Rodrigues was named Player of the Match, she acknowledged her teammates’ support, said she had put her faith in God, and thanked Jesus in the post-match interview. Criticising this, Gandhi argued that while wearing the Indian jersey, Rodrigues represents Indians and “not her church”.
In her older tweets dating back to 2012-13, she expressed disdain for her surname, saying she would rather have ‘Modi’ or ‘Godse’ as a surname. She has repeatedly praised Nathuram Godse, the assassin of Mahatma Gandhi, in her tweets.
Declaring herself as a “huge fan and follower” of Godse, she has multiple tweets announcing that she “misses him” and that there is a need for “1000 more Godse’s” and that “India misses him.” Much of that record, however, is no longer readily accessible, but screenshots of her past tweets are shown below:
Long-time BJP Supporter
Her association with BJP, however, predates her formal organisational role. Gandhi has been a pro-BJP voice since around 2012. Initially, her X (then Twitter) handle was @pritirules. Aafter her anti-Congress posts were being shared by prominent BJP leaders, she changed her handle to @MrsGandhi. “I realised this name has a lot of potential, as there would be one Gandhi questioning the other. So I changed my handle,” she explained to the Telegraph.
In 2012, Modi started following Priti Gandhi on Twitter. According to her, she put forward her opinions aggressively — which caught Modi’s attention. Gandhi was even invited to Gandhinagar to meet Modi. “He [Modi] liked that I, as an independent person, defend him on social media”, Gandhi told The Telegraph.
In January 2014, Gandhi had falsely claimed that Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, had stated that “Modi is incorruptible”. Gandhi allegedly amplified a fake endorsement of Modi by Assange, featuring a poster of Assange alongside a quote that read, “America fears Modi because they know he is incorruptible.”
WikiLeaks responded:
#India: Here is the BJP’s Pritti Ghandi pushing fake #Assange endorsement of #Modi to 40k people https://t.co/kh8HsMlgqi
— WikiLeaks (@wikileaks) March 17, 2014
History Of Misinformation
Gandhi’s rise within the BJP’s digital ecosystem closely coincided with a long record of disseminating and amplifying misinformation. Alt News has fact-checked her claims repeatedly over the years.
For instance, in 2019, Gandhi circulated an edited video suggesting that Rahul Gandhi wanted to leave India and settle abroad. In 2020, Gandhi revived the ‘potato-gold’ remark, a claim that stemmed from a clipped video with distorted context, to mock Rahul Gandhi and mislead people.
In 2021, during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, Gandhi also shared a misleading video purportedly showing an absence of crowds in Haridwar during the Kumbh Mela. The post appeared amid intense scrutiny of the religious gathering, where millions of pilgrims had assembled, and thousands of COVID-19 cases were subsequently reported among attendees and seers.
The video, however, did not depict the principal pilgrimage area around Har Ki Pauri. It was reportedly shot at Govind Ghat, several kilometres away, and at a time when the location did not see large crowds. The video was therefore misleadingly presented as evidence that Haridwar was not crowded during the Kumbh Mela.
During the 2021 West Bengal post-poll violence, Alt News had fact-checked a doctored video shared by Gandhi showing men wielding swords while dancing to the TMC election song, ‘Khela Hobe’.
In another instance, Gandhi shared a misleading video claiming that “Modi Modi” slogans were being raised inside Pakistan’s Parliament. Alt News found that the chants were actually “Voting Voting”.
More from the Archives: Propaganda & Disinformation
A recurring feature of Gandhi’s social media activity over the years has also been the amplification of communal or polarising misinformation.
In 2020, she shared an image of Priyanka Gandhi embracing the mother of the Hathras rape victim and described the woman as “fake Naxal-bhabi”. She falsely accused both Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi of consoling the “Naxal operative who had infiltrated the family’s home and was posing as the victim’s sister-in-law”.
The same year, she also circulated a clipped video of journalist Arfa Khanum Sherwani speaking about the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), using the edited clip to distort the context and present the speech in a communal light.
A Newslaundry article cites a 2021 Centre of the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH) paper, which identified Gandhi among BJP figures who amplified the ‘Love Jihad’ narrative in the aftermath of the killing of Nikita Tomar – a student who was shot outside her college in Ballabhgarh by a Muslim youth.
According to a 2020 report by Lokmat, Gandhi said in a tweet on October 27, 2020, “Those in denial of the existence of Love Jihad are only closing their eyes to reality, maybe even purposely. Unless we don’t accept the problem, finding a solution is impossible. Today it is Nikita, tomorrow it could be you!”
It is important to note that the chargesheet of the Nikita Tomar case had no sections of the IPC related to forced conversions and other associated crimes, as per a Times of India report.
In 2019, both Gandhi and Bengal BJP shared a clipped video to falsely claim a communal bias in a speech by then Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee. They shared a 12-second excerpt of her speech clipping out the part where Banerjee had recited Hindu scriptures. Alt News had fact-checked this.
In 2021, Gandhi shared a video of a man apparently blowing on food, suggesting that he was spitting on it, giving the footage an explicitly communal framing. In 2022, she claimed that participants at a Popular Front of India (PFI) protest in Pune had raised “Pakistan Zindabad” slogans. Fact-checkers found that the slogan was in actuality “Popular Front Zindabad”.
Again, in 2022, while sharing a photo of Rahul Gandhi with a girl, Gandhi falsely claimed that she was Amulya Leona, who raised ‘Pakistan Zindabad’ slogans during the anti-CAA protest in Bangalore in 2020. In reality, the girl with Rahul was Miva Jolly, an activist associated with the Kerala Students Union, the student wing of the Congress party.
During the 2024 farmers’ protest, Gandhi shared an image claiming a farmer was seen sitting on a Mercedes car worth Rs 3 crore, thereby portraying that the protesters were ‘rich’ and thus the movement was not legitimate. It was found in an investigation by Alt News that the car was actually an SUV Gurkha by Force Motors whicbh had been modified to look like a Mercedes vehicle. We spoke to the owner of the car as well.
In January 2022, Gandhi falsely claimed that Uttar Pradesh BJP MLA Vinay Shakya had been kidnapped after he had been pressured by Samajwadi Party to join them. Local police replied to her tweet clarifying that the abduction claim was entirely false. Gandhi, then, deleted her tweet.
Target of Misinformation Herself
Priti Gandhi herself became a target of misinformation when a viral thread in 2021 shared three genuine screenshots of her old posts alongside a fabricated tweet claiming that her husband had escaped the Capitol Hill riots. The thread, which gained over 10,000 likes and was amplified by several journalists and Congress members, falsely portrayed the manufactured tweet as part of a pattern in which Gandhi’s husband had narrowly escaped multiple major incidents. While three screenshots were genuine and referred to same incident (the 26/11 Mumbai attack), the Capitol Hill tweet was fake.

Dozens missing, 5 dead after migrant boat is found drifting near Spanish islands
At least five people have died after a boat carrying West African migrants ran into trouble in the Atlantic Ocean
BARCELONA, Spain -- At least five people died and dozens more were feared dead after a boat carrying West African migrants ran into trouble in the Atlantic Ocean. Forty-four people were brought to safety in the Canary Islands.
Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said Thursday that one of its planes had spotted a “precarious” boat drifting some 120 km (74 miles) south of the island of Gran Canaria on Wednesday afternoon.
Three survivors were immediately evacuated by helicopter to a hospital on the island. The remaining 41 migrants were brought to safety by boat and disembarked early Thursday in the port of Arguineguín, where they were cared for by the Red Cross. All survivors were men, some underage, and came from Mali or Senegal, said José Antonio Rodríguez Verona, a spokesperson for the Red Cross in the Canaries.
In a phone interview with The Associated Press, Rodríguez Verona said survivors were disoriented and dehydrated, with many collapsing or vomiting upon reaching land. While it was difficult to get precise information given their fragile state of health, migrants reported leaving Gambia and being stranded at sea for “many, many days.” Some estimated they had been at sea for nearly a month. Running out of provisions, they fell ill from drinking seawater.
Survivors also told the Red Cross that more than 100 people were originally on board, including women and a baby. As people died on the journey, their bodies were tossed in the ocean until they had no more strength to do so.
In an emailed statement, Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said that it was not able to retrieve the remains of the five dead found inside the boat due to strong winds and waves that were 2.5 metres (8 feet) high.
Separately, Helena Maleno, founder of the migrant rights group Walking Borders, which monitors deaths and disappearances on migration routes to Spain, reported that 83 people had died on the voyage, including three women and a baby. In a post on X, Maleno said the boat had departed Gambia 27 days ago.
Maleno and her NGO are frequently contacted by relatives of missing migrants and often relay calls for help and rescue to Spanish authorities. The AP reached out to Maleno and Walking Borders seeking further details but has not yet received a response.
The West African Atlantic route to Spain’s Canary Islands is one of the deadliest crossings to Europe. While arrivals to the Spanish archipelago have fallen significantly in the past year, tens of thousands of people have died or gone missing in recent years, with several migrant boats getting lost and drifting all the way across the Atlantic to the Americas.

I’ve also pulled some deals from competing sales at Backcountry and other cottage industry retailers. Below, find the best deals on all our favorite tents, backpacks, sleeping bags, sleeping pads, cookware, outdoor apparel, and more. Be sure to check out our outdoor gear guides, like the Best Tents, Best Sleeping Bags, Best Sleeping Pads, Best Backpacking Tents, Best Merino Wool, and Best Base Layers.

Sure. Here you go:
Deals on Tents
The REI Half Dome 2 is the best budget two-person backpacking tent. I’ve toted it on many backpacking trips and found it plenty sturdy, quick to set up, and capable of fitting two people along with their gear. It even comes with a footprint (which I never bother with, but it's nice to have it if you have to deal with pointy rocks).
The Big Agnes Copper Spur series is our top pick among freestanding ultralight tents. This is the bike-packing model, which features shorter pole segments that are easier to haul on a bike, but I really prefer it for the more subdued colors. The Copper Spur is a high-quality, well-designed tent that's lightweight, easy to set up, and roomy enough to be livable in the backcountry. The “awning” design (with trekking poles or sticks) is a nice extra.
Nemo's Dragonfly tents are roomy for the weight. There's a generous amount of mesh at the top, which provides some nice ventilation on warm summer nights and is perfect for falling asleep under the stars when the weather permits. The Osmo fabric is a blend of nylon and polyester that absorbs less water than pure nylon rainflies.
MSR's Groundhog stakes aren't cheap, but they're the best backpacking tent upgrade you can make. They're superstrong—I've never had one bend or pull out on me—and considering their strength, they're pretty lightweight. I suggest carrying a mix of stakes when backpacking—some of these, some carbon fiber pegs, and some shepherd hooks. That way, no matter the terrain, you've got something that'll work.
REI's Base Camp tent is my favorite car camping tent. It's a traditional dome tent design, with two crossed poles and two side poles, that hold up very well in wind. The floor is high-quality 150-denier polyester, which so far has not shown any signs of abrasion, despite quite a few nights on rough ground out West. Inside, there are loads of storage pockets, and the double doors make great vents in warmer weather, with huge windows that ensure you catch any whiffs of breeze on hot nights.
The Marmot Halo is my favorite all-weather four-person family tent. The low-profile design stands up better to wind, while the steep sidewalls maximize interior space. It also has a nearly full-length rain fly, which helps make this a real haven in a storm. The name comes from the unusual pole design. There are two cross poles, like every square, domed tent, but the side poles connect halfway up the tent body instead of at the ground. The only downside is that you can't stand up in it. If you want more room, the six-person version, which, with a 76-inch peak height, may be tall enough for you to stand up in, is also on sale.
Deals on Hiking Boots and Shoes
My favorite barefoot sandals are 25 percent off right now. I always call these the barefoot equivalent of Chaco sandals. They're not as robust, and I'd still bring Chacos if I were white-water rafting, but for everything else these are perfect. Z-Trails flex and bend as you walk, giving your feet the freedom of movement you'd expect from a barefoot shoe, though these do have 10 mm of cushioning, which makes them a good option if you're just starting out with barefoot shoes. The even more minimal Z-Trek sandals are also on sale.
The best all-around barefoot shoe, the Prios are your classic sneaker reimagined for barefoot shoe enthusiasts. When you were a kid, you had just one pair of shoes: The Prios are that pair. The toe box is wide enough for my toes to splay out nicely, and the heel cup is snug with no slipping. The ground feel is great too, enough feedback to feel barefoot, but you're not going to wince when you hit a sharp stone.
Altra's Lone Peak shoes have carried countless thru-hikers to the finish line. The Lone Peak first came on the scene in 2011 and quickly built a cult following. They're light (11.5 ounces) and very comfortable in our testing. The reinforced toe and heel offer excellent protection against rough, rocky trails, and while they're much more padded these days than early versions, they're still zero drop.
Keen's Targhee Apex has finally found a look that isn't bad by Targhee standards. Perhaps more than any other shoe we've tested, these look like the trail-running Gorpcore icons they are. At just 0.75 pounds each, they are light without being fragile, and the generous footbed lets your feet spread comfortably on long days.
The La Sportiva Prodigio combines trail-running agility with boot-level protection, delivering surprising versatility on rugged terrain. They're one of our favorite light hiking boots. The fit is a little on the snug side—much like La Sportiva climbing shoes—but they should be fine even for wide feet thanks to the generous footbed width. At 1.65 pounds for the pair, these aren't terribly bulky.
Camping Gear Deals
This camp chair is the coziest way to hang out around the fire. It is somewhat huge, heavy, and awkward to fold up and carry, but so long as you have room for it in your vehicle, there's no better way to relax under the stars with your loved ones.
The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI brand gear is the company's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works well and has produced some great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example: It's comfortable (it does wobble a little side-to-side when you move) and less than half the price of competitors.
I've noticed that when people try to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter backpack, they struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which smashes anything soft down to about half the size of the same item in a regular stuff sack. This works well with sleeping bags and clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino wool.
The Flash 22 is one of the best-value day packs on the market, especially on sale. It's surprisingly comfortable despite the lightweight straps and minimal padding. It carries loads up to 15 pounds without straining the shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. Note that this deal is only on the patterned colors.
WIRED staffers have North Face duffels that have been going strong for 25 years, earning a spot in our Buy It for Life guide. They're big ol' bags (this one is 62 liters), capable of swallowing gear like a whale, and unlike all the other identical cases on the luggage carousel, they’re always easy to spot. This version is made of phthalate-free, recycled PVC and recycled nylon that’s treated with a non-PFC water-repellent (DWR) finish.
Deals on Outdoor Clothing
Now is a great time to score some new base layers and mid layers ahead of the cooler months, or pick up one of our favorite rain jackets.
Arc'teryx's Beta AR rain jacket is one of the burliest rain jackets I've tested. The Beta AR uses 40D fabric for most of the face, with reinforced 80D patches in high-wear areas, all of it with a Gore-Tex Pro 3L membrane. It's been the only Gore-Tex jacket I've tested that hasn't wetted out yet, and the pit zips provide excellent ventilation. At 1 pound, 0.3 ounces, it's not the lightest jacket, but you'd be hard-pressed to find anything else this durable at this weight.
This is an REI Outlet deal because it's been discontinued, which is a shame (hopefully that just means new colors are coming next year). REI's 100 percent merino base layers are some of the best values around, even at full price. On sale, they're a true steal. I like this half-zip for the extra ventilation the zipper provides, but if you prefer, the regular top (on sale for $30) is also on sale, as is the base layer bottom (on sale for $30).
Nothing says outdoors like a hatchet loop on your pants. Fjällräven Vidda Pro trousers give you that and great ventilation. The Vidda Pro uses Fjällräven's G-1000 fabric, a 65 percent recycled polyester and 35 percent cotton blend, with pockets everywhere and extras like ventilation zippers, reinforced knees (with openings for pads), and that sweet, sweet hatchet loop on the leg.
Sleeping Bag and Sleeping Pad Deals
Our favorite backpacking sleeping bag, the Bishop Pass 15 offers the best warmth-to-weight ratio while packing down small and staying affordable. I have slept in this bag for more than two weeks, with nighttime temps ranging from 28 to 65 degrees Fahrenheit, and, yes, it was too warm in the heat, but on those warmer nights, I unzipped it and used it as a blanket. It isn't perfect, but it's a versatile bag.
REI's Magma line of down gear is some of the best value around. The Magma 15 sleeping bag has long been an affordable option that's perfect for shoulder-season trips when the temperature potentially swings lower than you expect (the comfort rating is 21). There are three lengths and three widths, which makes it easy to find a perfect fit for your body, and the 850-fill-power goose down (Bluesign-approved) packs down nicely and small. If you don't need the shoulder-season coverage, the Magma 30 is also on sale for $262 ($87 off), and it makes a great summer sleeping bag.
This down mummy bag has a spoon-shaped design for side sleepers and extra room in the elbows and knees so you can roll over onto your side without feeling like you're slipping into a straitjacket. It's built for temps down to 30 degrees Fahrenheit and has zippered gills you can open to avoid overheating when it's warmer.
The best budget ultralight quilt, the Magma Trail is a great value for the money. The lower price does mean that this one is a bit heavier (it uses 850-fill-power down), though at 24 ounces for the long, wide version I have, it’s competitive on the scale. The straps for attaching it to your sleep pad aren’t as nice as what you’ll get with something like the Enlightened Equipment's Revelation Quilt, but it’s just as warm and does a respectable job of keeping out drafts. There's even a zippered foot box with a drawstring for cooler nights.
Nemo's Pulse quilt uses RDS-certified, gold-infused 1,000-fill-power ExpeDRY down, which does a good job of shedding moisture from tent condensation and reportedly dries faster than standard down, though I've never figured out a good way to test this. The Karo Step baffle stitching keeps down well distributed, and at 12 ounces for the regular, this one is pretty dang lightweight.
This is our favorite sleeping bag for car camping. The REI Siesta is plenty warm and affordable. It's also not a mummy bag because you're not climbing Denali here. The rectangular cut makes for a much roomier, more comfortable sleeping experience. The 20-degree-Fahrenheit rating makes it warm enough for three seasons, and unlike most rectangular bags, the Siesta has a hood, which helps on those cold nights.
The Kindercamp makes a great car camping bag if you've got young children. Once your kids are about 4 feet tall, an adult sleeping bag works just fine. Prior to that, they'll benefit from a kids' sleeping bag like the Kindercamp, which is cut smaller so your little ones don't have to heat up a huge, adult-size sleeping bag to stay warm.
There are other good sleeping pads out there, but nothing compares to the Therm-a-Rest NeoLoft for comfort. This pad reinvigorated my love of backpacking by ensuring that I get a great night's sleep. It's cushy and comfortable, especially if you're careful not to overinflate it. The R-4.8 insulation keeps you warm down to about freezing, though I've used it in colder conditions by pairing it with a closed-cell foam pad.
The Z-Lite Sol weighs next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), folds up compact enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and will completely change your backpacking experience for the better. I am too old and too soft to sleep on just this anymore, but I use it as a chair, padding for a nap on the rocks, a table, extra padding on cold nights, and more. It's possibly the most versatile piece of gear I own.
If you want to feel like you never left your bed at home, this is the camping pad to get. You really have no idea how comfortable tent camping can be until you sleep on a Megamat. The firm, 4-inch-thick pad is both soft and surprisingly firm thanks to the closed-cell foam inside, which relieves pressure and feels about as close to the mattress in your bedroom as you're going to get in the woods.
Camp Stove and Water Filter Deals
Nothing says camping like roasting marshmallows over open flames and burning beans on the camp stove. Check out our guides to the best backpacking stoves and best camping stoves for more picks.
MSR's PocketRocket Deluxe is our top pick for a backpacking stove. It wins the title thanks to its larger burner area, which allows the flame to spread out for faster boil times and better fuel efficiency, especially with larger pots. It also fared better in the wind than smaller burners. The genius of the deluxe model is the small curved lip around the burner, which helps keep wind from getting to the base of the flame. It's a small design element, and one that you certainly want. During long-term testing, I found it more effective at maintaining a simmer in the wind, should you want to do any actual cooking.
You can put together a lighter cooking setup, but Jetboil's Stash is the lightest all-in-one system out there, and it does boil water a bit faster than the rest. The heat diffuser design speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I could only match indoors in still air), but the real appeal is how this kit packs down into itself and how simple it is to use.
Jetboil's larger all-in-one cooking system, the Flash, offers a larger-capacity 1-liter pot that combines an integrated pot and burner into an easy-to-use system. I prefer the more compact Stash above, but if you're cooking for two and are all-in on dehydrated meals, this stove is popular for good reason.
While I prefer the larger burner head of the Deluxe model above, the MSR PocketRocket 2 is lighter at 2.6 ounces compared to the Deluxe's 2.9. It still has wide enough arms to support just about any one- or two-person pot. It's simple to use, even while wearing gloves, and it's efficient. At 947-foot elevation, it boiled 1 liter of water in 3 minutes, 47 seconds. You can even get it to simmer, though the flame radius is small, so fancier cooking isn't easy.
MSR's WhisperLite series is probably the most popular backpacking stove ever made. They last forever (mine is over 30 years old and still works great), and this model, the Universal, can use just about any fuel you can imagine—white gas, kerosene, unleaded gasoline, and isobutane-propane canisters, to be precise. The only downside is that it can be fiddly compared to stoves like the Jetboil. But if you're headed out on a long trip, buying fuel as you go, this is the most flexible option out there.
This is by far the most compact two-burner stove I've tested. It's my pick for any situation where space is at a premium—whether that's canoeing or just because you have a small car. The burners are large, and with some practice, I could get a light, simmer-friendly flame. My main gripe is the windscreen, which is not the best. The Basecamp version, with fitted pots, is also on sale for $300 ($100 off).
My favorite stove in Coleman's current lineup, the Coleman Cascade 3-in-1 features heavy-duty cast-iron grates and comes with a cast-iron griddle and grill. It'll comfortably fit a 12-inch pan and a 10-inch pan side by side, and it's significantly sturdier and more robust than other Coleman stoves, making it worth the extra money if you use it often. That said, the much cheaper stove below will get you by if you're only using it a few nights a year.
This stove is ubiquitous at campgrounds for a reason. It's well-built, sturdy on a table, and just works. It's not the most powerful stove, and it lacks frills like push-button ignition, but it's capable of holding a low flame, simmering soups, and cooking scrambled eggs without browning them. It's also incredibly durable.
The MSR Gravity Autoflow filter is a must-have for backpacking with a group. To use this filter, scoop up 10 liters of water in the dirty water bag, attach the hose, connect your water bottle, and sit back and relax. The filter is good enough to keep you safe from all the usual protozoa and bacteria, and the flow rate is a solid 1.5 liters per minute when the filter is clean.
The MSR Guardian is our pick for trips with sketchy water sources because it filters down to 0.02 microns, which will even remove viruses. It is heavy at 22 ounces and may be overkill for trips in the US, but it's a great option for overseas adventures. I really like that it's designed to be self-cleaning, which makes field maintenance incredibly easy, and that it screws right onto a Nalgene bottle. Also, because it's a pump filter, it's very fast. You can crank out a couple of liters in hardly any time at all. The gravity-fed version is also on sale at Backcountry for $232 ($78 off).
Deals on Action Cameras and Gadgets
If you snap a selfie in the woods and Instagram isn't around to see it, did it happen? You'll never have to answer that question if you've got one of our favorite action cameras or 360 cameras with you.
Insta360's X6 360 camera just launched—our review will be coming soon—but the X5 is still a great option, especially on sale. The twin 1/1.28-inch sensors capture 8K video, which means you can reframe your footage to fit rectangular video formats and still have nearly 4K clips sharp enough to mix with footage shot with your phone. The dynamic range is impressive, and the X5 also has great battery life.
If you're going to turn your action camera on yourself, consider the Ace Pro 2, our top pick for vlogging. It has a great lens and sensor co-engineered with Leica, is capable of recording 8K video at up to 30 frames per second (fps), and has some pretty darn nice color even in the default settings. My guess is that the Ace Pro 3 is coming pretty soon, but this is still a good deal.
Sure, phones have some of the features you'll get with a satellite messenger, but we still think you're better off with a dedicated device. Garmin's new inReach Mini 3 Plus now offers some of those phone features—like voice messaging—along with the emergency features and excellent service worldwide. It's also still tiny, well-built, and it has great battery life. A non-Plus model, which doesn't have a speaker and mic, is also on sale.

Maltese tycoon acquitted of orchestrating murder of renowned journalist
- Published
A Maltese businessman on trial over the murder of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia has been acquitted.
Yorgen Fenech, 44, was accused of complicity in her murder and criminal association to commit murder. He denied all the charges.
In 2022, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio were jailed for 40 years over the killing of Caruana Galizia, who was an outspoken critic of the government and had uncovered networks of corruption in Malta and abroad.
She was killed by a car bomb in October 2017, with speculation at the time that senior establishment figures may have been involved.
Fenech was cleared of both counts by an 8-1 margin after eight hours of deliberation by the jury, the Reuters news agency reported.
His family members screamed with delight in the packed courtroom in Valletta, while Caruana Galizia's family wept, the agency said.
"Nine years after Daphne's brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed," her family said in a statement reported by local media.
"Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne's life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost."
Daphne Caruana Galizia gained international prominence for her investigations into corruption, money laundering and organised crime, which she published on her blog Running Commentary.
She was deeply involved in the 2016 Panama Papers investigation - a cache of confidential documents leaked from a Panamanian law firm. The investigation exposed offshore structures and triggered corruption allegations directed at top government officials in Malta.
Her shocking assassination prompted widespread public outrage and protests on the streets of Malta at the time. She was 53 years old.
During the trial, the jury heard that Fenech had wanted the journalist killed because she was about to reveal information about him.
One of Malta's richest men, Fenech is a well-known figure and was the owner of a company Caruana Galizia had written about months before her death.
Fenech denied the accusations, and during the trial he deflected blame towards his one-time close friend Keith Schembri, former chief of staff of then-prime minister Joseph Muscat and a target of Caruana Galizia's stories.
Muscat, who was never linked to the murder, stepped down in January 2020 due to the political fallout from the assassination.
Police told the court that Schembri had never been a suspect, and he has denied any role in the murder.
In 2025, two men - Robert Agius and Jamie Vella - were jailed for life by a Maltese judge for having supplied the bomb.

Since we were unable to identify the video's original source, we could not definitively confirm its authenticity. However, the clip predated the August 2026 flooding in Nepal and displayed visual inconsistencies that pointed to AI generation.
As Nepal suffered from catastrophic flooding that left more than 900 people dead and thousands of others missing in late August 2026, a video appearing to show an elephant wading into floodwaters to rescue a man and carrying him to shore circulated online.
The video spread on multiple platforms, including Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, Reddit and YouTube, garnering millions of views. Snopes readers also contacted us to ask whether it was real.
"In Nepal Elephants were saving people," one X post caption read (archived). "What an amazing world we live in."
(X user @TonyGunk123.)
The earliest version of the video that we could find was posted to YouTube on Aug. 5, 2026 (archived).
The video contained multiple anomalies commonly found in AI-generated media. Our analysis of screenshots revealed a lack of detail, harsh or unnatural shadows, inconsistent skin color and texture, degraded quaity, object bleeding and misshapen extremities.
(Snopes Illustration.)
Although the Aug. 5 video featured a song as the audio, in other iterations of the post, people spoke in the background and yelled as the man appeared to climb onto the elephant.
The text over one such video was in Hindi (archived), reading "Watch Nature's Display/View" and "How the elephant saved a human" (translation via native speaker). However, the audio was in Thai — further evidence it was not captured during the August 2026 flooding in Nepal. One man can be heard saying "flood" while another woman says, "It's an elephant" before asking, "What is it going to do?" (translation via native speaker).
Several commenters on Reddit and Facebook claimed the video depicted a real incident in which an elephant rescued her caretaker as a stunt at an elephant park in Thailand.
"The story originates from a genuine, widely celebrated 2016 video filmed at the Elephant Nature Park in Chiang Mai, Thailand," one Facebook user wrote. "The clip captures a real moment where a young elephant named Kham Lha rushed into a fast-flowing river to 'rescue' her favorite human caretaker, Darrick, whom she believed was drowning."
Although that story was authentic and KhamLa is a real elephant at Elephant Nature Park in Thailand, the widely shared video of the 2016 incident is not the same video that spread in August 2026.
Another article claimed the video was authentic and depicted a real 2017 incident in which elephants helped rescue hundreds of people from a flooded Nepali safari park. We found no proof the video was connected the the 2017 flooding. The image attached to the article was also AI-generated, as evidenced by the man's disfigured fingers and the merging of his arm and shirt sleeve (archived).
Unlike the 2016 video of KhamLa swimming to her caretaker or the 2017 news reports regarding elephants helping to rescue people, no reputable news outlets reported on the August 2026 video or confirmed it was authentic.
In sum, the video appearing to show an elephant rescuing a man from floodwaters is not from the August 2026 Nepal floods. The clip also displayed visual inconsistencies that pointed to AI generation, such as unnatural lighting, texture movement and shapes.
For further reading, we confirmed that CCTV footage authentically showed floodwaters destroying the Gyirong Port, a Nepal-China border crossing.

Gloria Steinem death: Pioneering voice of modern feminism, dies at 92
Steinem died away at her home in New York City, surrounded by loved ones Wednesday, her foundation announced in an Instagram post Thursday
Gloria Steinem, the journalist and women’s activist who became an icon of the modern feminist movement, died Wednesday at 92 years old, her foundation announced in an Instagram post.
Steinem was a leader of the second-wave feminist movement in the late 1960s, challenging traditional domestic roles, advocating for women to pursue higher education and careers as well as promoting reproductive freedom. Her leadership inspired generations of women to aim big and challenge the norm.
Recognized everywhere by her signature streaked hair, parted down the middle and large aviator glasses, Steinem was an unmistakable presence. She spent much of her life as an advocate, traveling and frequently speaking at universities, community centers, rallies and public marches.
“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” the post read in part, her foundation wrote in the social media post.
“Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor.”
Steinem passed away at her New York City home, surrounded by loved ones.
Before becoming a dedicated activist, Steinem’s career originated in journalism. That included a 1963 undercover assignment exposing degrading conditions in Hugh Hefner’s Playboy empire – an effort she ultimately regretted.
In 1971, she co-founded “Ms. Magazine,” the first major publication to be owned, run and written by women. It broke the traditional mold by publishing stories that raised awareness about issues facing women and girls at a time when most mainstream media were not.
But her focus shifted years later during a meeting where women forcefully advocated for abortion rights.
Following the reversal of Roe v Wade, Steinem, who had a secret illegal abortion at age 22, told the Associated Press in a 2022 email: “That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me.” She added, “Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy.”
Steinem viewed her role as “an entrepreneur of social change”.
Throughout her career, she launched the National Women's Political Caucus alongside former Reps. Bella Abzug and Shirley Chisholm, as well as author Betty Friedan, whose 1963 landmark The Feminine Mystique inaugurated second-wave feminism. Her organizational legacy also includes founding the Ms. Foundation for Women, Voters for Choice, the Women's Media Center and the Coalition of Labor Union Women.
“I want to do justice to the women I meet, to tell their stories,” she told The New Yorker magazine in 2015. “It’s making connections, and using myself to listen, because we can’t empower women without listening to their stories.”
Steinem also became a stylish icon of a feminist movement, which she stressed must represent women of every race.
“If you’ve suffered discrimination, you’re sensitive to it on every level. I learned feminism largely from Black women. Women of color basically invented feminism,” she told The New Yorker.
In 2013, then-President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor.
“From reluctant spokesperson to a beacon of positive change, hers is a singular journey – an American leader who can speak to us all,” film and theater director Julie Taymor said of Steinem in a 2017 New York Times interview.
Taymor later directed the 2020 movie The Glorias, adapted from Steinem’s 2015 best-selling autobiography My Life on the Road. Steinem was also the subject of the 2011 HBO documentary Gloria: In Her Own Words and a 2018 theatrical production, Gloria: A Life.
Steinem was born in Toledo, Ohio, on March 25, 1934, to a Presbyterian mother, Ruth, and a Jewish father, Leo.
In 2020, she told The Independent about her relationship with her father after her mother’s nervous breakdown.
“He was one of the most irresponsible people on Earth, and it didn't matter,” Gloria recalled fondly. “Because he was kind, he was funny, he treated me as his buddy and his companion. I am personally thankful to him that I’m friends with all my old lovers, because they were good men. [And] because I had a good father, I knew they were good men.”
Steinem began working as a freelance journalist after graduating from Smith College.
In 1963, she spent 11 days working undercover as a Playboy bunny for an assignment for Show magazine. Her seminal two-part investigation, “A Bunny’s Tale,” detailed the low pay and misogynistic conditions faced by Playboy bunnies—who were originally waitstaff. The article was later adapted into a 1985 television film starring Kirstie Alley.
She helped launch New York Magazine in 1968, where her essay “After Black Power, Women's Liberation” cemented her status as a prominent feminist voice during a period of turbulent social transition.
Ms. Magazine, which she co-founded in 1971, addressed topics like abortion, sexism, equal pay, and domestic abuse. This marked a significant departure from conventional women's publications focused primarily on beauty, cooking, and supporting husbands.
An early edition published the names of 52 women, including Steinem, who had undergone abortions. It demanded the legalization of the procedure ahead of the landmark 1973 Roe v Wade decision, which established the constitutional right to abortion in the U.S. for nearly five decades.
'QUINTESSENCE OF FEMALE REVOLUTION'
Steinem frequently challenged the traditional boundaries of marriage. “Women are not going to be equal outside the home until men are equal in it,” she said.
She had no children and remained unmarried until age 66, when she wed David Bale, a South African environmentalist and businessman who was the father of actor Christian Bale.
Reflecting on her decision, she stated: “I hope this proves what feminists have always said – that feminism is about the ability to choose what’s right at each time of our lives.” David Bale passed away from brain cancer in 2003.
Steinem maintained her active career into her eighties. Her written works include 1986’s Marilyn: Norma Jean, which focuses on Marilyn Monroe, alongside Revolution from Within: A Book of Self-Esteem, which explores personal growth, as well as multiple essay collections.
In 1993, she conceived and narrated Multiple Personalities: The Search for Deadly Memories, an Emmy Award-winning HBO documentary on child abuse, and produced Lifetime’s Better Off Dead. She also hosted Woman, a Viceland series documenting violence against women.
Biographer Carolyn Heilbrun, author of the 1995 book Education of a Woman: The Life of Gloria Steinem, described her as “the epitome of female beauty and the quintessence of female revolution”.

'Chavanni se rupiya' jibe draws Yogi's ire as CM attacks Akhilesh's 'cheap language'
At an event in Mathura, Yogi Adityanath accused Akhilesh Yadav of using cheap language in politics. He said the remarks insulted democracy, historical memory and Uttar Pradesh's public institutions.
Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Thursday launched a sharp attack on the Samajwadi Party and its leadership, accusing party chief Akhilesh Yadav of using “cheap language” and mocking democracy through his recent remarks against political leaders.
Speaking at the Panchayat AajTak event in Mathura, Yogi said that while the world was discussing education, skilling and deep technology, the Samajwadi Party was using words such as “dog” and “cat” for its own political leaders.
He also hit back at Akhilesh Yadav over his recent “from a 25-paise coin to a rupee” remark targeting RLD chief and Union Minister Jayant Chaudhary.
Yogi described the remark as an insult to democracy and said the language used by the SP chief reflected his mindset. “In a democracy, people are called Janardan. But the SP turns its own leaders into dogs and cats. This shows how it is making a mockery of democracy,” Yogi said.
YOGI HITS BACK OVER CHAVANNI REMARK
Referring to Akhilesh’s remark about Jayant Chaudhary, Yogi said BJP and NDA leaders had described it as an insult not only to the RLD chief but also to the legacy of former Prime Minister Chaudhary Charan Singh and the farming community.
Yogi said such remarks reflected the mindset that prevailed in Uttar Pradesh before 2017. Yogi also accused the Samajwadi Party of failing to respect historical figures and freedom fighters.
He recalled an old incident in Gorakhpur involving the inauguration of a park named after revolutionary freedom fighter Pandit Ram Prasad Bismil.
Yogi claimed that the then education minister in the SP government had referred to Bismil as “Bismillah Sahib” instead of using the revolutionary’s name.
According to Yogi, when someone on the stage pointed out that the reference was incorrect and that the park was named after revolutionary Pandit Ram Prasad Bismil, not shehnai maestro Ustad Bismillah Khan, the minister allegedly viewed the correction through a political lens.
“Those who could not even distinguish between revolutionary Pandit Ram Prasad Bismil and shehnai player Ustad Bismillah Khan, you can easily imagine where they must have taken school education in Uttar Pradesh,” Yogi said.
‘CHEATING WAS MADE A BIRTHRIGHT’
Yogi also accused the previous government of promoting cheating in examinations and irregularities in government recruitment.
He alleged that during that period, “recommendation slips” were given more importance than merit and diktats were given greater importance than reason.
He further accused the previous government of giving greater importance to sycophancy towards one family than to India’s heritage.
Yogi claimed that Uttar Pradesh had now moved beyond that era and said there was no “policy paralysis” in the state under his government.

A common cause given for leg pain is muscle strain, and this may be attributed to standing for a long time, exercising incorrectly, or getting older. But sometimes, there may be something different going on. A pain that begins in the lower back and radiates down the buttock and to the leg, may indicate irritation or pressure on the sciatic nerve, and is referred to as sciatica.
The largest nerve in the body is the sciatic nerve. It extends from the lower back through buttocks and down each leg. If a nerve in the lower back is compressed or inflamed, it may result in pain that radiates down this nerve.
How do you know if you have sciatica pain?
Sciatica isn’t always typical leg pain. It can cause a sudden electric-like, burning or tearing sensation down the back of the thigh and sometimes into the calf or foot from the lower back or buttock.
Some people may also experience tingling, numbness or weakness in the affected leg. The pain can worsen after sitting for prolonged periods, or after coughing, sneezing or certain movements.
In some cases, the discomfort may be primarily experienced in the leg, and there may be very little discomfort in the back. This can be one explanation as to why people may confuse sciatica with leg muscle or joint pain.
What causes sciatica?
A common cause of sciatica is a slipped disc or a bulging disc in the lower portion of the spine. The discs between the bones of our spine work like cushions. If one of them bulges or tears, it can compress an adjacent nerve.
Other reasons include changes in the spine with age, constriction of the spinal canal, bone growth and, less frequently, injury or other spinal diseases.
Not all people suffering from sciatica require a surgery. With the right kind of rest, and the use of the remedies as prescribed by a physician, physiotherapy and a gradual return to normal activity, many people get better. Treatment depends on the cause and severity of the symptoms.
When to det a doctor’s advice
Some back or leg pain may get better over time, but certain symptoms shouldn’t be ignored. You should seek medical advice if the pain is severe, keeps returning, lasts for several weeks or is affecting your ability to walk, work or perform everyday activities.
Numbness or worsening weakness in the leg, trouble with urination or defecation or numbness around the inner thighs and genitals are emergencies.
Avoiding making every leg ache a diagnosis of sciatica is also important. Similar symptoms can occur due to problems involving the muscles, joints, blood vessels or other nerves, which is why it is important to consult a doctor. Your doctor can evaluate your symptoms, motion, muscle strength and reflexes and might suggest imaging if needed.
In addition to this, keeping a healthy weight, being physically active, strengthening core muscles and avoiding long periods of sitting can help keep your spine healthy.
The bottom line is: leg pain that radiates from the back or buttock is not necessarily from the leg and can be from the spine. Early identification of warning signs and proper diagnosis can prevent symptoms from becoming severe and can help to expedite a return to normal life.
(Dr. Kalidutta Das is chief and director of spine services, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital. Kaliduttadas@gmail.com)

More than a kilometer underground, in what used to be a gold mine, inside a tank filled with tons of liquid xenon, “something” struck the nucleus of an atom. The tiny collision left an unusual energy signature that researchers are still unable to explain, but the scientists behind the experiment believe this could be the most convincing physical evidence of dark matter to date.
Dark matter is one of the most important and elusive substances in astrophysics. Though it makes up about 85 percent of the matter in the universe, we can’t observe it directly because it doesn’t interact with light or much else. Most of the evidence for its existence comes from its gravitational effects, the mass of dark matter having tugged on the atoms of the early universe to form stars, galaxies, and the vast web of intergalactic structures visible today.
But the enigma of dark matter is complex. Scientists don’t even know what it is made of, whether it’s a single type of particle or an entire set of particles that interact with one another in ways we do not yet understand. The most fantastical explanations even suggest that it consists of black holes. One of the most widely studied theories on dark matter has dubbed its components WIMPs, short for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles, meaning the particles have a mass and thus a gravitational pull but otherwise interact weakly with conventional matter.
If WIMPs exist and are part of the dark matter of our galaxy, enormous quantities of them could be passing through the Earth continuously without leaving a trace. However, it is possible that, very occasionally, one might interact with an atomic nucleus and transfer some of its energy to it, which is why an inexplicable collision is exciting in the world of particle physics.
In the strange disturbance recorded at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in South Dakota, the detector monitoring the tank recorded that a xenon nucleus received energy and recoiled. Though researchers have not yet been able to satisfactorily explain the cause, some models suggest a WIMP could produce such a reaction.
The scientists stated that this single event is statistically too small to be considered the discovery of a new particle. In 220 days of observations conducted between 2023 and 2024, only one such anomaly occurred. “With only one event, we don’t want to get ahead of ourselves. We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input,” Rick Gaitskell, a professor at Brown University and a member of the team leading the project, said in a press release.
The team behind the experiment has published their study as a preprint, meaning it has not yet been peer reviewed. They have, however, presented the results to the scientific community at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics Conference in Japan.
Discoveries made around dark matter tend to elicit this kind of restrained excitement. When in November 2025 a team of Japanese astronomers announced that they had seen signs of dark matter in the Milky Way, they too advised the research community not to count their chickens.
But even if cautious, there are reasons for enthusiasm. If the impact was caused by dark matter, there is enough evidence for researchers to begin characterizing the responsible particle. For example, the team has already calculated that, under the WIMP models they analyzed, the particle is about 200 times more massive than a proton. The impact could help us understand how this type of matter interacts with conventional matter.
The team has also been examining other possible explanations. Paradoxically, in experiments as sensitive as this one, atypical events are not all that uncommon. That’s why SURF has various methods of filtering out background noise and detecting interference caused by known particles or radiation. This event withstood that scrutiny. So far, the researchers have not found an explanation among these known sources that fits what they observed.
“We understand our detector and the backgrounds so well that even a single outstanding event, like the one we found, is important,” said Sam Eriksen, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol and the study’s lead author. “We expect dark matter events to be extremely rare, so only a handful could mark the first detection of WIMP dark matter.”

The world is whiffing on its biggest climate goal
So where, exactly, does the climate fight go next?
For more than a decade, 1.5 degrees Celsius has been the watchword — er, watch temperature? — of climate policy. If the world could hold warming at that level, it could stave off some of climate change’s worst effects, researchers believed.
Well…there’s bad news on that front. A major new assessment from the United Nations concludes the world will inevitably pass the 1.5-degree benchmark within the next few years, barring some celestial intervention. Under current policies, we’re on track to hit 2.6 degrees of warming between now and 2100. And while that’s not quite a Mad Max scenario, it will very much change how humans live. (More on that in just a minute!)
In many ways, the new report formalizes what researchers and policymakers have warned for years. Last November, UN Secretary-General António Guterres made international headlines when he acknowledged that a “temporary overshoot” of 1.5 degrees was “inevitable.”
People understandably fixated on that “inevitable” bit. But “temporary” matters, too. As this new assessment repeatedly stresses, the efforts we make now to cut emissions and remove carbon from the atmosphere will still ultimately determine the size and duration of the much-feared “overshoot.”
Go a little deeper
The realities of a rapidly warming world also point to a second, equally urgent task: Even as we strive to limit climate change, we need to brace for the warming we can no longer prevent.
That approach, known as “climate adaptation,” has not always been popular among advocates or philanthropists. Adaptation is “a kind of laziness, an arrogant faith in our ability to react in time to save our skins,” Al Gore wrote in his 1992 book Earth in the Balance.
Gore has since changed his tune, however, and so have many others. Among the most prominent converts is the billionaire philanthropist Bill Gates, who has gradually made adaptation a larger piece of his climate agenda.
Last October, Gates released a controversial memo arguing that climate policy should measure success by improvements in human welfare “even more than” changes in emissions or temperature. But there’s no reason we can’t advance both goals together.
Many countries and US states already have, in fact. After a 2003 heat wave killed roughly 15,000 people in France, the country created a “robust” national heat plan that included early warnings and checks on vulnerable residents. The system is credited with making subsequent heat waves less deadly (although a historic heat wave earlier this summer still caused 5,700 excess deaths).
Other adaptations will be far more disruptive. Fiji, for instance, has begun relocating coastal villages threatened by rising sea levels. And whatever adjustments society makes, life in a warming world will still be more difficult and more expensive.
Maybe that’s why “climate adaptation” no longer sounds like laziness: There is clearly no easy or low-effort way out of all of this.
One link for later
➨ Beware the “loneliness economy.” A booming cottage industry of paid apps, meet-ups, and clubs promise they can make you friends…for a fee. But many of these products and services do little more than sell the idea of community.

In my 20s, I fell in love with my partner's ambition.
His dream was to own a restaurant, and I admired his willingness to reject a traditional 9-to-5 to build something of his own.
He entered the industry as a teenager, worked his way up to general manager at a local restaurant by his mid-20s, and eventually became a partner there. By 30, he had achieved the dream he'd spent years pursuing: becoming the restaurant's sole owner.
Watching him move closer to that goal over the years was exciting, and I was proud to support him along the way — but now, in my early 30s, I'm realizing how much of my own future I've put on hold while waiting for that dream to financially pay off.
At times, the restaurant has felt like a third person in our relationship
At first, supporting him felt like laying the groundwork for the future we were building together.
When we were younger, money wasn't a major concern, and I believed that the financial instability we felt at times was a temporary trade-off.
But dating a restaurant owner means the business is often a third presence in our relationship. Anxieties about payroll, rent, equipment repairs, and loans don't go away when the workday ends.
During slower months, when every dollar he earned went back into the business, I became the one responsible for keeping us afloat. I paid our bills. Vacations were canceled. On more than one occasion, I had to borrow money from my parents to make rent.
Over time, his career began shaping mine, too. I'm a writer, and I've always wanted the freedom to pursue my own creative ambitions, but our circumstances required me to prioritize stability instead.
While my partner reinvested much of what he earned back into the restaurant, I spent years staying in corporate roles because we needed the security of a steady paycheck.
The irony isn't lost on me. One of the qualities that I was so attracted to in the first place was his willingness to reject a conventional career path and pursue his dreams.
Supporting his ability to do that, though, has often required me to choose a more conventional path myself.
Now, I've started to feel like we're running out of time
In our 20s, delaying major life milestones didn't feel particularly consequential. For years, I told myself that I could wait.
If we weren't ready to buy a house, there was always next year. If money that might have gone toward savings had to go back into the restaurant, I told myself it was temporary. Even through the setbacks and financial stress, I believed we were investing in our future.
Then I reached the end of my 20s.
Friends started buying homes, getting married, having children, and building wealth. I was genuinely happy for them, but watching them move forward also made me worry we'd fallen behind.
At times, it felt like I was standing on the sidelines, cheering on my partner's dream while waiting for our own life to begin.
Surviving cancer changed what I want from my future
Another turning point came when I was diagnosed with breast cancer at 30.
Before cancer, the future felt limitless. Afterward, I understood how dangerous it is to assume there will always be more time. Cancer taught me that "someday" isn't a guarantee, and I became less willing to postpone the life I wanted.
In the aftermath of treatment, I found myself craving stability in a way I never had before. I wanted to feel like my life was moving forward.
I started asking myself the questions that had been lingering in the back of my mind for years. Would we ever own a home? Would I be happier if money weren't always a source of stress? Had I spent so much energy supporting someone else's dream that I'd neglected parts of my own?
Eventually, I found myself asking a question that once would have felt unthinkable: Is love enough?
I've learned that multiple things can be true
These aren't feelings I've kept to myself.
Over the years, we've had countless conversations about money and the future we both want. My partner has never dismissed how I feel, and he's deeply appreciative of the sacrifices I've made.
I don't regret supporting his dream, but that doesn't cancel out my grief for the milestones I sometimes wish we'd reached by now: a home, more financial security, and a greater sense of certainty about the future.
I've realized I can be proud of what he's building and still wish our path required fewer sacrifices. I'm still figuring out what that means for us.
I don't want him to abandon what he's worked so hard to build, but I also don't want to confuse patience with postponement, or love with an indefinite willingness to wait. Most of all, I don't want to wake up one day and realize I spent too much of my life waiting for it to start.

England has experienced its driest July since records began in 1836, receiving only 6.5mm of rainfall – 10% of the country’s long-term meteorological average for the month. Wales also experienced its driest-ever July, while Northern Ireland recorded its eighth driest. Scotland was the only country in the UK not to set new records but still received only 69% of its average rainfall for July compared with the long-term average. Southern England faced the worst of the dry conditions with some areas, including the Sussex coast, receiving less than 0.2mm of rain in July. This resulted in widespread low moisture content within the soil, enabling temperatures to reach the high 30s celsius.
Looking ahead, despite notable spells of rain in the north, parts of southern England may receive only the odd shower for the rest of August. Throughout the summer, forecast models have hinted at more unsettled weather reaching the south-east of England at a 10-day range. However, as time edged closer the rain was largely confined to north-western parts of Britain, failing to reach the south-east with any significance. With much uncertainty within forecast models, the risk of this dry period persisting is not out of the question.
There is a disturbance in the Atlantic, approximately 1,000 miles east of the Lesser Antilles. The National Hurricane Centre has predicted an 80% chance of the cyclone forming in the next 48 hours as a short-lived tropical depression. If such a system does strengthen, it will become the fourth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season and would be named Dolly. Regardless of any development, there will be a risk of gusty winds and heavy rainfall in Lesser Antilles on Friday night and into Saturday. This year’s strong El Niño is expected to play a significant role in lessening hurricane activity within the Atlantic.
In India, the monsoon continues to cause devastation, particularly in eastern regions where flooding in Assam has caused 100 deaths as of 10 August. Flooding caused by rivers overflowing has resulted in 700,000 people being displaced over the last month. This includes 300,000 displaced near the Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in Asia. The monsoon also brought significant lightning, which resulted in the deaths of 14 people in eastern India on the 4 August, including 10 in the district of Giridih. Many of the dead were farm workers, caught in open agricultural fields where there is a lack of shelter to provide safety when such storms arrive.

Russians, sex tourism and now 5,000 US sailors: What to know about Pattaya as USS Abraham Lincoln finally docks
The Vietnam War launched the resort's sex tourism
US Navy aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln has steamed into Thailand's Laem Chabang on Wednesday with roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines who have spent 286 days at sea.
They arrive amid reports of mental health concerns and deteriorating conditions on board.
The Lincoln was deployed in November last year and was involved in the US naval blockade and combat operations in the war with Iran. It set a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea, according to Democratic lawmakers.
Typically naval deployments are for between six and nine months, but during times of conflict that can be extended.
There's no getting around the fact that Thailand's seaside resort of Pattaya has a lingering reputation for sex tourism, even though that's only part of the story for the city that's an expected shore leave destination of crew members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
The 5,000 or so sailors and Marines will be following in the wake of millions of other tourists, including a significant number of US military personnel who take part every year in major land and sea exercises nearby with their Thai counterparts.
Social media ahead of the Lincoln's visit has been awash with jibes about lusty sailors, but recent visitors say the development of more family-friendly attractions makes the new Pattaya overshadow its former seedy self.
Many US Navy ships dock at nearby deep-water facilities such as Laem Chabang Port and the Sattahip Royal Thai Navy Base, both less than an hour away by road.
Shore leave spending boosts the local economy, and mission duties often include community outreach in and around the city, such as specialized medical care for villagers or putting in volunteer time at orphanages.
But when hundreds or thousands of sailors have a chance to enjoy some onshore liberty, the navy deploys members of its Shore Patrol to work side by side with Thai police to defuse any trouble.
Navy personnel are likely to have been reminded that, though rarely enforced, the law in Thailand technically bans prostitution, and paying for sex is a punishable offense under Article 134 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the legal framework for the U.S. armed forces.
The military connection goes back at least to the Vietnam War era, when at its height, 40,000-50,000 U.S. service personnel were stationed in Thailand, largely in support of that conflict's air operations. Bases used by U.S. forces dotted Thailand, and all attracted their share of nightlife activities.
Pattaya was close to both the Sattahip naval base and the Thai Navy's U-Tapao airfield, which hosted U.S. Air Force B-52 bombers.
Elizabeth Becker, author of "Overbooked: The Exploding Business of Travel and Tourism," wrote that American GIs during the Vietnam War flocked to Pattaya, a once-quiet fishing village, "and it turned into a raunchy seaside playground."
The military facilities brought a continuous stream of personnel through Pattaya, while the 1966 Entertainment Places Act created a legal gray area allowing the sex trade to operate semiopenly in bars and massage parlors — as something of a private arrangement between customer and employee — despite a 1960 law criminalizing prostitution.
Pattaya also had a beach that could be reached relatively easily from Bangkok, which positioned it well for a transition to civilian visitors after the withdrawal of U.S. military forces in 1976.
Pattaya's infrastructure of go-go clubs and other entertainment venues was then marketed to travelers arriving in greater numbers due to cheaper air travel and a boom in package tours. Sex tourism became entrenched.
Severe economic disparities brought many young women and men from Thailand's poor northeastern Isan region to earn wages far exceeding rural agricultural incomes by working in Pattaya's lucrative nightlife sector, allowing them to send money home to their families.
Prostitution is culturally taboo, but sex work has quietly flourished in Thai society for centuries, with the domestic market dwarfing the more glitzy one for foreigners.
Pattaya underwent another evolution in the 1990s, with a new wave of tourists coming from what had been the Soviet Union, after communism there collapsed in late 1991.
Embracing modern globalized tourism, the newcomers came on direct charter flights, even from provincial cities, to the civilian airport at U-Tapao, benefiting from a 30-day visa-free agreement. Signs in Cyrillic sprouted around Pattaya as businesses catered to this new clientele.
Russians were not the only people calling Pattaya their home away from home.
The agreeable climate and allegedly laissez-faire attitude of local law enforcement attracted fugitives from justice and criminals from all over the world, including Russian, Eastern European, and Western European gangsters as well as drug-dealing motorcycle gangs from Australia.
Pattaya has tried with some success this century to rebrand itself as a family destination, with parks, malls and luxury resorts largely in surrounding areas that attract large numbers of Thais and visitors from other Asian nations.
A popular water park is themed around Cartoon Network shows. The Nong Nooch Tropical Botanical Garden displays vast stretches of flora and hosts cultural shows. The Sanctuary of Truth Museum is an ornate all-wood structure over 100 meters (yards) tall.
There are also golf courses, running events and day trips to nearby islands.
Travelers can still get a taste of old Pattaya with a nocturnal stroll down "Walking Street," at the heart of the city's racy nightlife district.

Jalgaon: In Bodwad town, an angry mob went on a rampage, vandalising property, pelting stones and torching vehicles after suspecting a private coaching class operator of sexually assaulting a minor female student. As the situation threatened to spiral out of control, police had to resort to tear gas and a lathi-charge to disperse the crowd. The situation was brought under control following the deployment of a large police force, and Superintendent of Police Shrikant Dhivare is monitoring the developments.
The suspect, a resident of Jamthi in Bodwad taluka, runs private coaching classes in Bodwad for students from Classes 5 to 12. On Wednesday evening, the operator allegedly engaged in obscene behaviour and made inappropriate demands of a minor girl, forcibly making her sit in his car.
Some youths spotted the pair in the car, and a mob, enraged by the suspicion that the girl was being sexually assaulted, vandalised the coaching centre and the vehicle. They subsequently proceeded to the operator's native village, Jamthi, where they allegedly engaged in arson and stone-pelting, causing damage to vehicles.

Man City buy costly new midfield - but have they overlooked Haaland cover?
- Published
Manchester City have completed their squad overhaul - including a fully revamped midfield - to the tune of £458m, a new Premier League record for a summer window.
But that eyewatering sum does not tell the full story.
New Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca received the full backing of director of football Hugo Viana in his first transfer window in charge after replacing Pep Guardiola. Indeed, City's record transfer fee was twice broken this summer.
A joint-British record £125m was spent on Maresca's former Chelsea skipper Enzo Fernandez after £116m was committed on Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest. Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi, 18, was also brought in for £86m. The trio accounted for the bulk of City's summer incomings.
The departures of captain Bernardo Silva, 2024 Ballon d'Or winner Rodri, Tijjani Reijnders and Nico Gonzalez means the City midfield has been completely transformed.
Senior club sources are said to be delighted by the business done not only during the past couple of months but in January too, when plans were brought forward to sign long-term targets Antoine Semenyo and Marc Guehi.
And if the clock is rewound further back, Manchester City's rebuild of the team that won the 2023 Champions League really began in January 2025 after a difficult start to that season.
Just four players remain from the starting eleven and substitutes from the night they beat Inter Milan in Istanbul to win the continent's biggest club prize.
Maresca now has the luxury of calling upon two established players in almost every position. City feel the squad is stronger at this point than at the beginning of last season which they believe has been achieved by remaining calm and trusting the transfer strategy.
However some big questions remain.
How will their new midfield signings all fit together?
And, despite the vast amount of money spent, have they actually left themselves without a back-up to Erling Haaland?
- Deadlines, acrimony and a record as Man City back Maresca for Fernandez deal 
  - Published23 hours ago
- Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to £65m Man City move 
  - Published1 day ago
Selection dilemmas for Maresca
City's expenditure of £542m on new signings since the turn of the year will grab the headlines, but it often goes under the radar how well they do at selling fringe players.
During this same period, they have recouped £334m, including £75m for Savinho, who scored only two Premier League goals during his time at City, as well as £65m for Rodri and £52m for Reijnders.
It gives City a net spend of £208m in 2026, which will be further bolstered by Tottenham's obligation to buy Omar Marmoush for £60m at the end of his loan spell next season.
Sources had said during the summer that they were operating on a one-out, one-in policy and Maresca managed to replace almost every player that departed, aside from Nico Gonzalez and Marmoush.
With the side well stocked at left-back, it is felt that Nico O'Reilly will play more in his natural midfield position to ease the Gonzalez gap.
The club believe the record fee for Fernandez is justified by acquiring a proven winner at the highest level that will strengthen the midfield. Anderson was the summer's number one target, while 18-year-old Bouaddi is seen as having all the attributes to develop into a world class talent.
City have won back-to-back games at the start of the Premier League season and Maresca will now have a selection dilemma each game as he possesses an embarrassment of riches to choose from.
The question is how the Italian will now fit them all together.
Analysis: How will Maresca use his new midfielders?
Fernandez, Bouaddi, and Anderson are all players comfortable across multiple positions in Maresca's system.
Maresca has moved between a box and a diamond shape in midfield at City. The main difference between the two shapes is that the former has two natural holding midfielders and the second a single holding midfielder.
Against Bournemouth, Guehi paired Anderson at the base of midfield. O'Reilly, the left-sided attacking midfielder, was joined by right-back Rico Lewis, moving in-field to form the box.
Against Crystal Palace, left-back Josko Gvardiol and attacking midfielder O'Reilly flanked number 10 Rayan Cherki as the three ahead of Anderson in what looked like a diamond.
1 of 2
Anderson anchoring the midfield suggests Maresca sees him as Rodri's successor.
While full of praise for Bouaddi, Maresca has stressed his youth, a nod to the fact that he will likely deputise for Anderson.
