Charles Perrottet has repeatedly denied taking payments from the property developer Jean Nassif to achieve political outcomes for him, telling a corruption inquiry he cannot explain a message sent after a Nassif development was refused, which said: “Charles fucked this whole thing.”
Charles, the brother of former New South Wales premier Dominic Perrottet, has previously told the Independent Commission Against Corruption he would lie to Nassif about doing political work for him. On Thursday, he said he may also have regularly lied to close friend Christian Ellis, who is named in Icac’s allegations. He rejected the accusation he was fabricating evidence to Icac.
As part of its inquiry into alleged corruption in the NSW Liberals, Icac is investigating the allegation that conservative factional figures Charles Perrottet, Jeremy Greenwood and Ellis received prohibited donations totalling $2m from Nassif or his company Toplace between 2020 and 2023 in exchange for political outcomes, as well as the recruitment or renewal of members to the Liberal party, a practice known as branch stacking. Branch stacking is not itself illegal.
Ellis is overseas and has not responded to Icac, while Greenwood will appear before the commission next week.
Charles Perrottet has previously said he would regularly mislead Nassif, adding a “political flavour” to advice in order to chase up payments for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, a company controlled by Ellis and Greenwood.
On Thursday, the commission heard an exchange sent by Greenwood to Ellis in April 2020, expressing concern about losing Toplace as a client when Nassif’s Cherrybrook development proposal was refused after the Hills shire council did not support it. Charles Perrottet said he did not know what the message – in which Greenwood wrote “Charles fucked this whole thing” – meant.
He was asked about a subsequent exchange between him and Ellis in which he detailed steps to assist with Toplace developments, including a call he wrote he would make to the NSW Liberal MP and former Hills shire councillor Robyn Preston.
On Thursday, Charles Perrottet said he could not recall calling Preston. The counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, asked if he would “regularly lie to Christian Ellis at that time to tell him you were doing some things and not others?”
“I may have,” said Charles Perrottet, suggesting it might have been “to sound supportive”.
Dwyer, noting he had also said he would lie to Nassif, suggested that “actually the fabrication is the evidence you’re giving to the commission because you want to make it sound like you didn’t take the active steps that are clearly set out in this text”.
“No,” said Charles Perrottet.
Later, he was asked about a message from Greenwood to the Toplace executive Sharangan Maheswaran, also named in Icac’s allegations, in 2021, asking for payment from Nassif, or “Charles is just going to cut the relationship”. After Maheswaran offered to pass on the message, Greenwood expressed concern that Nassif might see it as a threat.
“Most certainly, but sometimes JN [Jean Nassif] gives into threats,” Maheswaran wrote back. Greenwood wrote that he wanted Nassif to understand that “yes, sure, we’re all friends, but Charles can’t keep exhausting the capital he has, which he gets on the back of other people’s work in the faction … while then having to make excuses because our agreements weren’t honoured”.
Maheswaran, who is named in a separate allegation, has previously denied any wrongdoing. He will appear before Icac next week.
Under repeated questioning from Dwyer, Charles Perrottet rejected the suggestion it was “clear as day … that Mr Greenwood shared your view, as expressed to Jean Nassif, that he had to hand over the money in order to achieve the political outcomes”.
“No,” said Charles Perrottet.
‘Meeting of the minds’
On Thursday, Charles Perrottet was asked about a 2020 meeting to discuss the recruitment of conservative right members amid a factional fight with centre-right Liberals to take over branches in the Hills shire. He said he supported the plan “to have more balance” in branches, but repeatedly rejected that Nassif was financially supporting branch stacking efforts.
The inquiry has previously heard Charles Perrottet created a group chat called “Back to Basics” in August 2020, adding his brothers Dominic and Jean-Claude Perrottet, Damien Tudehope, Ellis and two other conservative faction members.
“Gents, I believe it’s time for a WPH [West Pennant Hills] meeting of the minds. Lots has been going on, and some concerning developments this week in both the left and right has accelerated the need for us to get together and discuss,” he wrote. “This group share the same values.”
Charles Perrottet was asked about an agenda he shared with the group before the meeting at Tudehope’s West Pennant Hills home, including the item “Staffing support or new models to ensure progress and open discussion”. The day after the September 2020 meeting, Ellis provided an update to the group saying the “short-term goals” moving forward included “private clients for retainers for staff”.
Charles Perrottet rejected the suggestion that his first message was setting the agenda for a potential plan for private individuals to pay retainers to support branch stacking efforts, saying it “may have been a point of discussion that Christian wanted to raise at the meeting”.
The commission heard that the day after Ellis’s message, $148,500 was deposited via cheque from Toplace to Beckington. Charles Perrottet said the timing of the payment was a “coincidence”, “unless you speak to Christian [Ellis] and ask him”.
After Dwyer said that Ellis was in the UK and had chosen not to participate in hearings, Charles Perrottet said: “I’m aware. I’m not sure he hasn’t chosen to participate. I’m aware he’s in the UK. If you can’t ask him, I would ask Jeremy.”
Tudehope, who gave evidence to the inquiry in its second week, told the commission he could not recall the meeting or what the reference to private clients meant. Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
Nassif, who fled Australia for Lebanon in 2022, has withdrawn from an expected appearance via video link on Friday after providing Icac with a medical certificate. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

That means thinner laptop designs and quieter operation, and the space savings allow for larger batteries. According to Lenovo, it could reimagine how future high-performance laptops are designed.
Under Pressure
Lenovo is the first computer manufacturer to unveil a laptop that uses Frore’s AirJet Mini fanless air-cooling technology. Frore is known for its liquid-cooling tech that’s used in data centers, but the AirJet is designed for consumer computers.
Dubbed the Lenovo Active Flow Thermal Solution, the AirJet module pulls ambient air that’s inside the laptop to create 2,000 Pascals of back pressure (around 124 miles per hour). This high-speed air is then spread onto a copper base layer through tiny jets in the AirJet module, which Frore claims will disrupt the boundary layer that causes heat buildup and throttling. Without a boundary layer, the processor’s heat is dissipated out the back. Lenovo had a motherboard sample from the AeroBlade concept laptop that showed four embedded AirJet modules, located along the top of the laptop.
Frore says each AirJet module can create 10 times the back pressure of a regular laptop fan and can pull and expel air without needing many vents. Lenovo claims the Active Flow Thermal Solution uses the same power as a traditional fan, but it’s debris- and water-resistant.
While Lenovo may be the first to demo a laptop using AirJet, it’s not an exclusive partnership, so we could see other laptop makers employ it.
So Light, It’s Dreamy
With its typical, unassuming laptop design, nothing about the AeroBlade Concept screams that it’s a concept. But at 10 mm thin and weighing 1.8 pounds, you can’t help but think there’s something special. With a magnesium-aluminum body, it’s so lightweight that it makes some of the current lightest laptops, like the Asus Zenbook A14 or MacBook Air, feel downright heavy. I spent longer than I should have just lifting it up and down, and marveling at its portability.
I expected Lenovo to show a non-functioning sample or one I couldn’t touch, but what I demoed felt like a production unit. Indeed, Lenovo told me it’s a “very mature and refined product in terms of sample stability.” The laptop has an OLED screen and USB-C ports that support Thunderbolt 4.
The engineering sample uses an Intel Lunar Lake processor, which suggests the cooling tech can support higher-performance CPUs, though with support for up to 20 watts of thermal design power (TDP), it may not suit really demanding machines (there is a more powerful version of the AirJet, called the AirJet Pro). We won’t fully know how effective this design will be until it’s in the real world. If it goes into production, Lenovo says that class of chipset won’t necessarily be what’s inside, or whether the AirJet tech will end up in a future variant of the company’s existing laptops and mini PCs.
Lenovo didn’t reveal any details like battery life, pricing, or availability. Still, the product feels so finished that I can’t help imagining an imminent release, especially since some of Lenovo’s concepts have made it into production.
Alongside Project AeroBlade, Lenovo’s wackier concept of the year is Project Swan. Like its rollable gaming laptop that debuted at CES 2026, Project Swan expands horizontally from 14 to 17 inches with the push of a button. The company says it took what it learned from previous projects and refined it. While Lenovo mentions it's suitable for travel in its press release, at 3.5 pounds, it's noticeably heavy. That means this model has fewer motors, but they’re more durable. While still very much a “watch this space” product, it’s an exciting showcase of how a compact laptop could provide the visual real estate of a larger machine.

Film Heritage Foundation’s 4K restoration of Kamal Amrohi’s 1972 classic Pakeezah, starring Meena Kumari, is set to receive its global premiere at France’s Festival Lumière in Lyon, followed by a gala screening at the BFI London Film Festival. The restoration marks a significant step in preserving one of Indian cinema’s most celebrated films.
Pakeezah 4K Restoration to premiere at Festival Lumière and BFI London Film Festival; Meena Kumari classic gets new lease of life
The restoration has been undertaken by Film Heritage Foundation (FHF) in association with the Amrohi family. The screening at the BFI IMAX in London will be presented by FHF director Shivendra Singh Dungarpur along with Kamal Amrohi’s children Tajdar and Rukhsaar Amrohi and grandson Bilal Amrohi.
The restoration took two years and presented several technical challenges, as the original camera negative was found to be almost melted and unusable. FHF subsequently worked with an interpositive, a CinemaScope print and a colour reversal internegative preserved by the NFDC-National Film Archive of India. Original film stills and memories shared by Tajdar and Rukhsaar Amrohi were also used to help recreate the colour palette and visual consistency of the film.
Speaking about the restoration, Shivendra Singh Dungarpur said, “Restoring Pakeezah has been a long-held dream, and I am so grateful to Bilal Amrohi for being the moving spirit and encouraging the family to support the restoration and bring the film back to life. Pakeezah is a film that has been etched in my memory since I was a child when I watched it for the first time with my grandmother in a darkened cinema in Dumraon, Bihar. The restoration of Pakeezah took two years. It has been one of the most exciting yet one of the most challenging restorations I have worked on. When I went to inspect the original camera negative and saw that it had almost melted, my heart sank. And the other film elements we had to work with were not in good condition with faded colours, scratches and mould. In my mind’s eye, I could see each frame like a painting saturated with colours, the opulent sets and the luminous beauty of Meena Kumari and the songs of Ghulam Mohammed were ringing in my ears as if it was yesterday, but not a single cast or crew member survived from the film and I wondered how I would be able to restore Kamal Amrohi’s original vision with what I had to work with. During our research we discovered original film stills which helped a great deal and I also consulted Tajdar and Rukhsaar Amrohi who had visited the sets and had vivid memories from the making of the film. I couldn’t have asked for a better showcase for the restored Pakeezah than the Festival Lumiere in Lyon, the birthplace of cinema followed by a gala screening at the London Film Festival.”
Tajdar Amrohi recalled his association with the film and his father’s dedication to the project. He said, “I was at the grand premiere of Pakeezah in 1972 with my father and Choti Ammi (Meena Kumari) and the film cans arrived at Maratha Mandir in a palanquin. I never imagined that I would be presenting the restored film with my family at the gala premiere in London fifty-four years later. I would like to thank Shivendra Singh Dungarpur and Film Heritage Foundation for restoring the film with so much passion and meticulous care and for bringing my father and his greatest work back to life so that new generations will see the unforgettable Meena Kumari and enjoy the beauty of the film. I remember when I was a child, my father was deep into the making of Pakeezah. Everything in our lives revolved around Pakeezah. My father had put in everything he had in the film and whenever we asked him for anything as children, his response would always be, “After Pakeezah.” Pakeezah was his life’s mission. I have so many memories of the film as I would regularly visit the sets on Floor No. 3 at Filmistan where much of the film was shot. The film has influenced generations of filmmakers and even today I am sometimes asked how he achieved some of the shots.”
Rukhsaar Amrohi also reflected on her father’s connection with the film and Meena Kumari. She said, “Pakeezah was my father’s obsession, his dream, his oxygen that gave meaning to his life. No one else could have played the role of Pakeezah, but Choti Ammi (Meena Kumari). She was Pakeezah. My father nurtured the film for over fifteen years like a child till it was fully matured and ready to be presented to the world. As a thirteen-year-old, I witnessed the countless sacrifices my father made and the relentless dedication and perfectionism in the face of almost insurmountable challenges to make his vision a reality. I have preserved every bit of his legacy that remains in Amroha, but for years, I felt that my father’s legacy as a great master of cinema had been forgotten. I would like to thank Shivendra Singh Dungarpur for taking the initiative to restore Pakeezah with so much love and care. I only wish my father were alive to see his creation restored and reborn for the world to see fifty-four years after it was released. I cannot wait to see the restored film back on the big screen and I will be travelling to London to present the film.”
Pakeezah, which was released on February 4, 1972, underwent a production journey spanning nearly 15 years. Originally conceived in the 1950s, the film began shooting in black-and-white before moving to Eastmancolor. The production was interrupted several times, including after Amrohi and Meena Kumari separated, before being revived in 1969.
The film went on to become one of the defining works of Indian cinema, with Meena Kumari’s performance as Sahibjaan becoming central to its enduring legacy. She passed away on March 31, 1972, just weeks after the film’s release.
The restored version of Pakeezah is presented in 4K with a 5.1 sound mix. The film runs for 153 minutes and features Meena Kumari alongside Ashok Kumar, Raaj Kumar and Nadira. The restoration was carried out by Film Heritage Foundation at L’Immagine Ritrovata laboratory in association with Bilal Amrohi of Lionheart Cinema.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet after an ice-and-rock avalanche triggered a surge of water and debris through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems. The disaster destroyed homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure. As of 03 September, at least 1,200 people have died, while over 4,000 remain missing and hundreds have been injured. Search and rescue operations continue across the worst-affected areas (here, here, and here).
Amid this, several videos are being shared on social media, claiming to show people being rescued from debris following the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The videos show people being rescued from debris following the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal.
Fact: None of these visuals are related to the August 2026 Nepal floods. They were recorded during different incidents in different locations. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
This video, showing a man trapped under mud and debris while several people attempt to pull him out, is being shared as a scene from the 2026 Nepal floods.
Our investigation found (here, here, and here) that the video shows a rescue operation following an accident at Adarsh Cold Storage in Phaphamau, Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh, on 23 March 2026. An ammonia gas chamber exploded, causing part of the facility to collapse and trapping workers under the debris. Rescue teams pulled 18 people from the rubble, while four people died and several others were injured.
Video 2
This video, showing a group of people on a concrete structure trying to prevent a man from being swept away by strong water currents, is being shared as a scene from the 2026 Nepal floods. News18 Rajasthan also shared it, claiming that it shows a rescue operation in Nepal.
Our investigation found (here, here, and here) that the video shows a motorcyclist being swept away by strong currents in the Los Pirules area of Valle de Santiago, Mexico. Locals rescued him from the water.
Video 3
This video, showing rescue workers pulling a woman trapped under debris to safety, is being shared as a scene from the 2026 Nepal floods.
Our investigation found (here, here, and here) that the video is from Venezuela, where a woman was rescued alive from the rubble of a collapsed house following earthquakes.
To sum up, these videos do not show rescue operations in Nepal after the flash floods.

In a bid to tackle alleged voter fraud, Immigration and Customs Enforcement is preparing to award a contract worth up to $5 million to a company that will create a massive national database of voters.
ICE first detailed what the contract would entail in a document published last week. “The purpose of this acquisition is for the handling and secure delivery of publicly available voter registration files and voter history files to support Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) fraud detection and data segmentation activities,” the document reads.
In the document, ICE says that the agency will initially provide a list of specific states it wants to acquire public voter registration files from, though the successful contractor will need to have the capability to obtain data from all 50 states. ICE is also seeking voting history data “for each federal election specified by the government, including general, primary, runoff, and special federal elections.” ICE is seeking publicly available information from each state, which each have their own rules around how it is obtained. This would include voter registration, and in many cases, voting history. Either could potentially include party affiliation—a move that experts believe will violate a right to privacy for US voters.
The document states that the successful contractor won’t be asked to collect and share party affiliation data fields for voters but that could change if “explicitly directed in writing by the contracting officer.” That contracting officer is listed as Michael Royer, section chief at Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative unit within ICE. ICE, DHS, and Royer did not respond to a request for comment.
On Monday, the agency published an acquisition forecast document that revealed the ICE contract would be worth between $2 million and $5 million. The final contract is expected to be published next Monday, and is likely to be awarded soon after, given that the term of the contract will expire on September 30.
ICE’s effort to create a national voter database is part of a much broader effort within the Department of Homeland Security and the Trump administration to undermine trust in the upcoming midterm elections. For more than a year, the Department of Justice has been seeking to create a national voter database by demanding states hand over unredacted voters rolls. States and courts, however, have pushed back.
DHS has already demanded states comply with its investigations. The agency has also said it would withhold emergency preparedness and counter terrorism funding from states who refused to implement White House policies on elections. And the agency has gone after voters directly, threatening to deport those suspected of voting illegally even when they have no criminal convictions. Despite assertions from DHS and the Trump administration, incidents of noncitizens voting are vanishingly rare, with an investigation in Georgia this week finding very few examples.
DHS also announced a new surge to investigate alleged voter fraud in certain states ahead of the midterms, to “pursue investigative leads, conduct field interviews, and support timely prosecutorial review,” according to internal DHS guidance that was first reported by CNN this week.
“It’s a joke,” Wisconsin governor Tony Evers said when asked about DHS’ plans. “I think it’s another thing that Trump is doing to make it look like there’s all sorts of problems that are not problems in Wisconsin. And frankly, he needs to stay out of it because voting is a state issue and not a federal issue.”
This is not the first time that ICE has issued a contract related to uncovering voter fraud. In July, 404 Media reported that ICE was set to pay Thomson Reuters $125 million for access to its CLEAR database, a platform that brings together names, addresses, property records, driver’s licenses, social media profiles, and voter registration records from both public and private sources.
And ICE has also sought a direct route to accessing voter files. In June, Axios reported that agents from ICE had obtained individual voter rolls from election officials in two counties in Texas and North Carolina.
Last year, WIRED reported that DOGE was building a master database using data from DHS as well as the Social Security Administration, the Internal Revenue Service, and voting data from Pennsylvania and Florida.
“They are trying to amass a huge amount of data,” a senior DHS official told WIRED at the time. “It has nothing to do with finding fraud or wasteful spending … They are already cross-referencing immigration with SSA and IRS as well as voter data.”

Nashik, Sep 03: Education is not a privilege, but the right of every student in India, and students from marginalised communities should not face neglect from the system, Congress MP Rahul Gandhi has said.
He met a delegation of tribal students, including those who were on a hunger strike to press for their demands, during his visit to Nashik in Maharashtra on Wednesday.
The students were protesting over a range of issues, including the condition of ashram schools meant for tribals.
Gandhi, in a post on X, later said, "Education is not a privilege -- it is the right of every student in India."
The Congress leader said during his Nashik visit, he met with a delegation of tribal students and carefully listened to their problems and demands.
Every student has the right to a respectful, safe, and conducive environment for their studies, the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha asserted.
"Students from marginalised communities should not face neglect from the system; they need its support and every possible assistance," he added.
During his Nashik visit, Gandhi interacted with district-level leaders of the Maharashtra Congress and asked them to stand firmly by the party's ideology and ensure justice for the people.

Brand sacks execs over ad showing woman pushed over
- Published
American golf brand Good Good has sacked two senior executives following backlash over an advert which showed a woman being pushed to the ground after reaching for a club.
The company, whose YouTube channel has 2.1m subscribers, said it had parted ways with chief executive Matt Kendrick and president Joe Flannery following the release last month of the advert created for golf club manufacturer Callaway.
Good Good vice-president of brand and marketing Jeffrey Lefkovits was sacked earlier this week.
Head of finance and operations at Good Good, Alex Puchala, said the dismissals on Wednesday were a "difficult day for the entire Good Good family".
Nahid Giga, a board member and investor in Good Good, has been installed as interim CEO.
The video drew widespread criticism and was accused of making light of violence against women.
Good Good and Callaway removed the advert and issued apologies.
Callaway ended its partnership with Good Good and said it was donating $1m (£736,000) to organisations working to prevent violence against women and support victims.
Good Good, whom Callaway has worked with since 2023, has stepped away from its sponsorship of a PGA Tour event in Austin, Texas, in November.
Good Good products have also been pulled from the shelves of several retailers.
The advert showed Good Good co-founder Garrett Clark rushing over to Alexis Miestowski - a professional golfer and regular content creator for Good Good - and pushing her to the ground before shouting: "Do not touch my new driver."
The brand, which has become one of the largest content creators in golf, launched its YouTube channel 2020. Regular clips include men and women competing in various golf challenges.
Good Good also creates made-for-TV shows as well as adverts for golf clothing and other merchandise.
Puchala said Good Good was "concouraged by the continued support" of its fans and said it is "focused on moving forward and building the next chapter of the company".

Suspect arrested after smashing 81 car windshields in Virginia parking lot
Most people who park in the lot reportedly work at the Virginia Commonwealth University Medical Center
An unhoused man has been arrested and charged with multiple counts of destruction of property after allegedly using a brick to smash the windshields and windows of dozens of vehicles in a Richmond, Virginia, parking lot.
Tyler Holtrust, 33, was charged with one felony and eight misdemeanor counts of destruction of property for allegedly damaging 81 vehicles Tuesday, the Richmond Police Department told The Independent Thursday. Earlier reports indicated the suspect may have damaged over 90 vehicles.
Holtrust could also face additional charges, authorities said.
Officers responded shortly after 11 a.m. Tuesday to East Grace and Ambler streets in Richmond’s Shockoe Bottom neighborhood, near Main Street Station, after receiving a report of a man damaging vehicles. Officers located Holtrust, who is reported to be homeless, and took him into custody without incident.
Witness Sydney Lee told WWBT that she watched the arrest unfold.
“I saw them putting him in cuffs and getting into the ambulance,” Sydney Lee said. “So I just pulled in and kept going down, and I hadn’t even noticed, but the second I parked, I noticed the car in front of me had their windshield out. And then all of a sudden you could just see the whole line, just everything gone.”
Most people who park in the lot work at the Virginia Commonwealth University Medical Center, according to WWBT. Investigators are working with VCU Police to identify the affected vehicle owners, who were notified of the investigation through flyers left on their cars, according to digital news platform Virginia Statewide Incidents LLC.
Laura Lee, a medical center employee who has parked in the lot for years, said she found her car’s windshield smashed Tuesday.
“It’s just a headache to have to deal with, but I’m just thankful that no one got hurt,” Lee told WWBT.
Meanwhile, frustrated drivers scrambled to find a way home after their windshields were smashed and questioned how so many vehicles could be vandalized without anyone intervening, the outlet reports.
“I wish that the surveillance here was a little bit better. I think 100 vehicles is kind of a lot to get vandalized without anyone catching it,” Lee said.
Drivers also criticized the lack of timely communication about the incident. Some VCU employees said they did not learn about the vandalism until several hours after it happened, while others said they were never notified at all, according to WWBT.
A VCU spokesperson told The Independent Thursday that Parking and Transportation notified A Lot subscribers about an hour after VCU Police were alerted to the vandalism. The department later sent a second message to those affected with additional guidance and offered private bus and rideshare transportation to affected VCU and VCU Health employees.
“VCU Police and VCU Parking & Transportation are actively reviewing security measures in all of our parking decks and lots. During that review, VCU Police are increasing high-visibility patrols in A Lot,” the spokesperson said.
A GoFundMe has been set up to help victims replace their smashed windshields, some of whom said their insurance will not fully cover the damage, WWBT reports.
Anyone who believes their vehicle was damaged in the area is asked to contact Richmond police officer S. McNeil at 804-646-3602 or Crime Stoppers at 804-780-1000.

From 2021 to 2023, more than 105,000 people in the U.S. died from a drug overdose each year — tens of thousands more than the already high rates seen in the lead-up to the Covid pandemic. Then, suddenly, the death rates dropped.
In 2024, U.S. overdose deaths decreased 27%. Preliminary data from 2025 show another meaningful drop, though overdose mortality is still quite high. Other countries with major overdose problems also saw fewer deaths: In Scotland, there was a 13% decrease in 2024, and in Canada, 9%.
“It is unprecedented to see overdose deaths come down so dramatically, so quickly,” said Brandon Marshall, an epidemiologist at Brown University who studies overdose trends. Still, “we’re nowhere near out of this crisis.”
It’s unclear what caused the decline. State health authorities who have been fighting the opioid crisis for decades are still surprised by the drop, said Evan Gumas, a senior research associate at the Commonwealth Fund.
He wrote a report, published Thursday, on the potential factors contributing to the change. Gumas spoke with public health and addiction authorities from at least two dozen U.S. states and other countries about what they were doing to combat the overdose crisis.
“The thing that every single one said … was there is no one thing that led to the decrease,” Gumas said. People he spoke to repeatedly mentioned a handful of initiatives: naloxone distribution and harm reduction responses, expanded access to medications for opioid use disorder, better treatment in and around prisons, and enhanced data infrastructure.
The progress is encouraging, but experts worry about the future: Medicaid cuts loom, and the Trump administration, while generally supportive of medications to treat opioid use disorder, has positioned itself against some proven harm reduction measures.
Behind the numbers
One factor behind the decline in overdose deaths may be wider availability of the opioid overdose reversal drug naloxone.
In 2022 the federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration required states receiving opioid response funding to develop a “naloxone saturation” plan to ensure wide availability of the drug.
From 2023 to 2024, Virginia saw a 40% decrease in overdose deaths after implementing such a plan. Maryland more than doubled its naloxone distribution between 2021 and 2025, including via vending machines, emergency medical services, and programs in which public safety personnel provide the drug to people at the scene of an overdose. The state saw a 25% decrease in overdose deaths from 2019 to 2024, per the report.
“Every single overdose death is really a failure, because no one should die from an opioid-related overdose when we have an antidote,” said Sarah Wakeman, an addiction medicine physician who directs the Mass General Hospital Substance Use Disorder Initiative in Boston and did not contribute to the report.
For people in recovery, medications for opioid use disorder like methadone and buprenorphine are still drastically underutilized in the U.S., but access is improving. That may have contributed to the decline in deaths as well.
Medicaid expansion “is the single most influential lever for coverage and access to medication for opioid use disorders,” Gumas wrote in the report. In Colorado, the number of methadone clinics more than doubled, from 25 to 54 in five years. New York saw similar growth. Meanwhile, health authorities in Sweden told Gumas that a decade of concentrated expansion of access to these medications contributed to about a 25% reduction in deaths since 2017.
Jurisdictions that Gumas communicated with also frequently mentioned increased access to medication for incarcerated people as an important way to reduce overdose deaths. Substance use disorders are 12 times more common in the prison system than in the general population, and the weeks immediately after a person’s release are especially risky. In New York prisons and jails, the use of medications for opioid use disorder increased seven times over between 2022 and 2025.
There are some more sobering contributing factors as well, per Wakeman. “So many people died during the years of really accelerating death rates that actually, there’s not as large of a population at risk of dying,” she said.
Additionally, the drug supply is always changing, with the potency of fentanyl declining in recent years. These shifts are difficult to track, but state surveillance systems can provide insight, Gumas wrote.
Overdose deaths decreased in every U.S. state in 2024, except for South Dakota, which had three more deaths than the year before. Still, there was a wide and largely unexplainable range of geographical variety.
“We need a lot more research rapidly to tease apart what is going on in terms of driving the variation,” said Marshall, who reviewed the Commonwealth Fund report and provided feedback before publication. “Right now the dominant hypothesis is that it’s mostly a function of the drug supply.”
Emerging contaminants in the drug supply, including “tranqs” like xylazine and medetomidine, are still dangerous, but may not have the immediate risk of fatality that fentanyl does.
Looking ahead
While there’s hope that the number of overdose deaths will continue to decrease, it’s not necessarily expected. Provisional data for 2025 show that in Scotland, which has the second-highest overdose death rate in the world after the U.S., rates may have crept back up.
In the U.S., many experts are worried that the progress states have made is at risk under the Trump administration.
“They claim this as a priority for the administration, but then their actions — particularly funding decisions — risk and compromise much of the progress we have made so far,” Marshall said.
SAMHSA, the federal mental health and addiction agency, was decimated in the first year of this Trump administration. More than half of the agency’s staff was cut, and roughly $1.7 billion in block grant funding was canceled, while another $350 million in addiction and overdose prevention funding was also cut.
Earlier this year, an open letter from agency leadership warned against using federal funds to buy harm reduction supplies like sterile syringes and pipes, or to distribute test strips for common drug supply contaminants. Many states are still trying to figure out how to handle that directive, Gumas said.
Experts agreed that the biggest threat to progress on overdose deaths is the looming Medicaid cuts. Researchers at Penn’s Leonard Davis Institute of Health Economics and Boston University estimated last year that the cuts would cause 156,000 people to lose access to opioid treatment, then lead the overdose rate to double among that group.
“These cuts are going to be pretty catastrophic in a lot of cases,” Gumas said.

  Russia has begun importing fuel, its government has confirmed, as a shipload of gasoline arrived from India. A fuel exporter in peacetime, Russia has been forced to turn to imports after Ukrainian strikes on its refineries and depots in response to the Russian invasion. The campaign by Kyiv’s military has been a major success, causing fuel shortages across Russia and in illegally occupied Crimea. At least one cargo of gasoline from India has just entered Russia’s domestic market, three industry sources told Reuters and shipping data showed. Russia is also arranging rail imports of gasoline from Belarus and Kazakhstan, and has placed a ban on fuel exports. Reuters reported last week that Russia had also begun shipping in diesel from Asia.

The tanker unloaded at Russia’s Arctic port of Vitino in early August, shipping data showed. India has been one of the keenest customers of Russian oil held at low prices by war sanctions.

Ranking the most game-changing transfers in Premier League history
- Published
The 'here we go' is on hold, the 'bombas' are done and dusted and the window panes are reverberating after being forcefully closed on Tuesday night.
Now comes the moment for new arrivals to make their mark on the pitch rather than the balance sheet.
Throughout the Premier League era there have been hordes of transfer hits and misses, but today we're looking at those signings who proved game-changing for their club and the competition, the ones who really moved the needle.
I've ranked my top 10 below. You can have your say in the comments.
You could make an argument for plenty of players who were left off this list. Thierry Henry is probably the one quibbled over the most, Arsene Wenger turning him from misfiring winger to one of the generation's greatest forwards.
But Arsenal had been champions 12 months before he arrived, and it took until Henry's third season for the Gunners to reclaim that crown.
You could point to Cristiano Ronaldo, who won a Ballon d'Or at Manchester United, or Wayne Rooney, who became the club's record goalscorer.
But a teenage Ronaldo took time to bed in, while Rooney, despite a debut hat-trick in Europe, had to wait until his third season for a Premier League winners' medal.
Then there's a plethora of Manchester City signings. Erling Haaland announced himself with 36 goals in 35 top-flight games but arrived in the middle of City's four-year title-winning streak. Yaya Toure, Kevin de Bruyne and Rodri all had big impacts.
However, the list can only be 10 names long. So here it is...
10. Petr Cech - Rennes to Chelsea, £7m, July 2004
Austrian goalkeeper Jurgen Macho was one of first faces through the door as the Roman Abramovich era began at Chelsea, arriving on a free transfer from Sunderland, only to tear his cruciate ligament and never play for the club.
A keeper signed the following summer would prove far more influential at Stamford Bridge.
While prising Claude Makelele from Real Madrid's Galacticos was a huge statement - likewise Hernan Crespo from Inter Milan - Petr Cech was the wall on which back-to-back titles were built.
Cech conceded only 15 goals in his debut league campaign, going on a run of 1,025 minutes without being beaten and ending the season with a record 24 clean sheets.
His Chelsea career spanned 11 seasons and included four Premier League titles and a Champions League. The Blues made back the £7m they paid - and then some.
9. Alan Shearer - Southampton to Blackburn, £3.6m, July 1992
Blackburn Rovers, fresh off a sixth-placed finish in Division Two, immediately set out their intentions after promotion via the play-offs guaranteed them a spot in the inaugural Premier League season.
Southampton striker Alan Shearer had interest from Manchester United, but Rovers - bankrolled by local businessman Jack Walker - tabled a British record £3.6m for the 21-year-old and enjoyed an almost immediate return.
Shearer scored 16 times in his first 21 Premier League games before injury, helping Blackburn finish fourth in their first top-flight season for 27 years. He bagged 31 as they finished runners-up the following term, and 34 in 1994-95 as Rovers were crowned champions for the first time since 1914.
Chris Sutton, another British record buy at £5m from Norwich City, may argue he was the signing who got Blackburn over the line, forming a formidable 'SAS' frontline, but it was Shearer's arrival that set the ball rolling.
8. Carlos Tevez - Corinthians to West Ham, undisclosed, August 2006
West Ham fans frantically refreshing Ceefax on 31 August 2006 must have thought they'd landed on the jokes page when news broke of a double swoop for a pair of Argentina's top young stars.
It was a huge coup for the Hammers, pipping the world's best clubs to add 22-year-olds Carlos Tevez and Javier Mascherano to Alan Pardew's squad.
With West Ham struggling near the bottom of the league, Mascherano left for Liverpool on loan after Christmas. Tevez, meanwhile, would have a huge impact.
West Ham were bottom with 11 games to go - nine points adrift of Sheffield United - but won seven games and Tevez netted seven times, including the winner against Manchester United on the final day, to relegate the Blades.
Sheffield United claimed foul play over the third-party ownership of Tevez and Mascherano, and West Ham were eventually ordered to pay £20m in compensation, having initially been fined £5.5m rather than being docked points.
7. Robinho - Real Madrid to Manchester City, £32.5m, August 2008
It gets somewhat lost in the cloudy narrative of the past, but Robinho had a decent first season at Manchester City, scoring on his Premier League debut and netting 14 times in 31 top-flight games to finish as their top scorer.
Things went downhill from there, but Robinho's performance was less important than what his arrival meant for the future of English football. It was City laying down a marker.
On the day the club were bought by the Abu Dhabi United Group - it also happened to be transfer deadline day - they nabbed one of the world's most prominent players from under the noses of Chelsea for a British record fee.
City finished 10th that season. But 18 years and more than £3bn on transfers later, they have become the most dominant club in England, winning eight titles.
6. Virgil van Dijk, Southampton to Liverpool, £75m, January 2018
Mohamed Salah might feel hard done by here. After all, he did score 32 Premier League goals in his first season at Liverpool after arriving from Roma in 2017.
But that didn't immediately move the needle in terms of pushing Liverpool further up the league table - they finished fourth again and scored only six more goals as a team compared to the previous season.
Instead, it was the £75m signing of Virgil van Dijk in January 2018 - and arguably goalkeeper Alisson Becker that summer too - that really raised the bar for Jurgen Klopp's side, who lost only once the following season and conceded only 22 goals as they racked up 97 points.
Incredibly, Liverpool were beaten to the title by Manchester City, but they became European champions the following season and won a first league title in 30 years a year later.
5. Robin van Persie, Arsenal to Manchester United, £22.5m, August 2012
It was a sign of how the Manchester United and Arsenal rivalry had cooled.
Once the key protagonists in Premier League heavyweight contests, the Gunners would seemingly never contemplate allowing their top scorer to join United.
Yet on the back of a season in which he netted 30 goals to finish as the league's top scorer, Robin van Persie left Arsene Wenger's outfit to line up for Sir Alex Ferguson, who was scorned by Manchester City's emergence and desperate to return the title to Old Trafford.
Van Persie went on to score 26 times as United reclaimed the throne in Ferguson's final season - the club's 20th title - while Arsenal slipped to a distant fourth.
4. Sol Campbell, Tottenham to Arsenal, free transfer, July 2001
A handful of journalists gathered at Arsenal's London Colney training base expecting the unveiling of goalkeeper Richard Wright from Ipswich. Instead they were stunned to see former Tottenham skipper Sol Campbell walk in.
The England defender, who joined Spurs as a youngster more than a decade earlier, had lucrative offers from Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Inter Milan.
There was no inkling that he would end up down the road at Highbury instead, the deal sealed during clandestine meetings with Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger and vice-chairman David Dein.
"I have kept my head when other people around me were losing it," Campbell said at the unveiling of a transfer that was both seismic in the north London rivalry and the direction of the Premier League trophy.
He proved a phenomenal presence at the heart of Arsenal's defence, winning the league and FA Cup double that season and adding another Premier League crown as one of the 'Invincibles' two years later - a title clinched, of all places, at White Hart Lane.
3. N'Golo Kante, Caen to Leicester, £5.6m, August 2015
N'Golo Kante was playing in France's regional amateur leagues until his late teens. Only three years before he joined Leicester City in 2015, the tireless midfielder was turning out in his country's third tier.
The Foxes thought they'd found a bargain, but did not realise quite what an impact his arrival would have.
Kante became the beating heart of Claudio Ranieri's midfield as Leicester went on their astonishing title-winning run. While Jamie Vardy scored the goals and Riyad Mahrez brought the flair, it was the diminutive Frenchman's energy and ability to always be in the right place that set the tone.
Kante missed only one game and made more tackles and interceptions than anyone in the division on his way to becoming a Premier League champion, before Chelsea paid the Foxes almost five times what they nabbed him from Caen for a year earlier.
2. Sergio Aguero, Atletico Madrid to Manchester City, £35m, July 2011
Sergio Aguero set out on his debut as he meant to go on, scoring twice and setting up another in a 30-minute cameo off the bench against Swansea City.
Manchester City were without a top-flight title since 1968 when the Argentine arrived from Atletico Madrid.
Ten months later he had netted 23 goals in 34 Premier League games, including the one deep into stoppage time that crowned City champions.
City had spent lavishly on forwards previously but the prolific Aguero was a game-changer.
His goals shifted the power balance in Manchester and, after a decade in sky blue, he departed as the club's all-time record scorer with 260 goals to complement his five league titles.
1. Eric Cantona, Leeds United to Manchester United, £1.6m, November 1992
Where do you start with Eric Cantona? The maverick Frenchman arrived in England having won the title with Marseille, which was followed by a two-month ban for throwing a ball at a referee and a fallout with the hierarchy.
Advised to move to England, he rocked up at Leeds - via a trial at Sheffield Wednesday - in January 1991 and swiftly helped them clinch the First Division.
A few months into the new season, Cantona's relationship with manager Howard Wilkinson broke down.
Manchester United, languishing in mid-table by late November, without a league title in 26 years and having been dumped out of the Uefa Cup by Torpedo Moscow, came calling - after their bid for Wednesday striker David Hirst was rejected.
Cantona proved a revelation. He scored nine times in 23 games and was influential as United ended up winning the inaugural Premier League title by 10 points.
The forward would win four titles in five years at Old Trafford, including two league and cup doubles, laying the foundations for a generation of success before his shock retirement in 1997.

In the summer of 2026, a rumor spread that singer-songwriter Olivia Rodrigo had donated $10 million to abortion organizations after U.S. President Donald Trump cut funding for reproductive healthcare.
The claim appeared on Facebook and X. One X post said that based on the alleged amount Rodrigo donated and the supposed cost of an abortion of $580, she was "responsible for the murder of 17,241 babies" (archived). (It's worth noting that, according to Planned Parenthood, the actual average cost of all types of abortion is higher than the post claimed.)
The claim spread following a music festival Rodrigo hosted on Aug. 29, 2026. It's true that the festival, which had an all-women lineup, brought in $10 million in proceeds that Rodrigo said would be donated to several organizations, one of which was Planned Parenthood, which provides reproductive healthcare, including abortions. Other beneficiaries did not directly provide reproductive healthcare, but advocated for it and defended it in courts.
However, the list also included organizations not involved with abortion or reproductive healthcare. In addition, philanthropist Melinda French Gates pledged to match the $10 million Rodrigo raised with the festival, bringing the total amount for donations to $20 million. For this reason, we rated this claim a mixture of true and false information.
The Daisy Chain Fields festival
The singer first announced the Daisy Chain Fields festival on June 22, 2026, in an Instagram post that listed an all-women group of performers, including Generation Z favorites such as Rodrigo herself, Chappell Roan, Eli and Katseye, as well as older acts such as Sarah McLachlan, alternative rock band The Breeders, which started in 1989, and 78-year-old singer-songwriter Stevie Nicks.
"Daisy Chain Fields features an all-women lineup and 100 percent of the net proceeds will go to charities dedicated to advancing and advocating for women and girls," Rodrigo's Instagram post read (archived):
The Daisy Chain Fields festival website listed organizations that would benefit from the proceeds of the event. Planned Parenthood, known for providing reproductive healthcare including birth control, screenings and care for sexually transmitted infections, prenatal care or abortions, was one of them.
The Center for Reproductive Rights, also listed, does not offer healthcare. Instead, its mission is to defend reproductive rights in courts across the U.S. Meanwhile, the National Institute for Reproductive Rights is an advocacy group dedicated to creating access to reproductive healthcare at city and state level.
But among the organizations set to benefit, some had nothing to do with reproductive healthcare or reproductive justice. These included Baby2Baby, a charity that provides essential items to very children living in poverty — it is known, in particular, for distributing diapers, formula and clothing, but also school supplies, backpacks and hygiene items.
Another organization poised to receive a donation from the festival was FreeFrom, which helps survivors of gender-based violence build financial independence.
The Domestic Workers Alliance, meanwhile, defends the rights of domestic workers.
In other words, only a portion of the proceeds was destined to fund reproductive healthcare, including abortion.
French Gates gets involved
The festival took place on Aug. 29, as scheduled. Near the end of the evening, Rodrigo called French Gates to the stage, announcing that the billionaire philanthropist had matched the amount set for donation, bringing the total to $20 million (archived):
French Gates confirmed this through her social media accounts. The same day, she posted a photo of herself with Rodrigo, saying she would donate the money through her organization, Pivotal (archived):

Arunachal Pradesh – A Living Treasure of Biodiversity
Arunachal Pradesh is one of India’s most biologically diverse states, where forests, rivers, wetlands, mountains and communities are part of one interconnected ecological landscape. Its extraordinary range of habitats supports thousands of plant and animal species, including several rare, endemic and threatened species.
The State’s biodiversity is shaped by its remarkable variation in altitude and climate. From tropical forests in the foothills to temperate forests, alpine meadows and high-altitude ecosystems, Arunachal Pradesh offers a continuous range of habitats within a relatively compact geographical area.
With more than 80 per cent of its geographical area under forest cover, the State plays an important role in maintaining the ecological balance of the Eastern Himalayas. It is also part of the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, one of the world’s globally recognised regions of exceptional biological richness and conservation importance.
A Landscape of Remarkable Ecological Diversity
The geographical diversity of Arunachal Pradesh is reflected in its forests. Depending on altitude and climatic conditions, the State has tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, moist deciduous forests, subtropical broad-leaved forests, pine forests, temperate forests, coniferous forests, sub-alpine vegetation and alpine meadows.
This remarkable transition from the warm foothills to the high Himalayas creates habitats for species with very different ecological requirements.
The State is home to more than 5,000 species of flowering plants, around 600 species of orchids, about 75 species of rhododendrons, 45 species of bamboo, 17 species of cane and hundreds of medicinal plants. Arunachal Pradesh is particularly renowned for its orchid and rhododendron diversity.
The forests also support a remarkable variety of mammals, including the tiger, leopard, clouded leopard, snow leopard, golden cat, marbled cat, Asiatic elephant, red panda, takin, hoolock gibbon and several other rare and threatened species.
A Paradise for Birds
Arunachal Pradesh is equally celebrated for its avian diversity. Its forests and mountain ecosystems provide habitats for hundreds of bird species, making the State one of the most important birding regions in India.
The Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary in West Kameng is one of the best examples of this extraordinary richness. Located within the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, Eaglenest is home to a wide variety of hornbills, pheasants, kingfishers and other birds. The sanctuary is also known for the discovery of the Bugun liocichla, a bird named after the Bugun community that lives in the region.
Protecting Arunachal’s Wildlife
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is protected through an extensive network of national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, tiger reserves and other conservation landscapes.
The state is home to important protected areas such as Namdapha National Park and Tiger Reserve, Kamlang Tiger Reserve, Pakke Tiger Reserve, Mouling National Park, Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary, Sessa Orchid Sanctuary, Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary and Mehao Wildlife Sanctuary, among others.
These landscapes support an exceptional range of wildlife, from high-altitude species such as the snow leopard and red panda to tropical forest species including the clouded leopard, hoolock gibbon and numerous birds, reptiles and amphibians.
Recent wildlife surveys have continued to expand scientific knowledge of these ecosystems. A 2024 WWF-India survey in Arunachal’s high-altitude rangelands recorded six wild cat species, including photographic evidence of the elusive Pallas’s cat, marking the first such photographic record from the state. The survey used 136 camera traps across 83 locations, covering approximately 2,000 sq km.
The Orchids of Arunachal Pradesh
Among the many botanical treasures of the State, orchids hold a special place.
Arunachal Pradesh has one of the richest orchid assemblages in India, with hundreds of species occurring across its varied habitats. The Sessa Orchid Sanctuary in West Kameng was established in 1979 to conserve and study orchids in their natural habitats. The sanctuary has recorded a remarkable diversity of orchid species, including epiphytic and terrestrial orchids.
The Orchid Research and Development Centre at Tipi further strengthens conservation and research efforts. Its facilities include orchid species houses, natural orchidaria, a herbarium, tissue culture laboratory, museum and hardening units. These initiatives support both ex-situ conservation and the rehabilitation of orchids in their natural habitats.
Glaw Lake: Arunachal Pradesh’s First Ramsar Site
A landmark development came in August 2026, when Glaw Lake, located within the Kamlang Tiger Reserve in Lohit district, was designated as India’s 101st Ramsar Site and became Arunachal Pradesh’s first Ramsar Site.
Situated at an elevation of around 1,168 metres, Glaw Lake covers approximately 82 hectares and forms part of the catchment of the Kamlang, Lang and Lati rivers, which flow into the Lohit River. The lake is recognised by the State Forest Department as an important repository of aquatic biodiversity.
Its Ramsar designation gives international recognition to the ecological importance of the wetland and strengthens the focus on its conservation and sustainable management. The recognition is also significant for Arunachal Pradesh’s wider efforts to protect wetlands and the ecosystems and communities that depend on them.
A State Where New Discoveries Continue
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity story is still being written.
Recent scientific discoveries demonstrate how much remains to be documented within the State’s forests and mountains. The rare plant Vaccinium piliferum, a relative of the wild blueberry that had not been documented for nearly 188 years, was rediscovered in Vijoynagar in Changlang district recently.
New orchid species have also been identified in different parts of the State, while researchers have recorded new cascade frog species from Arunachal Pradesh. In 2026, scientists also identified a new butterfly species, Euthalia zubeengargi, from Basar in Leparada district.
Such discoveries are a reminder that Arunachal Pradesh is not merely a repository of known species. Its forests and mountains continue to offer opportunities for scientific research and the discovery of life forms that may not yet be fully documented.
Biodiversity and Indigenous Knowledge
For generations, the indigenous communities of Arunachal Pradesh have lived closely with their natural surroundings. Forests provide food, medicinal plants, fibres, fuel and other resources, while traditional knowledge has helped communities understand seasonal changes, plants, wildlife and sustainable use of natural resources.
Today, this relationship is increasingly important to conservation.
A recent example comes from West Kameng, where indigenous communities are sustainably harvesting Zanthoxylum, locally known as Khagi, a wild Himalayan spice. The initiative has reportedly involved around 200 families while contributing to the protection of approximately 100 square kilometres of forest and generating livelihood opportunities.
Such efforts demonstrate that conservation and livelihoods can move together when local knowledge and sustainable practices are placed at the centre of biodiversity management.
Conservation: Protecting a Living Legacy
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is a natural asset of national and global importance. At the same time, ecosystems across the world are facing growing pressures from habitat loss, climate change, pollution, invasive species and unsustainable exploitation of natural resources.
Protecting Arunachal’s biodiversity therefore requires more than creating protected areas. It calls for habitat restoration, scientific research, responsible tourism, community participation, sustainable livelihoods and greater awareness among citizens.
The State’s protected areas, community conservation initiatives, biodiversity documentation programmes and institutions dedicated to research and conservation all contribute to this larger effort.
Looking Ahead
The story of Arunachal Pradesh is inseparable from its forests, rivers, mountains and wildlife. Its biodiversity sustains ecosystems, supports livelihoods, enriches traditional knowledge and strengthens the ecological security of the Eastern Himalayas.
From the orchids of Sessa to the forests of Namdapha, from the bird-rich landscapes of Eaglenest to the wetlands of Glaw Lake, every ecosystem adds another chapter to the State’s natural heritage.
The recent recognition of Glaw Lake as a Ramsar Site is an important milestone, but it is also a reminder of the responsibility that comes with being home to such extraordinary natural wealth.
Arunachal Pradesh is a living treasury of biodiversity and conserving it is not only about protecting nature today, but ensuring that its forests continue to breathe, its rivers continue to flow, and its remarkable species continue to thrive for generations.

Democrats demand Homeland Security officials fund election security ahead of midterms
Two Democrats tasked with overseeing federal elections are asking why the Trump administration hasn't distributed money to protect state and local elections as directed by Congress.
Sen. Alex Padilla of California and Rep. Joseph Morelle of New York authored a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and the acting head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Nick Anderson, to demand they restore over $39.6 million in funds to a range of specific election security efforts as legislated in the fiscal year 2026 DHS Appropriations bill passed in April. NPR was provided an exclusive copy of the letter.
"With the midterm elections occurring in two months, we write with grave concern that time is running out … to assist state and local election officials in protecting our elections from cyber and mis-and disinformation threats," the lawmakers wrote.
DHS and CISA did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment.
Padilla is the ranking member of the Senate Rules Committee and Morelle is the ranking member on the Committee on House Administration. The authors specifically pointed to gaps in funding for the Election Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center. The center had been a free, voluntary resource for state, local, tribal and territorial election office employees to receive the latest intelligence how bad actors are targeting election infrastructure. While hackers haven't managed to hack voting machines at scale, hack-and-leak and mis-and disinformation campaigns on social media have garnered widespread attention and influenced media coverage. After funding cuts in March 2025, the center was only able to provide limited services through a paid membership model, something "under-resourced communities" cannot afford, Padilla and Morelle wrote.
Major concern over foreign election meddling spiked during the 2016 presidential election when the U.S. intelligence community concluded that Russia was trying to interfere including by leaking damaging information about Hillary Clinton to sway American voters in favor of Donald Trump. However, the threat has only grown in complexity, as other foreign adversaries, including Iran, have ramped up efforts to undermine confidence in the American electoral system and advocate for their preferred candidates and policies.
The Trump administration has historically focused on election security as a political issue. President Trump has dedicated a significant chunk of federal resources to attempt to cast doubt on the intelligence community's 2016 assessments and prove his false claims of election fraud in 2020, most recently in July during a primetime speech about election vulnerabilities where he offered no new evidence the election won by President Joe Biden was somehow compromised.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration has slashed federal funding for election security programs and cut a range of federal jobs focused on the issue, including at DHS's CISA.
Padilla and Morelle cite "the removal of hundreds of CISA personnel and attempts by the Trump administration to slash the agency's budget" as a major concern, particularly as the midterm elections draw near.
Additionally, the lawmakers argue the need is particularly urgent, given ongoing conflicts the U.S. is embroiled in, the rapid increase in cyberattacks targeting American critical infrastructure, as well as rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models that are uncovering vulnerabilities in code faster than ever before.
"This is particularly disturbing at a time when our nation is at war with the Republic of Iran, which has reportedly engaged in sophisticated cybersecurity attacks, including on water infrastructure in the United States and nuclear energy facilities in the United Kingdom," they wrote. "Russia, China, and other foreign and non-state actors also have significant cyber and online election interference capabilities, which are likely increasing with advances in artificial intelligence."
The lawmakers conclude that the Trump administration is unlikely to "repair trust with election officials" before the November elections. However, they say federal officials have an obligation to distribute funds to the information sharing center and to support local election security advisory positions in regions across the country.
"The failure to restore this funding as directed by Congress is a disservice to the thousands of election jurisdictions across this country," they wrote.

Channel smuggling gangs resort to 'mega-dinghies' as crackdown limits small boat supply
- Published
A drop in small boats illegally reaching the UK is forcing people smuggling gangs to adopt new tactics, a BBC investigation has found.
And there are claims of more "mega-dinghies" being prepared, of the type seen arriving on UK shores in recent weeks.
The image of a 15-metre long small boat carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK drew condemnation from both newspapers and politicians.
Ministers were accused of "losing control" of illegal Channel crossings, and the French police again found themselves criticised for not intervening.
But evocative as the picture was, it also represented a new strategy by the increasingly frustrated people smugglers we encountered on France's northern shores - who attacked our crew with stones, and injured our cameraman.
They are running low on small boats, we have found. And once rival criminal groups are now having to work together by loading more migrants on fewer, larger vessels - just like the "mega dinghy".
The UK and France are announcing measures to increase the number of police officers on the French coast in order to try to stop the migrants.
The latest initiative comes as Andy Burnham prepares to host French President Emmanuel Macron at Downing Street for the first time since becoming prime minister.
- Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats 
  - Published13 hours ago
- Inside secret police warehouse as Germany targets small boats gangs 
  - Published18 August
- Hundreds of migrants enter UK after 10-day lull 
  - Published5 days ago
Gang members have told our sources that others are being prepared, to the concern of emergency teams on both sides of the Channel, because of the increased risk to more lives. On 4 August 170 people had to be rescued after theirs caught fire in the middle of the Channel.
With French officers claiming they are now intercepting two-thirds of small boats before they can reach the coast, that means fewer crossing opportunities. And for those hoping to make the journey, it means a higher price.
Today, the gangs are quoting up to €2,000 (£1,700) per person. It used to be around €1,300 just a year ago. Their passengers also have to now pay in cash, to ensure commitment.
During one early low tide on Gravelines beach, we saw the only small boat to launch that day, and it was not what we expected.
At 09:30, a dozen or so migrants emerged from the sand dunes. Their distinctive orange life jackets, purchased from a local sports shop, made them easy to identify.
A need for speed at this point would be a fair assumption, but this was not to be the case. There was no running. It was almost orderly. A refined process where instructions were obeyed.
As they waded into the calm shallows of the Channel, their "taxi boat" came into view. It is simply a small boat that has departed from further along the coastline to avoid detection. Only now, they are being forced to set off from even greater distances. This one had left from Belgium.
The reason for the group not rushing was because the boat was already in the water. French police argue they are prevented from intervening at this point over fears of people drowning. It is to the long frustration of the British authorities, who would like their neighbours to at least adopt a more "case-by-case" approach.
As they clutch their phones in plastic wrapping, the group patiently waits for what they hope will be a voyage to a better life in the UK. Some tell me they are from Afghanistan. They are eager to catch their ride. Those who make it on are visibly elated.
After the last passenger, a young boy, is almost thrown on board, it inches out to sea, but it is not leaving yet.
At 09:49, another group of migrants move into the water and wait to be collected. An hour later, the boat indeed does return, but to another gathering that has emerged on a different part of the beach. A few run the vast distance across the sand to try to secure a spot. Most manage to clamber on.
As police officers watch from the shore, the small boat goes on to make five collections like this over three hours. The boarding becomes more frantic as the window of opportunity shrinks.
By 12:11, the small boat, with 82 people on board, finally moves off into the busiest shipping lane in the world. It is dwarfed by the passenger ferries in the background.
Everyone successfully made it to the UK. Small boats typically radio for help once they are in British waters, as the coastguard is compelled to rescue them and take them to shore.
What they leave behind in Gravelines is a scene of dejection and exhaustion. A limp toddler is carried past me towards a police officer, who revives him with a light shake.
This all unfolds next to four or so men casting their fishing rods into the increasingly choppy waters. It is peak holiday season here. They and other dogwalkers barely glance at the crestfallen migrants wading back to the stand.
Before, the gangs would often launch boats in the dead of night, but with increased police patrols, charity workers tell us the gangs now see the middle of the day as a better opportunity, as it takes taxi boats longer to arrive and it allows them to better co-ordinate boarding.
"You feel guilty being there - going to the beach and having a good time, while these families are in such terrible situations," observes a woman with her young daughter. They had been playing with a bucket and spade.
"It's hard," she admits. "We regularly see people on the beach attempting the crossing. It feels like living in two parallel worlds that have nothing to do with each other; it's really strange."
The migrants remaining will wait for their next opportunity, as per their agreement with the gangs. But because of more robust policing that wait is now typically weeks, even months, rather than days.
They also need a favourable weather window: the wind needs to ideally be under 5 knots and waves need to be less than 0.8m for a small boat to have a chance of making it across.
To improve their chances of avoiding detection and to be closer to a taxi boat, charity workers tell us migrants are also sleeping closer to the beach in the woods or among the dunes, instead of at the larger camps where they can wash, or receive food, water and medication.
It is after arriving at the largest settlement at Loon-Plage, near Dunkirk, that we soon find ourselves in direct confrontation with the people smugglers.
As the intense heat bears down on a tent where people can charge their devices, we initially meet two young Egyptian men who are visibly tired and disheartened. They have been staying in squalid conditions for months and have made several unsuccessful attempts to cross.
"The police stopped us from leaving and destroyed the boats," explains one. He says he wants to go to the UK so he can work and obtain legal papers.
A young Sudanese woman and Afghan man also told us they had also tried to cross dozens of times. We have been to the camp on several occasions over the past year, but this time there was a perceptible unease.
Riot police had cleared out the tents in the same week, and the day before around 400 migrants preparing for a taxi boat in the nearby Hardelot forest were forced to return after several fires broke out.
It is evident the migrants and the gangs have been repeatedly frustrated, and the sight of our camera in one corner of the camp leads to us being attacked.
After agreeing to stop filming, one smuggler, around 5'8" tall (172cm) and in a new grey tracksuit, tries to grab our camera. He then repeatedly throws rocks at us from close range, striking our cameraman above the eye.
We're chased to the car and make it away. Pol would later receive a few stitches.
The UK has been quick to praise the French police for reducing crossing numbers to a six-year low. Officials also cite a deeper, more coordinated level of coordination between the two countries.
But changes in immigration policy, the movement of people and the weather means the broader picture is more complicated.
Thousands are still illegally entering the UK every month on small boats. The numbers remain significant. And motivations to make this journey still run deep in this stretch of northern France.
For the people smuggling gangs that still means money, and a need to evolve.
Additional reporting by Marianne Baisnée

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.
